articles.title: DOH to deploy over 24k health workers in 2027 to address manpower shortage
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) plans to deploy 24,381 health professionals nationwide in 2027 as the government works to address continuing shortages of healthcare workers, particularly in…

blocks.text: The Department of Health (DOH) plans to deploy 24,381 health professionals nationwide in 2027 as the government works to address continuing shortages of healthcare workers, particularly in underserved areas.
Health Secretary Edwin Mercado gave the figure during the Senate Finance Committee’s budget briefing on the DOH’s proposed 2027 budget on Friday.
Mercado said the deployment would include doctors, nurses, radiologic technologists, and medical technologists, among other health professionals.
“Our budget for next year is 24,381 health professionals ang ide-deploy natin. Various cadres lang po ’yan: nurses, doctors, radtech, medtech.”
(Our budget for next year is for the deployment of 24,381 health professionals. These are from various cadres, including nurses, doctors, radiologic technologists and medical technologists.)
'No municipality now without a doctor'

Mercado said the government had already addressed the previous gap in basic physician access, saying that there are now no municipalities without a doctor, including geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas.
“Actually po, wala nang bayang ngayon na walang doktor. So zero na po. Wala na pong ating mga bayan kahit po doon sa mga IDA areas.”
(Actually, there is now no municipality without a doctor. So it’s zero. There are no municipalities without doctors, including those in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas.)
Sen. Joel Villanueva had raised the issue of healthcare-worker distribution, recalling that several years ago, the DOH had reported 209 municipalities without a single doctor.
Villanueva asked whether the proposed budget would be enough to recruit, deploy, train and retain the healthcare workers needed to address the country’s shortage.
7 years to meet target ratios
Mercado said the country still faces a significant shortage of health professionals when compared with the DOH’s target ratios.
Based on an estimated population of 116.9 million, Mercado said the desired ratios are 14.3 physicians, 27.4 nurses, and 2.8 midwives per 10,000 population.
At the current rate of producing health professionals, he said it could take seven years to meet those ratios, taking into account population growth and attrition among healthcare workers.

“Sa current rate nga po ng ating production ng ating health manpower, ay aabutin po tayo ng pitong taon bago po natin ma-meet yung ganitong ratio. Taking into account the population increases din. Taking into account ding yung attrition…”
(At our current rate of producing health manpower, it would take us seven years to meet these ratios, taking into account population growth as well as attrition.)
DOH eyes task shifting

As a short-term measure, Mercado said the DOH is studying task shifting, or allowing lower-level health workers with appropriate training to perform certain tasks currently handled by higher-level professionals.
He said the approach could help address manpower gaps while the country waits for more doctors and other specialized health professionals to be trained.
Mercado said the DOH is coordinating with professional organizations and other agencies to determine which functions can be assigned to other cadres while maintaining appropriate referral systems.
For the longer term, he said the department wants to reduce attrition and provide healthcare workers with clearer career paths.
Senators flag shortage of specialists

Villanueva also raised the shortage of occupational therapists, physical therapists and speech therapists, saying many Filipino health professionals leave the country for better pay and opportunities.
Mercado said producing specialized professionals takes several years, making it difficult to immediately address the shortage.
He said the DOH is working on a system where initial screening and intervention can be performed at the primary-care level, with patients referred to specialists when necessary.
The department is also looking at practice-based accreditation to expand access to services without requiring every professional to establish a full facility.
Villanueva said the government also needs to make these professions more attractive to students by ensuring that graduates have places where they can practice.
Mercado said a planned expansion of PhilHealth benefits and higher professional fees could serve as a “market signal” that these professions offer viable career opportunities.
Deployment breakdown
Villanueva asked the DOH to submit a detailed breakdown of its 2027 deployment plan, including the number of workers to be hired and deployed to rural, underserved, and remote areas.
He also asked that the data be broken down by region and, if possible, by province, to allow lawmakers to assess whether healthcare workers are reaching areas with the greatest need. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Jury in Lindsay Clancy murder trial told to follow law 'whether you agree with it or not'
articles.summary: The deadlocked jury in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial has returned for a seventh day of deliberations on Friday after strict instructions from the judge to apply the rules of reasonable doubt.

image.caption: Judge William Sullivan looks over the courtroom during the Lindsay Clancy murder trial in Plymouth, Mass., on Sept. 3, 2026. On Friday, jurors began their 7th day of deliberations. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
The deadlocked jury in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial has returned for a seventh day of deliberations on Friday after strict instructions from the judge to apply the rules of reasonable doubt.
Dramatic scenes unfold on 7th day of deliberations over U.S. mom's fate
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

"You must follow the law as I give it to you whether you agree with it or not," Judge William Sullivan told jurors before they filed out of the courtroom in Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass.

This comes after a dramatic turn of events in court the day before revealed a single juror as the only holdout. In a note delivered to Sullivan, the jury's foreperson told the judge one juror among the 12 won't follow the court's instructions about reasonable doubt.

During Thursday's sidebar with legal teams and eventually Clancy herself, observers noted defence attorney Kevin Reddington became heated, slamming documents down on the desk and gesticulating as he spoke to the judge. During sidebars, no one in court can hear what is being discussed.
Proceedings once again became heated on Friday, before the jury was brought in, as the lawyers and Sullivan argued about how to handle Thursday's letter from the jury.

Prosecutors argued the jurors should be instructed to return to deliberations, while Reddington disagreed, arguing the juror in question "looked you in the eye, and lied" about following Sullivan's instructions.
Every defendant is entitled to have a juror who is "true to their oath," Reddington said.
Sullivan ultimately ruled that he will not do a further inquiry of the juror, saying he would remind them to follow the law "whether they like it not."
In an objection, Reddington requested that Sullivan be less "soft" in his instructions, adding that he didn't do it "forcefully" Thursday. And the exchange once again became heated.
"What do you want me to do?" Sullivan said, his voice rising. "I'm not an actor. I'm just giving the instruction."
To which Reddington suggested that Sullivan was "glossing over" the imperative to apply the law of reasonable doubt.
"I'll try to do this with more pizazz than I did yesterday," Sullivan added later.
Tempers rise on deadlocked Clancy jury as single holdout refuses to budge
Judge could declare mistrial

Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children in 2023 while her then-husband was running an errand. Over the past five weeks, jurors have heard that she strangled Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

Clancy's defence doesn't dispute the killings. But they argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.

items: Judge lectures Lindsay Clancy jury on reasonable doubt, tells them to keep deliberating
Lindsay Clancy supporter arrested outside court, and other dramatic moments from the murder trial

blocks.text: Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.

articles.title: Russian attack hits Ukraine's security service headquarters
articles.summary: For much of the war, Russian drone and missile attacks in Kyiv followed a particular rhythm. They almost always came at night. But not, they're taking place during the day and in Kyiv. A Russian…

image.caption: A firefighter works at the site of a warehouse hit by a Russian drone strike in the town of Brovary, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv region on Friday. The last week has been marked by Russia stepping up daytime attacks. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

For much of the war, Russian drone and missile attacks in Kyiv followed a particular rhythm. They almost always came at night. But not, they're taking place during the day and in Kyiv. A Russian drone attack on Friday targeted the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in central Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said.
Moscow making more daytime strikes with fast, jet-powered drones
A Russian drone attack on Friday targeted the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in central Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

"Unfortunately, a Russian drone struck the central building of the Security Service of Ukraine on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, across from St. Sophia Cathedral," he said on X after speaking with acting head of the service Oleksandr Poklad.
"The drone was aimed directly at the office of the head of the Security Service in that building."
Five people were injured in the attack, Kyiv's mayor added on the Telegram app. Heavy black smoke rose from the site.
The news comes as Russia changes its tactics in the war.

Russia has typically attacked Ukraine at night. But now, daytime strikes are becoming more frequent with Russia's use of fast-flying, jet-powered drones. Since last week, attacks have come day and night, compounding the terror of overnight strikes with the exhaustion of constant daytime disruption.
In Kyiv, the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life, and the relentless alerts are exhausting residents, some of whom are left wondering how long they can stay.
Intelligence warns Putin is preparing escalation in Ukraine

Getting the shopping done has become a nightmare for Volodymyr Bovsunovskyi, who recounts a recent family trip to a mall to buy clothes for his nearly four-year-old daughter. They had been inside for about 20 minutes when the alert sounded. They rushed out without buying clothes and saw smoke rising nearby.
"A lot has changed in the last seven days," he said. Like many residents, he hopes the attacks will relent. For now, Ukraine is struggling to find an effective way to counter them.
Carney's message to Putin: 'End this war'
Bovsunovskyi is now considering leaving the city for a while, hoping to give his family — including his pregnant wife — a chance to rest.

Ivan Datsiv, an IT worker, was in his apartment in Kyiv's Podil district when a Russian drone tore through the floor on Tuesday, charring the ceilings and walls of his apartment and completely destroying the one next door.

items: Russia is rattling NATO’s nerves, but how far will Moscow go?

blocks.text: Datsiv tries to joke about it, saying he had been meaning to repaint the walls anyway.
The alerts have become so frequent that he no longer sees the point of repeatedly going to a shelter. At this rate, he said, the only alternative would be to live in the basement.
"The alarms sound constantly," he said. "You don't even have time to go down and come back up. It's just a waste of time running back and forth."
He, too, is thinking of leaving Kyiv for "another city — somewhere quiet and without this danger."

articles.title: Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices
articles.summary:
Russian and Ukrainian strikes in July killed more crew than in whole war to that month, preventing grain exports

A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as…

blocks.text: A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher.

More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as the conflict has intensified, making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in the strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası.

Attacks on vessels continued into August and escalation in the Ukraine war has prompted the head of the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization, to condemn the “deterioration of maritime security around the globe”.

Russia first launched waves of attacks on port infrastructure and vessels anchored in Ukrainian Black Sea ports in the months after its invasion in 2022, preventing Kyiv from exporting grain. In July, Russia again struck Ukraine’s main grain export hubs of Odesa and Chornomorsk.

blocks.caption: Firefighters tackle a blaze on a civilian vessel hit during Russian missile strikes on Chornomorsk last December. Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/Reuters

blocks.text: However, the recent escalation in the Black Sea and neighbouring Sea of Azov – connected by the Kerch strait – has also resulted from Ukrainian retaliatory attacks. Drones have hit Russian vessels, including tankers Kyiv says belong to a shadow fleet of hundreds of ships used by Russia to evade sanctions on its oil exports. Ukraine has targeted ships and port buildings at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, vital for oil and grain exports.

In a grim illustration of the danger to vessels and their crew, an abandoned Russian-flagged cargo ship – with a burned-out command deck – recently ran aground on Turkey’s Black Sea coast as startled holidaymakers looked on.

The Omskiy-107’s crew abandoned ship after it was hit by a Ukrainian drone near Novorossiysk, leaving the unmanned vessel to drift hundreds of miles and end up close to the Bosphorus, the narrow strait straddled by Istanbul that is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.

blocks.caption: A damaged Liberian-flagged bulk carrier is escorted by a safety boat through the Bosphorus this week. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

blocks.text: Shipping in the region is under increased threat, according to analysts at the maritime risk intelligence firm Vanguard. “Merchant vessels are now more likely to be affected because of the ports they visit, their trading activity and the cargoes they carry. Attacks have also extended beyond ports and their immediate approaches, increasing the risk to vessels across a wider area of the Black Sea,” they said.

The precarious maritime situation has already significantly reduced Russian and Ukrainian grain exports, raising concerns the disruption will worsen the impact of other food price shocks and hurt countries reliant on imported wheat, barley and maize.
Russia is the world’s largest grain exporter, with its produce mostly going to the Middle East and north Africa, particularly Turkey and Egypt, while Ukraine is the fifth-largest.

In July, Russia suspended shipping in the Sea of Azov after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, before deciding to redirect some grain exports to alternative routes such as via the Caspian and Baltic seas and the Pacific. However, more than 70% of Russia’s seaborne grain exports are shipped from Black Sea ports, and a further 20% from the Sea of Azov, according to analysis from Oxford Economics.
“I have seen estimates that Russian grain exports were down to 40% of normal export capacity in August,” said Tatiana Orlova, the lead emerging markets economist at Oxford Economics.

blocks.caption: A satellite image shows damage to a grain conveyor, after a Ukrainian drone and missile attack on Novorossiysk last month. Photograph: Vantor/Reuters

blocks.text: Ukraine, which had a bumper and early grain harvest this year, has also found itself unable to export large volumes through its Black Sea ports. Kyiv exported only a third – about 1.4m tonnes – of the grain it could have exported, using sea, rail, river and road, according to recent comments from Ukraine’s food minister.
Global wheat prices have been trading higher in recent weeks, but remain below levels at the beginning of the Ukraine war in 2022.

However, analysts say the latest disruption to seaborne grain exports is likely to push prices higher and exacerbate other food supply shocks, including the Iran war and lower European grain yields after extreme summer heat and the rapidly developing El Niño weather system.
Global food prices are forecast by Oxford Economics to rise by nearly 12% this year and a further 4.8% in 2027.

Unlike in 2022, when many big food importing countries were caught napping by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, “a lot of countries have grain stocks, which should help, so there is better preparedness for this kind of shock”, said Orlova. “But it is pretty clear the food price is going to be affected.”

articles.title: Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv over weekend, reports say
articles.summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have led President Donald Trump's efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war - but talks have stalled.

blocks.text: US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war appear to be gathering pace.
The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials.
Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, but a gulf remains between the two warring sides.
Earlier on Friday, Zelensky said a Russian drone hit the office of Ukraine's security chief Oleksandr Poklad in Kyiv. Poklad appears to be unharmed.
In a post on social media, Zelensky said he had ordered Poklad, who head the SBU security service, to respond "adequately" to the attack.
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Russia multiple times, but the purported talks will be the first in Ukraine.
Zelensky said on Thursday that "tentative dates have been set" and the US envoys would be in Kyiv "in the coming days".
But Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksiy Honcharenko said the pair were expected in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday. He added that this would happen after their visit to Moscow on Saturday.
Russia's state news agency Tass said Witkoff and Kushner were "expected to arrive in Moscow and then to Kyiv... on 5-6 September", quoting a source.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later told reporters: "I wouldn't announce anything, but when these contacts take place, we will inform you."
Meanwhile, Putin told an international economic forum on Thursday that "there are chances" a peace deal could be reached.
"First of all, Moscow and Kyiv must agree between themselves," he said.
But he showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine.
Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly rejected Putin's terms saying they are tantamount to capitulation.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and currently controls about 20% of its territory.

articles.title: PhilHealth paid only 482 claims for developmental disability benefits since 2017
articles.summary: PhilHealth has paid only 482 claims under its benefit package for individuals with developmental disabilities since the program was introduced in 2017, with the insurer citing the limited number of…

blocks.text: PhilHealth has paid only 482 claims under its benefit package for individuals with developmental disabilities since the program was introduced in 2017, with the insurer citing the limited number of contracted facilities as a major reason for the low utilization.
On Friday, PhilHealth president and CEO Beverly Ho disclosed the figure during the Senate Finance Committee’s briefing on the Department of Health’s proposed 2027 budget.

Ho was responding to Sen. Joel Villanueva, who asked whether the National Health Insurance Program’s proposed funding would cover individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and other developmental disabilities.
“2017 pa lang may benefit package na po yung PhilHealth all. Unfortunately, in these many years, we only paid 482 claims on this.”
(Since 2017, PhilHealth has already had a benefit package for this. Unfortunately, over these years, we have only paid 482 claims.)
Ho said one reason for the low number of claims was that only five facilities were contracted to provide the covered services.
“And the reason for that being one, we only have five contracted facilities. So we know very stringent yung rules namin," she said.
(And one reason for that is that we only have five contracted facilities. We know that our rules are very stringent.)
PhilHealth to ease accreditation requirements
Ho said PhilHealth was preparing to change its accreditation rules to allow more facilities and professionals to participate in the program.
She said a policy to decouple accreditation standards was expected to be released by the end of the week, allowing more providers to participate.
PhilHealth was also looking at allowing occupational and physical therapists and other professionals to obtain practice-based accreditation rather than being limited to facility-based accreditation.
Ho added that many therapists operate in freestanding clinics, which may not meet the existing facility-based accreditation setup.
She said PhilHealth had already begun discussions with professional groups and expected these changes to be addressed before the end of the year.
Ho also said PhilHealth was working with developmental pediatricians to expand early screening for children with developmental concerns.
She noted that developmental pediatricians could not personally screen children in every school and community.

The Philippine Society for Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics had already piloted a training module for barangay health workers (BHWs) and daycare center workers to serve as the first level of screening, she said.
Training is also being prepared for primary care physicians and general pediatricians before patients are referred to developmental pediatricians.
Ho said the approach was necessary to ensure that specialists would receive patients who had already undergone initial screening.
Villanueva flags specialist shortage
Villanueva earlier asked the available DOH programs to increase the number of healthcare professionals and specialists serving individuals with ASD and other developmental disabilities.

He said there was a serious shortage of occupational therapists, physical therapists and speech therapists, with many Filipino healthcare professionals leaving the country for better pay and opportunities.
Villanueva said the shortage could discourage students from pursuing these courses if there were not enough facilities and opportunities for them to practice after graduation.

Acting Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said the DOH was looking at short-term measures, including task shifting and strengthening primary-level screening and referral systems, while recognizing that producing specialized professionals could take four to five years.
He added that the planned expansion of PhilHealth benefits and potentially higher professional fees could also encourage more professionals to enter these fields. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: SC: Drug search warrant can't be used to seize credit card hacking evidence
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a warrant authorizing the search for illegal drugs and drug paraphernalia cannot be used to obtain evidence of credit card hacking, absent an exception…

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 10:21pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a warrant authorizing the search for illegal drugs and drug paraphernalia cannot be used to obtain evidence of credit card hacking, absent an exception recognized by law.

In a decision, the SC Third Division acquitted an individual of violating the Access Devices Regulation Act of 1998, which prohibits the possession of counterfeit access devices, including fake credit cards.

“A violation of Republic Act No. 8484 is unrelated to drug offenses. Thus, the seizure of any evidence for such a violation would have to fall within any of the exceptions recognized by law, which is absent here,” it said.

The case stemmed from an operation against the individual after the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) received information that he was involved in illegal drug activities, computer hacking, and credit card hacking.
The NBI later applied for and obtained a search warrant for drug offenses.

During the warrant’s execution, agents seized several credit cards placed inside a bag, including two credit cards that were later confirmed to be fake because their numbers did not match the records of the original account holder.
According to the SC, only items described in a search warrant may be seized.
Items that are not described in a warrant cannot be seized unless justified by a recognized exception, the court said.
The SC said the plain view doctrine, which allows the seizure and presentation as evidence of objects that are in “plain view,” could not apply.
It said that because the credit cards were placed inside a non-transparent bag, their incriminating character, if at all, was not in plain view.

“Even after opening, and even assuming that the bag was open to begin with, a mere deck of credit cards is not, by itself, a contraband. Were it not for the tip they received beforehand, the law enforcement officers could not have perceived that the credit cards themselves were counterfeit,” it said.

The court also noted that authorities did not apply for a search warrant for access device fraud or related cybercrime activities despite being aware that the individual was engaged in such activities.

“Despite this, they did not act on the information regarding [his] hacking and credit card fraud activities by forwarding it to the proper division or applying for a search warrant covering possible violations of Republic Act No. 8484 or any cybercrime,” it said.
Meanwhile, the SC said the individual’s conviction could not be sustained following the exclusion of the credit cards as evidence.

“Thus, to successfully sustain a conviction for the possession and use of a counterfeit access device, the prosecution must present not only the access device but also any evidence that proves that the access device is counterfeit,” it said.
“With the exclusion in evidence of the two American Express credit cards, the prosecution utterly failed to present the very access device itself,” it added.
The decision was penned by Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao.
It was promulgated in February 2026 and made public in September 2026. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Part of Marilaque Highway closed due to landslide
articles.summary: A massive landslide blocked off a major highway connecting Metro Manila to Rizal, Laguna, and Quezon.

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 10:19pm
A massive landslide blocked off a major highway connecting Metro Manila to Rizal, Laguna, and Quezon.

In a 24 Oras report from Jonathan Andal on Friday, a portion of the Marilaque Highway in Baras, Rizal, has been closed for around 12 hours because of a landslide. Personnel from Meralco could also be seen at the scene attempting to fix an affected electrical post, which caused a barangay to lose electricity.
However, there were no recorded casualties in the landslide.
The displaced land spanned 50 meters in Rizal. Giant rocks and pieces of land scattered around the road, with a jeepney nearly getting toppled.
The landslide occurred after continuous rains caused by the Southwest Monsoon.
“Akala po namin may lindol, yun pala, pagtingin po namin doon, may umuusok doon, yung parang may fog. Yun pala, bumubulusok na yung mga bato saka lupa,” witness Shiela Peralta said.
(We thought there was an earthquake; it turned out, when we looked there, there was smoke, it seemed like fog. It turned out, the rock and ground were coming down.)

Johnnel Ferrero of the Baras Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office said that the water had saturated the ground, loosening the rocks. The trees, also being whipped around by the winds, could further contribute to the loosening of the ground.
Nearly four kilometers of the road was blocked off. Some motorists were stranded or forced to take longer, alternative routes. Some of them were vendors; others were students on the way home.
While vehicles could not pass, people could pass on foot through a cleared path on the side of the road.
Officials from the Department of Public Works and Highways and other pertinent authorities began clearing operations by noon. However, the area is still dangerous due to the continued rains.
By evening, one lane had been cleared enough for vehicles to pass. –Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
articles.summary: German Interior Minister Dobrindt said "technical discussions" were underway with countries outside the EU. He was meeting Danish, Greek, Austrian and Dutch counterparts to agree on the controversial…

image.caption: The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the 'return hubs'Image: Liselotte Sabroe/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP

blocks.text: Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year.
The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs."

"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday.
He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries.
What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?'
The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs."
Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities, two autocratically ruled countries.
"Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov.
Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027.
"We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement.

The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power.
In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges.
How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance
Are EU 'return hubs' legal?
The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law.
A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law.
EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory.
However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities.

Andreas Grünewald, a migration expert with the German evangelical charity Brot für die Welt (Bread for the World), questioned the feasibility of the plans, calling them "practically difficult to implement and highly problematic in terms of human rights."
He said ministers risked running into "political dead ends."
Rights organizations criticize EU 'return hubs'

The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups, including children's charities and church organizations, who have criticized the plans for what they see as the "criminalization of migration."

Marta Welander from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian aid, relief and development NGO, said the plans risk "normalizing detainment in prison-like facilities" and warned that deportees may face "persecution, torture or worse" in their destination countries.

Caritas, a Catholic charity operating in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Slovakia, said that migrants risked becoming trapped in a "legal grey area" if "arbitrarily and indefinitely detained" in the hubs.
Florian Westphal, CEO of Save The Children Germany, warned of the risks faced in particular by children and young people.
"The planned return centers in third countries are places of uncertainty and carry the risk of massive violations of children's rights," he said.

"Transferring children to states with which they have no connection, and where they face the risk of deprivation of liberty and are cut off from key figures in their lives, cannot be in their best interests. Children deserve unconditional protection, no matter where they come from or where they live."

articles.title: DOH eyes incentivizing child vaccination amid high wastage, stunting rates
articles.summary: Officials of the Department of Health (DOH) and its attached agency, the National Nutrition Council (NNC), said on Friday that they are looking into incentivizing the provision and uptake of…

blocks.text: Officials of the Department of Health (DOH) and its attached agency, the National Nutrition Council (NNC), said on Friday that they are looking into incentivizing the provision and uptake of vaccinations for children amid high vaccine wastage and stunting rates among children aged zero to five years old.

During the DOH budget deliberations, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian raised concerns over the high vaccine wastage rate in 2025, amounting to P590.3 million, which involved seven different types of vaccines intended for children to be classified as Fully Immunized Children (FIC).
Gatchalian also highlighted that according to EDCOM II data, only 65% of children achieved FIC status in 2025.

Health Secretary Edwin Mercado pointed out that every Filipino newborn automatically receives a PhilHealth ID upon undergoing newborn screening, and explained that they are looking into linking this system to YAKAP (Yaman ng Kalusugan Program), so that the child's chosen YAKAP clinic will have a care coordinator to monitor their vaccination schedule.
“Itatahi na rin natin na ma-register sa YAKAP para doon sa yakap clinic of choice nila, may care coordinator na babantayan kung nabakunahan, kung 'yung growth chart po ay nagagawa,” Mercado said.

(We will also integrate their registration into YAKAP so that at their chosen YAKAP clinic, a care coordinator will track whether the child has been vaccinated and if their growth chart is being maintained.)

“At kami po ay gumagawa ng care coordinator top-up para ma-incentivize ang mga YAKAP clinic na gawin ang monitoring at tiyakin na ‘yung mga bata ay nababakunahan. At kami naman po sa DOH ay mag-i-integrate sa PhilHealth para nga po ‘yung kanilang yakap clinics ay mababaan ng mga bakuna,” he added.

(We are also establishing a care coordinator top-up incentive so YAKAP clinics are motivated to conduct monitoring and ensure children receive their vaccines. On the DOH side, we will integrate with PhilHealth so that these YAKAP clinics receive a steady supply of vaccines.)
Mercado said that he plans to increase pediatric vaccination rates, keeping in mind the critical first 1,000 days of a child.
He added that the goal was to lower stunting rates early on so that schools will not have to catch up on nutritional supplementation later.
The DOH chief mentioned that their ultimate objective is to enroll 80% of the population in YAKAP by 2028.
Incentivizing families

During the budget deliberations, Gatchalian also raised the issue of malnutrition among children aged 0 to 59 months (under 5 years old), pointing out that in 2025, 25.3% of this age group, or around two million children, suffered from stunting or being short for their age.

“Ang delikado dito, this is 0 to 59 months… So in other words, 20% of our 0-5 [years old], bansot or stunted and pagpasok nila ng school, like I said, wala nang laban eh wala nang laban 'yung bata,” Gatchalian said.

(What makes this critical is that it affects children aged 0 to 59 months… In other words, 20% of our 0 to 5-year-olds are stunted, and by the time they start school, as I’ve said, the child is already at a disadvantage.)
He added that data showed wasting rates at 5.1% and underweight rates at 16.2%.
Gatchalian addressed these concerns to the NNC, which holds a P340 million allocation under the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program.
He specifically asked for the agency's proposal on how they plan to reach zero to five-year-olds and effectively address these health issues.

NNC Executive Director and DOH Undersecretary Albert Francis Domingo proposed linking vaccination to incentives such as food stamps, or utilizing dedicated Barangay Nutrition Scholars to conduct house-to-house visits.

This vaccination incentive structure is similar to the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps), which Domingo noted requires families to meet specific health metrics before cash grants are released.

“The idea is kailangan siyang i-link sa isang incentive na makukuha ng pamilya—maybe baka mga food stamps program or walang gutom program… na pwedeng ikabit ho para meron talagang malaking panghikayat don sa mga pamilya na bumisita sa mga health center,” Domingo said.

(The idea is to link it to an incentive that the family can receive—perhaps through the food stamp program or the Walang Gutom program… which can serve as a strong encouragement for families to visit health centers.)

“Or, another alternative, Mr. Chair, is we have around 42,000 to 45,000 barangay nutrition scholars na andiyan po dedicated… 'Yun po ay talagang nagbabahay-bahay sila… They can point to the exact bahay… kung nasaan ang mga malnourished na bata,” he added.

(Alternatively, Mr. Chair, we have around 42,000 to 45,000 dedicated Barangay Nutrition Scholars on the ground… They actively go house-to-house and can identify the exact households where malnourished children live.) –NB, GMA News

articles.title: DOH says UHC rollout delayed 2-3 years, cites health facility gaps
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) on Friday acknowledged that the implementation of the Universal Health Care (UHC) law had been delayed by two to three years, citing the COVID-19 pandemic and…

blocks.text: The Department of Health (DOH) on Friday acknowledged that the implementation of the Universal Health Care (UHC) Law had been delayed by two to three years, citing the COVID-19 pandemic and continuing gaps in the country’s health care infrastructure and services.

Health Secretary Edwin Mercado made the admission during the Senate Committee on Finance’s hearing on the DOH’s proposed 2027 budget, where Senator Panfilo Lacson questioned the department’s progress in implementing the UHC Law, which was passed in 2019.
Lacson noted that under the law’s original timeline, the Philippines was expected to reach the advanced stage of UHC implementation after six years, covering the period from 2020 to 2026.
“Medyo nung pong na-launch na, nagkaroon po ng hindi inaasahang COVID, kaya po medyo na-delay yung ating implementation na medyo na-push back ng two to even three years,” Mercado said.
(When it was launched, the unexpected COVID-19 pandemic occurred, so our implementation was delayed and pushed back by two to even three years.)
Universal coverage achieved, but services remain uneven
Mercado said the government had already achieved universal coverage in terms of enrollment, since Filipinos no longer needed to make individual contributions to be covered.
However, he said the country still needed to strengthen the capacity of the health system to actually provide the benefits covered by PhilHealth.

“Ang kaso po, yung supply side, yung nagbibigay ng mga benepisyo, ’yun pa po yung kailangan nating pagtutuunan, kasi hindi pa rin po equal yung presence ng mga accredited health facilities ng PhilHealth na magbigay, lalo na po yung mga matatataas na uri po ng sakit,” he said.

(The issue is on the supply side—the facilities providing the benefits—which we still need to focus on because PhilHealth-accredited health facilities are still unevenly distributed, particularly those capable of treating more serious illnesses.)

Mercado cited procedures such as open-heart surgery and organ transplants, which are covered by PhilHealth packages but may not be readily available in some areas because of a lack of capable facilities.
He also pointed to differences in the capacity of local government units to finance and manage their respective health systems.
DOH targets stronger local health financing
Mercado said the DOH was working to strengthen local health systems through a special health fund (SHF) that would allow local chief executives to better plan and allocate their health budgets.

He said the DOH’s goal was for local health units and local chief executives to have their own SHFs by 2028, alongside a proper financing analysis to determine how much funding would actually be needed to achieve UHC.
“Hindi pa po natin na-achieve. Hindi ko lang po mabibigyan yung actual percentage base po dun sa ating targets,” he said.
(We have not achieved it yet. I just cannot give the actual percentage based on our targets.)
Out-of-pocket spending down, but still above target
DOH data presented during the hearing showed that household out-of-pocket health spending fell to 41.2% of total health expenditure in 2025, from about 55% a decade earlier.
PhilHealth’s share, meanwhile, increased from 13.4% to 19.5% in 2025.

PhilHealth President and CEO Beverly Ho said the government’s share of total health expenditure had reached 46.5% in 2025, while the DOH was now working toward the Philippine Development Plan target of reducing out-of-pocket spending to 37% by 2028.

Lacson, however, questioned the composition of the government’s 46.5% share, noting that it includes spending from the national government, local governments and PhilHealth, among other government health financing sources.
He called for a clearer accounting of the different funding sources supporting UHC, including funds earmarked under special laws.

The health department is seeking a P353.8-billion allocation in 2027, with the proposed spending plan focused on strengthening hospitals and primary care, improving community health, and advancing the implementation of universal health care.
Mercado said the department also wanted greater coordination among agencies within the health sector rather than having them operate in silos.
“Ang aking push ay hindi siya silo, dapat mag-usap-usap lahat ng sectors within the agencies within the health sector," he said.
(My push is that agencies should not operate in silos; all sectors within the health sector should communicate and coordinate with one another.)
He added that the goal was to make the health system fast, fair, and trustworthy. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Go on Duterte arrest order: The timing is suspect; why only now?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Bong Go said he is puzzled by the timing of the arrest warrant issued against Vice President Sara Duterte over her cases of grave threats. “I’m just puzzled by the timing.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Bong Go said he is puzzled by the timing of the arrest warrant issued against Vice President Sara Duterte over her cases of grave threats.
“I’m just puzzled by the timing. Why now when the deliberations here are ongoing?” Go said in an ambush interview with Senate reporters on Friday.
“Didn’t it happen almost two years ago already? Given the length of time that has passed, why is it being released now? Why was it only filed at this time?” he wondered.
“The timing (is suspect), considering that there is an ongoing impeachment,” he noted.
According to Go, who also sits as a senator-judge, the impeachment court has just finished deliberating on the first article presented by the prosecution team against the vice president.
This part involved the same allegation of grave threats, while the presentation for the next article concerning confidential funds is still ongoing.
“That’s all. There’s just this question that keeps nagging at me. Why now? Why this kind of timing?” Go asked.
Go made the statement when asked about the warrant of arrest issued against the vice president by the Quezon City Regional Trial court on Friday.
Duterte’s grave threats case was in relation to her statements in an online press conference in November 2024.

In this forum, she said that she had instructed a person to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, if she would be assassinated.

The warrant, dated Sept. 4, was issued after the court found probable cause to hold Duterte for trial on all three counts of grave threats, with bail set at P120,000 for each count, for a total of P360,000.
Asked whether the warrant could be seen as a form of pressure against Duterte, Go declined to comment, saying the matter is already before the court.
“It’s now a matter in court. We have courts that we follow. We also have our own process here. Impeachment is different from a court proceeding,’ the senator said.
Asked again how Duterte might handle the arrest, Go said, “Vice President Duterte is used to situations like these… She can handle it. I believe she can.”
Meanwhile, Go also declined to comment on the possibility of Duterte undergoing the same booking and mugshot procedures just like other arrested persons.
“I have no further comment on the procedures,” Go said.
The senator, a known ally of the Duterte family, said he is sure that Duterte’s lawyers are preparing to pursue all legal remedies available to her. /apl

articles.title: LOOK: Photos of expired medicines ‘buried’ by DOH shown in hearing
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Photos of expired medicines worth millions of pesos allegedly being buried by the Department of Health (DOH) were shown during the Senate Finance Committee’s budget hearing on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Photos of expired medicines worth millions of pesos allegedly being buried by the Department of Health (DOH) were shown during the Senate Finance Committee’s budget hearing on Friday.
The photos were presented by Sen. Raffy Tulfo as he questioned DOH officials about the agency’s expired medicines, saying they were a waste of public funds.
Today, the finance panel scrutinized the proposed budget of DOH and its attached agencies and corporations for the year 2027.

blocks.caption: Millions worth of expired medicines from the Department of Health allegedly being buried. - Photos from the Office of Sen. Raffy Tulfo

blocks.text: Tulfo said he has long criticized the DOH during yearly budget deliberations over billions worth of medicines that expire.
“The DOH always says that this is due to some oversight on their part. That’s the reason,” the senator recalled.
“And then, number two – they say that medicines that expire are returned to the supplier, and the suppliers replace them. I’m going to debunk that today… that lie by the DOH,” he pointed out.
“I have evidence that those medicines are being buried. I have pictures here that will show that those medicines are being buried,” Tulfo revealed.

blocks.caption: Millions worth of expired medicines from the Department of Health allegedly being buried. - Photos from the Office of Sen. Raffy Tulfo

blocks.text: When Tulfo demanded documentation on the return of expired medicines to it their sources, DOH Undersecretary Gloria Balboa explained that the DOH has an arrangement with suppliers that allow medicines nearing their expiration date to be taken back.
However, she clarified that she was not personally aware of such agreement covering medicines that have already expired.
In response, new Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said they are looking into the procurement and supply chain processes of the agency.

Mercado confirmed that in 2025, P217 million worth of medicines expired, prompting senators at the hearing to ask for previous data that showed how much were the medicines that had expired in prior years and their volumes.
The new secretary said he does not have these pieces of information at the moment. He said he will look for answers.

blocks.caption: Millions worth of expired medicines from the Department of Health allegedly being buried. – Photos from the Office of Sen. Raffy Tulfo

blocks.text: He told the senators that he will give the lawmakers a complete record once this becomes available.
Nevertheless, the secretary said that stricter rules now apply to DOH suppliers.
The secretary said that they currently require that medicines to be delivered by suppliers must have at least 18 months of shelf life before the drugs’ expiration date.
He also told the senators that he will create an investigating committee to also look into this matter. /apl

articles.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
articles.summary: The devastating Himalayan glacial floods have raised broader questions about who should bear the costs and responsibility for the impacts of climate-related disasters.

image.caption: Nepal, a country of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming [FILE: August 31, 2026]Image: Ambir Tolang/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.
More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.

Buildings, bridges, roads and over a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.
The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
Nepal floods trap hundreds in hydropower tunnels
A global responsibility?
For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.

It's about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a "global responsibility."

"As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?" Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.
"Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community," he stressed.
Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.

"We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it," Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. "We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns."
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes
Highly vulnerable to climate impacts
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a "negligible contributor to climate change," according to the World Bank.

But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.
Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

The country's government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.
Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.

In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant "this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums."
"Earlier, we were advocating only about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it," she told DW.
Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice efforts.
In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing
An opportunity for global climate action?
Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed "Loss and Damage Fund" for assistance over the latest floods.
But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.

The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.
Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.

"Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action," Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. "For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors."

According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.
Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.

"Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence," he said. "This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility."

articles.title: Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August
articles.summary:
Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella

A 45-year-old woman has been killed and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence, in the seventh…

blocks.text: A 45-year-old woman has been killed and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence, in the seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August.

Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards the bridge on the A1 motorway.
Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.
Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge. He then killed himself by jumping off the bridge.

After her call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal to the scene but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Police are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge.

Isceri’s mother told SkyTg24 that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”.

Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026. As of 8 August, there were 40 femicide cases so far this year, according to figures compiled by the feminist alliance Non Una di Meno.
But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner.

Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing of Giulia Cecchetin, a 22-year-old medical student, by her former boyfriend in November 2023.

Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent.
However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval.

Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results.

“The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.”

items: In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.org
