articles.title: Only 52% of LGUs have accredited PhilHealth Gamot providers
articles.summary: Only 52% of local government units (LGUs) currently have accredited providers under PhilHealth"s Gamot Program, highlighting continuing gaps in access to medicines, particularly for patients in areas…

blocks.text: Only 52% of local government units (LGUs) currently have accredited providers under PhilHealth’s Gamot Program, highlighting continuing gaps in access to medicines, particularly for patients in areas far from hospitals and pharmacies.
PhilHealth president and CEO Beverly Lorraine Ho disclosed the figure during the Senate Finance Committee’s briefing on the Department of Health’s proposed 2027 budget on Friday.
The Gamot Program had 2,984 accredited providers as of August 2026—2,472 private pharmacies and 512 government pharmacies—and had served around 788,000 patients, Ho said.
“52% lang po ng LGUs currently yung may accredited gamot providers. So this is something that we will really work hard on po,” she said.
(Only 52% of LGUs currently have accredited Gamot providers. So this is something that we will really work hard on.)
PhilHealth eyes wider pharmacy network
Senator Joel Villanueva questioned whether Gamot providers were concentrated mainly in urban areas, saying patients in communities outside major cities still have to travel to access the program.
He cited complaints from constituents who had to spend additional money on transportation just to reach an accredited provider.
Villanueva asked PhilHealth to provide its target for expanding the network, particularly in rural, underserved, and remote areas.
Ho said PhilHealth aims to expand the number of participating pharmacies to around 20,000.
The current network, however, remains far below that target, with only 2,984 providers as of August.
Nearly 788,000 patients served
Ho said the Gamot Program was still in its pilot stage in 2025 but had expanded in 2026.

“As of this August, we already have 2,984 providers, so that would be our pharmacies po, of which 2,472 are private and 512 are government, and we’ve served around 788,000 patients already,” she said.(As of this August, we already have 2,984 providers, which are our pharmacies—2,472 private and 512 government—and we have served around 788,000 patients already.)
Ho noted that PhilHealth also plans to expand the medicines covered by the program.

She added that 21 medicines currently under the YAKAP program are planned to be moved to Gamot to make them more accessible to patients, while the Gamot medicine list is expected to expand from 54 to around 120 medicines.
DOH eyes different way of distributing medicines
Meanwhile, Acting Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said the DOH is also considering changes to how medicines are procured and distributed, partly to address the recurring problem of expired stocks.

One proposal is to redirect some of the DOH’s budget for medicines and commodities into additional subsidies for PhilHealth, allowing patients to access medicines through accredited providers rather than relying as heavily on centralized government stockpiles.
“Isa rin namang plano ng DOH, kanina nga po napag-usapan yung expired meds at yung hirap, mga expired meds po at yung pagbaba galing sa central warehouse,” he noted.
(Another plan of the DOH, as we discussed earlier, concerns expired medicines and the difficulties involved in bringing medicines down from the central warehouse.)

Mercado said about 40% of medicines are currently procured centrally, while around 60%, particularly common essential medicines available locally, are procured through the DOH’s Centers for Health Development.
He also explained that expanding the Gamot Program could encourage more pharmacies to participate as they see PhilHealth paying providers on time.

The DOH and PhilHealth said they intend to continue expanding the program to improve access to medicines, particularly for Filipinos who have limited access to hospitals and pharmacies. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Colombian president posts video purporting to show 23 ‘neutralised’ guerrillas in body bags
articles.summary:
Footage provokes outrage as bellicose and performative far-right politics continue to spread across Americas

Colombia’s hardline president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has provoked outrage…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Colombia’s hardline president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has provoked outrage after posting a video on social media in which he strides through rows of white body bags that he says contained the corpses of 23 “neutralised” guerrillas.
De La Espriella took power last month vowing “all-out war” against illegal armed groups and he published the footage on Thursday in an apparent attempt to show he was fulfilling that pledge.

“I promised to confront terrorism without hesitation and I’m keeping that promise,” the far-right politician wrote above the video. “I did not come to play nice with murderers, extortionists and child recruiters. I came to defeat them … Long live Christ the king!”
Celebrating the military operation in the Colombian Amazon during which the 23 alleged terrorists were killed, De La Espriella declared: “We are utterly determined to destroy you, who are a cancer.”
The body bag footage, set to a stirring Hollywood-style score, was condemned by human rights activists and the president’s political opponents.

Iván Cepeda, the leftwing candidate beaten by De La Espriella in June’s election, wrote on X: “He strolls among the bags with the corpses. He nearly treads on them with contempt. He calls himself a Christian but in reality he’s an unscrupulous being lacking the slightest sense of humanity.”

blocks.caption: Iván Cepeda at a campaign rally in Bogotá in June. Photograph: Mauricio Dueñas Castañeda/EPA

blocks.text: The leftwing lawmaker Daniel Monroy accused the president of “necropolitics”. He wrote: “This is one of the most bizarre things we’ve seen. Strolling among the dead, while invoking the name of God, just to justify an unnecessary spectacle.”
De La Espriella’s predecessor Gustavo Petro tweeted: “This is called turning death into a trophy – something only soulless people can do … The soulless find it easy to kill for the sake of killing.”
De La Espriella hit back at his critics, posting: “Forgiving terrorists is God’s business. Sending them to meet him – if that’s where they’re headed – is the president’s job.”

De La Espriella’s post captured the bellicose and performative political zeitgeist sweeping the Americas, where a growing number of rightwing populists are seeking to woo voters with promises of ferocious, TikTokable crackdowns on crime.

The genre has been pioneered by El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, with slick videos of his notorious mega-prison, and Donald Trump, who has repeatedly published footage showing alleged drug boats being blitzed in the Caribbean and Pacific.

Ahead of Brazil’s October elections, several candidates are promising lethal attacks on the drug traffickers who control Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. “We’re going to stain the ground red with the blood of these lowlifes,” one candidate, Renan Santos, said recently, promising “a bloodbath” if he won power.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the main challenger to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has vowed to wage war on “narco-terrorists”, although he and close allies have themselves been accused of having ties to organised crime. “Criminals will be taken out of circulation, either standing up or lying down,” Bolsonaro has said.

In Rio, Felipe Curi, a former police chief running for congress, has posted AI-generated videos depicting him shooting armed men in the favelas. Campaign propaganda features his image superimposed on pictures of the corpses of some of the 122 people killed during the city’s deadliest ever police raids. “I arrest crooks,” Curi boasts in one video, “and I neutralise them if they react.”

articles.title: How can African retailers compete with Shein and Temu?
articles.summary: Shein and Temu are expanding across Africa with low prices and vast product ranges. Businesses and unions warn the growth could come at a cost for local jobs.

image.caption: Shein and Temu have gained a significant market share in a short period of time, putting local manufacturers under pressureImage: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: A T-shirt for a few dollars, along with jewelry, shoes and accessories — all delivered straight to your door. For many young people in African cities, shopping no longer starts in a store.
They scroll through Instagram or TikTok, see influencers showing off their latest purchases, and place an order with just a few clicks.
This combination of extremely low prices, a huge selection and aggressive social media marketing has made Chinese company Shein one of the world's most successful online fashion retailers.
Temu, also from China, follows a similar model with an even broader range of products.

For Africa's young, urban consumers, the appeal is obvious. But as more purchasing power flows directly to Asia through these platforms, another question is becoming increasingly important: What happens to local retailers, manufacturers and jobs?
South Africa shows the impact
South Africa is currently the clearest test case. Shein launched there in 2020, followed by Temu in 2024.

According to a study commissioned by the Localization Support Fund, the two platforms generated around 7.3 billion rand (about $405 million) in 2024. That represents 3.6% of the total market for clothing, textiles, footwear and leather, but already around 37% of online sales in the sector.

The study also estimates that 2,818 manufacturing jobs and 5,282 retail jobs failed to materialize during that period, a combined impact of about 8,100 jobs. By 2030, more than 34,000 additional retail and manufacturing jobs could be at risk under the study's modeled scenarios.
China's fast-fashion giant Shein opens first store in Paris
Simon Eppel, a research director with the South African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union (SACTWU), sees this as a growing threat to the domestic industry.
He says Shein and Temu have gained a significant market share in a short period of time and put local manufacturers under pressure.
"They sucked up billions of rands […] in sales, and undercut local manufacturers," Eppel said. The union is calling for stricter controls.
"In fact, we propose to ban these apps in South Africa," added Eppel, noting that the SACTWU sees such a move as one possible measure to counter the effects of the price pressure.
Aggressive price competition
Industry experts have cautioned that online giants such as Shein can operate at a speed that is difficult for a small African retailer to match.
Digital data shows which products are in demand, while influencers, discounts and a constant stream of new offers encourage consumers to buy.
For users, the line between entertainment and shopping is becoming increasingly blurred. But price is a crucial factor for many consumers.
Tsonam Cleanse Akpeloo, chairman of the Association of Ghana Industries, Accra chapter (AGI Accra), stresses that the offers are particularly attractive in price-sensitive markets.
"Their prices are attractive in price-sensitive economies where consumers naturally look for products that fit their budgets," he told DW.
Local business owners say that problems arise when they can no longer compete on price.
Companies that rely on high-quality materials and higher standards are put at a competitive disadvantage.
In Ghana, Akpeloo has observed similar developments in sectors such as aluminum and hardware.
Nigeria: Cheap imports for urban youth

Nigeria is also an important market for the major Chinese online retailers. Temu has a dedicated platform for the market there, while Shein is building its reach primarily through influencers and fashion content.
The appeal is clear: a wide selection, low prices and access to international trends. But Nigeria has already experienced what cheap imports can do to a local industry.
For governments, therefore, the issue is not just fashion. It is also about the conditions under which local businesses can compete with global platforms.
New tariffs on low-cost goods from China

Shein and Temu do not have a direct presence everywhere in Africa. Their strongest presence so far is in countries such as South Africa and Nigeria, and to some extent in Ghana and Kenya. But their products also reach customers indirectly in many other African countries.

So-called freight forwarders play an important role. They provide customers with a delivery address in a country where Shein or Temu delivers directly. The package is initially sent there and then forwarded to Africa.

This is how it works for Mariama Sow from Guinea-Bissau. She orders shoes, accessories and human hair for hair salons from Shein. She uses a freight forwarder in Portugal, which then forwards her orders to Guinea-Bissau.
"Underwear, shoes, clothes and school supplies, and above all the human hair, live up to their promise," Sow said.

At the same time, she says she has heard complaints from other customers about poor quality or incorrect sizes. Another problem, she says, is that local retailers are losing customers, particularly younger ones.
The tax dispute shows the political dimension

For governments, the issue is also about taxes and fair competition. South Africa has therefore tightened the rules governing small online imports. The government wanted to prevent international platforms from enjoying a tax advantage over local retailers.
For a local retailer who pays rent, staff costs and taxes, such differences can be significant.
The conflict is therefore not simply a matter of China versus Africa. It is about whether local businesses can compete under comparable conditions.
Akpeloo from AGI Accra is also calling for better controls.

"We need stronger action against smuggling, better enforcement of customs and quality standards," he told DW. Goods entering the market without the required duties and taxes can put additional pressure on local businesses.
Beyond cheap imports
Despite all the criticism, it would be too simplistic to portray the platforms solely as a threat.The key question is where the economic value is created.
A delivery driver earns money from an order placed in China. A textile worker, by contrast, can support an entire local value chain — from the fabric producer to the sewing factory and retailer.
For African governments, the challenge will therefore be to provide access to affordable products and digital commerce without weakening their own industrial base.

The real competition is no longer just between Shein, Temu and local retailers. It is also over the shopping habits of a young generation — and over whether Africa will remain primarily a consumer in the new digital economy or become a producer itself.
How fast fashion is killing the planet

articles.title: Populism poses serious challenge to independent central banks, Bailey says
articles.summary:
Bank of England governor says central bankers must explain decisions or risk being seen as ‘unrepresentative elite’

The governor of the Bank of England has said the rise of populist…

blocks.text: The governor of the Bank of England has said the rise of populist politicians presents a serious challenge to independent central banks.

As Nigel Farage’s Reform UK gathered for its annual conference in Birmingham, Andrew Bailey said central bankers must be prepared to explain their decisions to the public or risk being attacked as an “unrepresentative elite”.

Bailey was speaking at a conference at the London School of Economics. In an address peppered with historical references, from Alexander Hamilton to Thomas Hobbes, he said central banks must not take their “legitimacy for granted”.

Bailey said populist parties’ pitch for power “often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people. Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty.”

He added: “This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it.”

Populist parties, especially of the right, have been riding high on both sides of the Atlantic in recent years. Attacking traditional institutions – including central banks – often forms part of their platform.

Farage has previously suggested he would like to replace Bailey if Reform comes to power. In the US, Donald Trump repeatedly launched tirades against the former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell over the central bank’s failure to cut interest rates.

blocks.caption: Nigel Farage has previously suggested he would like to replace Andrew Bailey if Reform came to power Photograph: Thomas Krych/AP

blocks.text: Bailey was among the international central bankers who signed a joint statement defending Powell against Trump’s criticism and stressing the importance of independence.

The Bank of England was made independent by the Labour government in 1997, handing decisions on interest rates from the chancellor to a nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) chaired by the governor.

After the 2008 global financial crisis, which led to a significant proportion of the UK banking sector being nationalised at taxpayer expense, the Bank of England was given additional responsibilities for financial stability.
Bailey said on Friday that insulating the Bank from politics had made it better able to fulfil its role of maintaining “the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible”.
He said: “Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.”
after newsletter promotion

The MPC is split over how to respond to rising inflation as a result of the Iran war. Bailey has stressed that in a weak jobs market, he does not yet see signs of the “second-round effects” that can embed inflation throughout the economy as workers bid up their wages to keep pace.

The MPC voted to keep interest rates on hold at 3.75% at its last meeting in July. But three members voted for a rate rise, including the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, Huw Pill, who used a speech on Thursday to reiterate that in the face of rising inflation, Threadneedle Street should act “clearly, promptly and decisively”.

At its next policy meeting on 17 September, the Bank is also expected to announce whether it will press ahead with its controversial policy of quantitative tightening. The Bank has been progressively selling off the bonds it acquired though the emergency policy of quantitative easing – creating money to help stave off recession.

Critics, from Reform to leftwing thinktanks, have argued that these sales tend to drive up the yield, or interest rate, on government bonds, which move in the opposite direction to prices. That makes it more expensive for the government to borrow, a pressing issue at a time of febrile bond markets.
Bailey will appear before MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee next week to explain his thinking.

Edmonton organizers said in a Thursday statement the Boston Marathon will accept the finishing times of 92 competitors to qualify but not the 13.
The Aug. 16 race in Edmonton was about two-thirds of a kilometre longer than necessary.
The organizers initially stood by their calculated course length but simultaneously held a review that found they had miscalculated it, citing an issue with a mapped detour.

items: Edmonton Marathon apologizes, says detour error lengthened 2026 race distances

blocks.text: The Boston Athletics Association, which runs the Boston Marathon, had said even though the runners in Edmonton had to go farther, they would be eligible if their final times still met the Boston qualifying time.
However, it said it would not accept race times from Edmonton that had been adjusted to accommodate the extra distance, ultimately leading to the 13 rejections.

items: Organizer says Edmonton Marathon routes were accurate. Elite, amateur runners disagree

blocks.text: Organizers in Edmonton say they will be contacting the 13 people and working with Athletics Canada to review the course certification process.

"It is evident the community that gathers through this event is resilient, passionate, kind and deserving of nothing less than our very best," said Tom Keogh, Edmonton Marathon race director, in a statement Thursday.
"We commit that this distance miscalculation does not happen again."
Edmonton Marathon apologizes for lengthening course by mistake

Before, during and after the event, several racers said their own distance calculators put the racecourse longer than the regulation 42.2 kilometres for the full marathon and 21.1 kilometres for the half marathon.
Race officials confirmed in the days after that the course was 674.7 metres longer than required.
Despite the added length, the Edmonton Marathon said two course records were broken in both the men's and women's marathons.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Dayne Patterson is a Calgary-based reporter for The Canadian Press

articles.title: U.S. sailors hit the streets of Thailand after record-setting Middle East deployment
articles.summary: Buses carrying crew members of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier streamed into Thailand's seaside resort city of Pattaya, as part of a port call after a lengthy deployment to the Middle East.

image.caption: Pedestrians walk past a LED display welcoming the arrival of U.S. service personnel of the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln in Pattaya on Wednesday. (Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·Photos
Buses carrying crew members of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier streamed into Thailand's seaside resort city of Pattaya, as part of a port call after a lengthy deployment to the Middle East.
USS Abraham Lincoln's lengthy deployment drew concerns about deteriorating mental health, food shortages

Buses carrying crew members of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier streamed into Thailand's seaside resort city of Pattaya on Thursday as part of a port call after a lengthy deployment to the Middle East.

The Lincoln was supporting the U.S. war against Iran, and its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 260 days. This drew concerns last month about deteriorating mental health among the crew as well as shortages of key food supplies on board.
The U.S. Navy downplayed any problems, and President Donald Trump said the deployment was "not nearly long enough."
The ship has been deployed for a total of 286 days, according to the U.S. Embassy in Bangkok. Its total uninterrupted time at sea before Wednesday's arrival in Chonburi province was 264 days.
The ship is expected to depart Thailand this weekend and continue its journey back to the U.S.
After clambering down from buses, laden with luggage, several service members told The Associated Press they were excited to be in Thailand.
Vendors and travel agents gathered outside the Hard Rock Hotel, the designated pickup and drop-off point for troops travelling from the Lincoln, which is docked nearby at Laem Chabang Port.
They swarmed service members as they arrived, offering a range of souvenirs and services. Many sailors waved them away while waiting for their rides.

Two other ships from the Lincoln's strike group are docked elsewhere in Thailand, with the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. at Chonburi's Sriracha port and the cruiser USS Robert Smalls in Map Ta Phut in neighbouring Rayong province.

A-ngoon Sombat travelled 200 kilometres between Pattaya and the central province of Ayutthaya to sell colourful braided bracelets to the visiting crew, as she does every time she hears a U.S. ship is coming for a port call in Chonburi province.
She set up opposite the hotel entrance and had managed to make some sales, but said she is still unsure if business will be good this week.
"There are many vendors around. It's really up to how lucky each of us are," she said.
Dozens of service members could be spotted strolling around Pattaya's Terminal 21 mall with shopping bags in their hands as the afternoon sun was blazing outside.

A 20-year-old serving as a navigator aboard the Petersen, who declined to give his name because he was told not to speak to media while ashore, said the morale among his crew members was really high now that they had arrived in Thailand.
The sailor said it was his first deployment for the U.S. Navy. He said it was a bit of an ordeal but he was happy to finally be on his way home.

items: Hegseth pushes back on reports of poor conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln in Middle East
Can Trump's 'gunboat diplomacy' stop Iran from blocking the flow of oil? Not likely, say experts

blocks.text: He declined to comment when asked about the reports about the conditions on the Lincoln.
A spot just outside the Laem Chabang Port had turned into a small attraction by Wednesday evening, as people gathered to catch a glimpse of the Lincoln.

People arrived by car and motorcycle to peer through a mesh fence at the ship, which is as long as about three American football fields. They took photos and videos and excitedly chatted with strangers about their chance to see the vessel.

American Keith Eldridge, who has lived in Thailand for five years, travelled from the neighbouring province of Chachoengsao to see the ship. He was too late to catch the Lincoln docking but found the viewing spot through a recommendation from other enthusiasts he met along the way.
He said it was impressive to be able to lay his eyes on this "engineering marvel."

"When you get to look at something so big, wrapped up with so much technology, the radars, the sonars, the weapon systems, the propulsion systems, it is truly amazing that we can build it, float it, and we fight from it," he said.
The Lincoln's commanding officer, Capt. Dan Keeler, said the ship will be heading home soon, but may make further supply stops.
He declined to comment on the exact date the strike group is expected back in the U.S.

articles.title: Legarda seeks permanent fuel-security framework
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Loren Legarda is pushing for a permanent fuel-security framework that would allow the government to closely monitor the fuel market and act quickly when prices and supply…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Loren Legarda is pushing for a permanent fuel-security framework that would allow the government to closely monitor the fuel market and act quickly when prices and supply are threatened by a crisis.

Legarda filed Senate Bill No. 2435, or the proposed Philippine Fuel Security and Strategic Petroleum Reserve Act, on Sept. 1. The measure would strengthen regular monitoring and verification while giving the government temporary powers during a declared fuel emergency.

The proposal follows issues raised during the recent oil crisis and Senate PROTECT Committee hearings involving fuel inventories, actual acquisition costs, industry margins and the basis for price adjustments.

“During the hearings, we saw how quickly prices could rise, while the government and the public had limited information on the actual cost of fuel already in the country, existing inventories, industry margins and the basis for each adjustment,” Legarda said.
“Families felt the increase immediately, but many basic questions could not be answered with the same speed,” she added.

Oil companies explained during the hearings that pump prices may be based on replacement cost, or the expected cost of the next shipment, even when fuel being sold had been acquired earlier at a lower price.
The government, however, did not always have ready access to records needed to independently verify the costs and margins involved.

“We are not saying that companies should not earn. But when there is a crisis and prices are rising quickly, the government should be able to determine whether the increase is reasonable or whether someone is profiting excessively while families are tightening their belts,” Legarda said.
“No one should take unfair advantage during a crisis,” she added.
Under the bill, the Department of Energy (DOE) would continuously monitor fuel supply, inventories, acquisition and landed costs, price movements, distribution and market behavior.
When verification is needed, the DOE may require contracts, invoices, bills of lading, import entries and documents covering freight, insurance, storage and hauling costs.
The authority would apply even without a declared emergency but would be limited to monitoring, verification, planning, consumer protection and enforcement.
The bill states that this would not amount to ordinary price control, while commercially sensitive information would have to remain confidential.
“Monitoring is different from regulating. During normal times, the DOE needs to know the true state of supply, costs and prices,” Legarda said.
“When a crisis comes, only then may clear, limited and temporary powers be used to protect the public,” she added.

During a declared fuel emergency, the DOE may impose temporary pricing and supply measures, including price or margin limits, priority allocation for essential services, inventory requirements, distribution directives and emergency procurement.

The agency may also limit, adjust, suspend or require verification of replacement-cost pricing when its continued use is likely to result in premature price increases, delayed rollbacks, excessive margins or market abuse.
An emergency pricing method may instead consider actual acquisition cost, average inventory cost, landed cost, reasonable logistics expenses and reasonable margins.
The measure also seeks to address questions raised during the hearings over additional government revenues when higher fuel prices increase value-added tax and other fuel-related collections.
It would require the publication of a Fuel Tax Transparency Report comparing actual collections with official revenue assumptions.
“As prices rise and families can afford less, it should also be clear how much additional revenue the government is collecting,” Legarda said.
“The public deserves to know whether the government is receiving windfall collections from the same crisis that is causing them hardship,” she added.
If substantial additional or windfall collections are identified, the Department of Finance and the Department of Budget and Management would be required to recommend appropriate relief.
Possible measures include temporary fuel-tax reductions, public transport support, assistance for farmers and fisherfolk, food logistics or disaster response.
The bill would also create a Strategic Petroleum Reserve for major national supply disruptions and a Government Operational Fuel Reserve to keep essential services running.
The DOE would lead the program, while the Philippine National Oil Co. would serve as the state’s fuel-security agent.
“We should not repeat in the next crisis the same search for data, disputes over the basis of prices and scramble for separate responses,” Legarda said.
“We have seen where the gaps lie. This bill puts the information, safeguards, emergency powers, tax accountability and fuel reserves into one permanent system,” she added.

articles.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
articles.summary: The growing number of attacks on substations and railway lines in Germany is raising concern. Experts say that people will have to get used to the likelihood that such incidents will continue.

image.caption: Germany is registering an increasing number of attempted sabotage attempts on its critical infrastructureImage: Thilo Schmuelgen/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage.
On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators.

In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received.
While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals.
Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year

What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors.

Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year.
People in Berlin express concern over Russia

Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin.

One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?"

One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening."
Is Germany's civil defense prepared for crisis?
A freeze in German-Russian relations

The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4.

The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years.
"We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year.

The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war.
Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive?
Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe.

Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it.

He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure."
At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war.
Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security

But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists.

A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS" aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force.

Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police. As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection."

Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves: "Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said. What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: MWIS cuts water losses at PEZA-Cavite by 1.7 million liters daily
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Infratech Solutions (MWIS) said it recovered about 1.7 million liters of water per day after completing a four-month non-revenue water optimization program for the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Infratech Solutions (MWIS) said it recovered about 1.7 million liters of water per day after completing a four-month non-revenue water optimization program for the Philippine Economic Zone Authority-Cavite (PEZA-Cavite).

MWIS, an operating unit of Manila Water’s Non-East Zone, said the program sought to improve water system efficiency, operational reliability and resource sustainability across PEZA-Cavite’s facilities.
The program involved network diagnostics, hydraulic engineering and field investigations to assess PEZA-Cavite’s water production, transmission and distribution facilities.
MWIS also established two district metered areas, or DMAs, to provide greater visibility into water movement across the network and allow more precise monitoring of consumption and system losses.
The DMAs enabled MWIS to isolate service zones, improve water balance analysis and identify areas requiring operational intervention.
The company also conducted step-testing and acoustic leak detection activities to identify hidden leaks and other inefficiencies in the distribution system.
MWIS replaced critical gate valves to improve network control, zone isolation and operational flexibility during maintenance and repairs.
These measures allowed the program to recover about 1.7 million liters of water per day, reducing losses and improving system efficiency during the four-month implementation period.
MWIS also developed and calibrated a hydraulic model of the network to simulate water flow and pressure under different operating conditions.
According to the company, the model was used to optimize water distribution, identify operational bottlenecks and evaluate possible infrastructure improvements.
The hydraulic simulations also guided operational adjustments aimed at improving network efficiency and reducing reliance on energy-intensive facilities.

“At MWIS, we believe that effective water management begins with a clear understanding of system performance. Through a combination of data-driven analysis, hydraulic modeling, and targeted field interventions, we were able to help PEZA-Cavite recover significant water losses and improve overall network efficiency,” MWIS General Manager Adrian Bryan Magallanes said.
“This project demonstrates how innovative NRW management strategies can strengthen operational reliability while supporting long-term resource sustainability,” he added.
Magallanes said MWIS was also committed to helping PEZA-Cavite improve the efficiency and resilience of its water distribution system.

“We are proud to partner with PEZA-Cavite in enhancing the efficiency and resilience of its water distribution system. We remain committed to delivering solutions that drive efficiency, sustainability, and operational excellence for our partners,” he said.

PEZA-Cavite, also known as the Cavite Export Processing Zone, is a 275-hectare industrial park in Rosario and General Trias City in Cavite. It hosts hundreds of export-oriented manufacturing, electronics, logistics and warehousing companies.

articles.title: Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to Gaza
articles.summary:
Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is striving to help Palestinians gain sovereignty over their food security

Salama Ayesh Muhanna still remembers the first seeds he planted on his family’s land…

blocks.text: Salama Ayesh Muhanna still remembers the first seeds he planted on his family’s land in al-Qarara, Gaza. At just 17, Muhanna had proudly sprouted cucumbers.
“I was very happy because I saw the results,” Muhanna says. “We were farmers at heart.”
Now 71, he is an agronomist, a community leader and the founder of the Al-Qarara Seed Bank.

The original project, founded in 2017, was situated near the eastern border of Gaza in al-Qarara, an area now completely flattened and inaccessible. Muhanna had a large home back then, olive trees, land of his own, and a successful seed bank operation with dedicated storage and equipment. Everything was destroyed early on during Israel’s brutal military campaign, but after being displaced to Deir al-Balah in 2024, Muhanna and his daughter Hanadi, 38, are now hard at work, regrowing seed collections at Gaza’s only seed bank.

Outside the tent where they currently live in a displacement camp, summer temperatures climb to almost 35C. Another tent houses their small but growing collection of open-pollinated, non-GMO seeds, including local wheat and vegetables such as okra and spinach.

blocks.caption: Salama Muhanna with his daughter Hanadi inside the seed bank. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: Each day, Muhanna rises early to check on the project, a 200-metre-wide plot of land where the family lives, collects seeds, and experiments with new crops. He inspects the seeds to assess their quality, waters crops and checks on seedlings. As the manager of the seed bank, Hanadi deals with local farmers and oversees the growing seed collection – all while studying agriculture and food sovereignty online via a programme partially tied to Coventry University and the Gaza Urban Agriculture Forum. Muhanna jokes that his hard-working daughter will be “managing her father” by next year.

The aim of the project is two-fold; firstly to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape. “The war forced farmers to resort to local seeds,” explains Hanadi, because of the ongoing blockades on seed imports, sky-rocketing food prices and growing hunger across Gaza. Yet it appears that a focus on local seed varieties – “baladi” seeds – may prove more effective. That, Muhanna says, is because “local seeds are resistant to drought, fungi, and pests”.
“During the war, they’ve been our lifeline,” he adds.

The projects other aim is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny. The seeds, once collected, are distributed among Palestinian farmers and families in Deir al-Balah who then return the same amount after harvest. Approximately 200 farmers have so far benefited thanks to Muhanna and Hanadi’s seeds, with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). And beyond multiplying seed collections, it is helping Palestinian farmers reclaim agricultural agency and self-reliance – providing for families despite devastating restrictions on resources including vital humanitarian aid.

blocks.caption: Muhanna says the seeds could be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: The seeds are deeply connected to memories of the Palestinian land Muhanna has always called home – and could, he hopes, be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza. “The pumpkin plant reminds me of my father and mother,” he says. “It grew on the vineyard where we lived when I was little.”

The needs have never been more urgent. At least 1.2 million people in Gaza now face acute food insecurity amid an escalating humanitarian crisis, according to a new report by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). Despite growing alarm among humanitarian organisations, Israel continues to block access to agricultural land, the imports of seeds and organic fertiliser. Meanwhile, dwindling water supplies, degraded soil and deadly remnants of explosives make farming a treacherous practice.
“Walking in the streets is unsafe, and walking on the land is unsafe,” Muhanna adds, admitting the psychological impact affects their work. “The war destroyed my hope.”

Despite immense challenges, the family know their seeds are helping the community while preserving indigenous seeds against agricultural monopolies, and safeguarding Palestine’s agricultural heritage.
As Muhanna puts it, seeds are “my identity, my patriotism, my nationality”.

“This is about agency. It’s about dignity. It’s about being less dependent on what is or is not allowed to enter Gaza,” says Pat Griffiths, ICRC spokesperson in Jerusalem. “As the occupying power, Israel has an obligation to make sure that Palestinians in Gaza have access to the food, goods and items that they need to live.”
There’s still a long way to go in returning the seed bank to its former size. Muhanna says that before the war, they had about 42 types of local seeds. “Now we have about 28.”
There is also another looming challenge that could affect the seed bank’s future.

blocks.caption: Salama Muhanna inside the seed bank: ‘During the war, they’ve been our lifeline.’ Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: “Climate change is what controls us,” Muhanna says as he sips on his tea and shelters inside from the sun. “When the weather is hot, the seeds spoil.” Sometimes he has to plant almost a month later than normal, delaying harvests in a race against time to gather resilient seeds for the future. Still they keep going, experimenting in their fields to see which local seeds produce the best yields. And with almost 2.5 tonnes of seeds collected so far – better than last year – there are signs that the efforts are working.
With each seed, there is hope in Gaza that sovereignty over food security can soon take root.
“Any country in the world that doesn’t have sovereignty over food security isn’t a country,” Muhanna says. “If we establish sovereignty over food security, then we’ll be a real country.”

articles.title: Duterte not yet guilty, but arrest order shows probable cause – solon
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — While the arrest order issued against Vice President Sara Duterte for charges of grave threats does not indicate guilt yet, Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said that courts…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — While the arrest order issued against Vice President Sara Duterte for charges of grave threats does not indicate guilt yet, Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said that courts do not make such decisions without finding probable cause.
Adiong, in a statement on Friday, said that due process must be observed at each phase of the legal process.
However, he said that the determination of probable cause has already been made — which is why a warrant of arrest was issued by a Quezon City court.
“The issuance of an arrest warrant is not a finding of guilt. Due process must be observed at every stage,” he said.
“A court, however, does not issue a warrant without probable cause. That determination has now been made,” he pointed out.
According to the lawmaker, every legal remedy must be made available to Duterte, but she should avail of those remedies within the court, and not outside it.
“The vice president remains entitled to every legal remedy available under the law. Those remedies should be pursued through the courts, not outside them,” Adiong said.
“The rule of law applies equally to all,” he noted.
Earlier, Duterte’s lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim said in a statement that the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 has issued an arrest order against Duterte for three counts of grave threats.
This covers the supposed threat she made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Lim is the vice president’s counsel in the grave threats charges filed by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
“Today, the Quezon City RTC has issued a warrant of arrest against the vice president,” Lim said in a statement.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” he added.
A photo of the arrest order issued by Branch 98 Presiding Judge Maria Angelica de Ramos showed that bail was set at P120,000 for each of the three counts of grave threats, or a total of P360,000.
The NBI cases stemmed from Duterte’s threats against the president, the first lady and the former house speaker during an online press briefing on November 23, 2024.
As she criticized the House for detaining her chief of staff, Undersecretary Zuleika Lopez, Duterte went to berate the First Couple and Romualdez.
In the same briefing, Duterte was told by a vlogger to take care as she may be in danger.
The vice president replied by urging people not to worry as she has talked with a person about killing the Marcos couple and Romualdez if she herself would get killed.
“Do not worry about my security because I already spoke to someone. I said, ‘If I am killed, kill BBM, Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez.’ No joke. No joke,” Duterte said in the briefing.
The same matter has been the subject of the impeachment complaints against Duterte, which eventually was included in the Articles of Impeachment transmitted to the Senate last May 13.
The alleged threats were included as Article IV, which the House prosecution panel has finished tackling.
The defense panel for Duterte’s impeachment has maintained that Duterte’s statements were part of free speech.
But the prosecution team believes her remarks constituted grave threats — regardless of whether or not the vice president executed a contract with an assassin to kill the three. /apl

articles.title: PVL: PLDT stays focused amid noise as title defense hits rough patch
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines— Defending champion PLDT got the brunt of criticism on social media after absorbing back-to-back losses in the PVL Invitational Conference. After sweeping 13 games en route to…

blocks.text: Savi Davison and the PLDT High Speed Hitters during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference. –MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net
MANILA, Philippines— Defending champion PLDT got the brunt of criticism on social media after absorbing back-to-back losses in the PVL Invitational Conference.
After sweeping 13 games en route to back-to-back titles in the PVL on Tour and Invitational last year, PLDT lost two of its first three games in its title defense.

Savi Davison, however, came to the rescue, dropping 32 points as the High Speed Hitters revived their title hopes with a 25-16, 25-22, 23-25, 25-20 win over Farm Fresh on Friday at Smart Araneta Coliseum.
Aware of the outside noise, coach Rald Ricafort is trying to ease the pressure by focusing on one game at a time rather than defending their title.

“The defending champion tag isn’t really relevant to us this conference because it just adds hype and becomes a distraction,” said PLDT coach Rald Ricafort in Filipino. “What’s more important for us is how we responded after the losses to Nxled and Vietnam, which were really tough for us, especially because we didn’t have much time to recover mentally.”

“I told them before the game that if that’s the lesson we’re going to get from this conference, then we have to maximize it. There are so many distractions outside of the game, but this is our job, so we really have to stay focused,” he added.

blocks.caption: PLDT High Speed Hitters' Savi Davison during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference.

blocks.text: PLDT High Speed Hitters’ Savi Davison during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference. –MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net
Team captain Kath Arado, who had 24 digs, said the High Speed Hitters have also learned to lean on one another amid the criticism.

“Honestly, you can’t really avoid it because social media is huge now and fans are really invested in volleyball. Personally, I’m not really active on social media, so that helps me avoid the noise,” said Arado in Filipino.
“It also helps that we have our coaches handling the technical side. We check on each other whenever we see each other and ask, ‘How are you?’ From there, we can tell if everyone is doing okay.”

“But what we really want to build is our relationship as a team. Whatever we hear outside or whatever happens within the team, we need to stay together. We’ll just listen to what the coaches tell us because that’s what will help us grow as a team,” she added.
Ricafort also credited the squad’s growth after three seasons together, particularly in handling adversity.
Kath Arado and Savi Davison on PLDT’s final elimination game against Creamline. #PVL2026 @inquirersports pic.twitter.com/H4bdXo4WT8 — Lance Agcaoili (@LanceAgcaoilINQ) September 4, 2026

“The team is definitely growing, and credit to all the teams because the games have been really tough. I think the biggest growth I’ve seen from us is that we’re now able to pinpoint the technical things we need to fix. Before, there were still a lot of differences among the players, but now we’re more solid even when we lose,” the PLDT coach said.

“We’re already at the point where we need to focus on growing as volleyball players. We really want this conference, but because of what happened, we weren’t able to get the games and results we wanted. It’s not over yet, though. We still have to fight until Tuesday,” he added.
PLDT hopes to stay in finals contention against Creamline on Sunday.

“They’re champions, they’ve been together for a long time, and they know each other really well. They’re a tough team to play against, but that’s our job. If we want to win, we have to work harder and stay focused,” Arado said.

“Creamline won’t give us an easy win. It’s not going to be like previous conferences where we could just expect to win. We have to think that we’re back to zero. We won today, but now we’re back to zero. We have to keep working and study them.”

articles.title: PhilHealth requests P170B for 2027 to enhance benefits, lower costs
articles.summary: Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) is seeking an additional P170 billion in the proposed 2027 national budget to help cover the projected cost of health insurance claims and expand…

blocks.text: Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) is seeking an additional P170 billion in the proposed 2027 national budget to help cover the projected cost of health insurance claims and expand benefits, as the government seeks to reduce the amount Filipinos pay out of pocket for medical care.

During the Senate Finance Committee’s budget briefing for the Department of Health (DOH) on Friday, PhilHealth president and CEO Beverly Lorraine Ho said the agency currently has P74 billion allocated under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
However, PhilHealth expects its payments for claims of indirect contributors to reach around P244 billion, prompting its appeal for an additional P170 billion.

“For next year, currently, ang allocation po sa amin ay total 74 billion, but we expect, based on the projected payout po namin this year, our payments for the claims of indirect contributors will already be around P244 billion. So next year po, our appeal would be 170 billion on top of the 74 billion that has currently been provided to us by the NEC," said Ho.

(For next year, our current allocation is a total of ₱74 billion, but based on our projected payouts this year, our payments for the claims of indirect contributors will already be around ₱244 billion. So next year, our appeal would be for ₱170 billion on top of the ₱74 billion that has currently been provided to us by the NEP.)
Ho said the additional funding would support efforts to expand PhilHealth coverage and increase its share of the country’s total health expenditure.

Senator Joel Villanueva pointed out that 41.2% of total health expenditure in 2025 came from out-of-pocket payments, asking how the government could ensure that the proposed health budget would translate into lower costs for patients.
PhilHealth said its share of total health expenditure is currently around 19%, intending to increase it to as much as 30%.
“Yes, Chair. Yung increasing ng PhilHealth share to as much as 30% of the total health expenditure. Ngayon po kasi nasa 19% siya,” said Ho.
(Yes, Chair. Increasing PhilHealth’s share to as much as 30% of total health expenditure. Right now, it is around 19%.)
Ho also said the agency’s realistic target is to bring the out-of-pocket share down to 37% by 2028, from 41% at present.

“For the CARE hours, currently, as of end 2025, the percentage of out-of-pocket payment as share of total health expenditure is currently at 41%. Our realistic, I guess, target, based on the trend of how much is being allocated to PhilHealth and our payouts, realistically at 37% of total health expenditure by 2028,” she added.

(Currently, as of the end of 2025, out-of-pocket payments as a share of total health expenditure are at 41%. Our realistic target, based on the trend of how much is being allocated to PhilHealth and our payouts, is 37% of total health expenditure by 2028.)
Zero balance billing
Ho said PhilHealth also wants to expand no-balance-billing (NBB) coverage, particularly in public hospitals.
Under the current policy, 90% of beds in public hospitals, except GOCC hospitals, are supposed to be NBB beds, while 10% of private hospital beds are covered by the mandate.
PhilHealth said this translates to a target of 66,055 NBB beds nationwide—59,790 in government hospitals and 6,265 in private hospitals.
Ho acknowledged, however, that implementation has been difficult in the past because hospital reimbursements were not always commensurate with the cost of services.
She said PhilHealth is now working with hospitals to make NBB more workable, including through negotiations on rates and payment arrangements.
P19B proposed for LGU hospitals and other programs
Ho also said the proposed 2027 budget includes an additional P19 billion for PhilHealth, primarily covering LGU hospitals, but clarified that the amount is not solely for zero balance billing.
The funding would also cover other programs, including mental health and severe malnutrition.
She said the proposed amount would cover 368 LGU hospitals.
PhilHealth’s data showed that it currently covers around 80% to 85% of the total bill in LGU hospitals.

Ho noted that the agency is still working out the details of how the additional funding would be used, including agreements with hospitals to ensure that patients actually receive zero-balance billing where applicable.
Villanueva, meanwhile, stressed the need for clearer communication so patients would know whether they would still need to prepare money for hospital bills.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Majority of Germans see Russia as a threat
articles.summary: More than half of German citizens believe that Germany's security is threatened by Russia, according to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey.

image.caption: The German government has accused Russia of hybrid attacksImage: Florian Gaertner/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the past few weeks, Germany has seen a drone attack on Leipzig Airport and an arson attack near defense contractors in Bavaria, while explosive devices and pyrotechnics were found at two substations in Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia.
As the country enters a September featuring three vital state elections, attacks on critical infrastructure appear to be on the rise, and defense contractors are apparently in the crosshairs.

After some initial hesitation, the German government has now publicly blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack, but could the Kremlin also be behind the other attacks? "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the Bavaria's conservatives, the Christian Social Union (CSU), has also warned that Germany has now become a "daily target of hybrid warfare," referring to measures that are not military, but are nonetheless meant to destabilize a country and unsettle the population — including cyberattacks, espionage, propaganda, disinformation, and acts of sabotage.

The developments seem to have alarmed the German people. Some 56% of the eligible voters polled now see Germany's security as threatened by Russia, according to the latest Deutschlandtrend, for which the polling firm infratest-dimap conducted a representative survey of 1,319 German voters for public broadcaster ARD between August 31 and September 2.
East Germans are significantly less concerned

But not all Germans feel this way. Nearly half of citizens in eastern Germany, for instance, feel only slightly threatened, or not at all, by Russia. The same goes for supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), some of whose prominent figures have expressed support for Russia. The survey found that two-thirds of AfD supporters consider the threat from Russia to be low.

The same divisions in the German population emerge on the question of arms exports to Ukraine. Just over half of Germans consider the country's military support for Ukraine appropriate, or think it should even be expanded, but for just over four in ten Germans, that support goes too far. Opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine predominates in eastern Germany and among AfD supporters.
AfD holds steady lead nationwide

The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state parliament on Sunday, and the AfD continues to be way ahead in the polls and could even win an absolute majority — usually unheard of in German elections.

The party also continues to enjoy strong support at the national level. The new poll suggests that if a general election were held this coming Sunday, the AfD would receive 27% of the vote, one point less than in August, which would make it the largest party in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.

The CDU/CSU, meanwhile, remains in second place at 21%, well below the 28.5% it managed in the Bundestag election in February 2025. The Greens would receive 15%, while the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the socialist Left Party have seen slight improvements compared to August, reaching 13% and 12%, respectively (+1 each). All other parties would fail to clear the 5% threshold.
Unpopular government, unpopular chancellor
The latest poll also suggests that the current governing coalition of the CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats would no longer have a majority if an election were held now.

Only 15% of those surveyed are satisfied with the government's performance, and even among supporters of the governing parties themselves, a majority is disappointed with the incumbent coalition's performance. Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz fares even worse: Only 13% approve of his work.
This is consistent with how citizens assess the CDU/CSU's competence.

Also notable is that significantly fewer voters believe the CDU/CSU is capable of finding solutions in key policy areas. While just over a year ago, 31% still considered those parties competent to ensure peace in Europe, that figure has now dropped to just 23%.
A similar loss of confidence in the CDU/CSU is apparent elsewhere: On asylum and refugee policy, on pension reform, and on climate and environmental policy.
On the topic of the economy, the CDU/CSU still enjoys the highest level of public confidence at 24%, but here too, the figure has dropped significantly from 31% in February 2026.
In eastern Germany, the AfD is now the party in which citizens place the most confidence across all policy areas surveyed, with the exception of climate and environmental policy.
Is Germany's weak economy boosting the right-wing AfD?
Economy causing concern

For many months now, Germans have viewed the economic situation as the most pressing problem to be solved. As many as 79% of respondents in the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey say the economy is doing poorly or very poorly. Here, too, however, there are significant differences depending on party affiliation.

As many as 41% of SPD supporters view the economic situation as good or very good, and 37% of Green Party supporters say the same. In contrast, only 3% of AfD supporters share this view — they are much more pessimistic, with 96% saying the economy is poor or very poor.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: VP Sara's 2 ex-security officers, alleged bagman dropped as witnesses
articles.summary: MANILA- The House prosecution has dropped plans to present two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s former security officers and alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga as witnesses in her impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA- The House prosecution has dropped plans to present two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s former security officers and alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga as witnesses in her impeachment trial, saying evidence already presented is sufficient to support allegations of misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds.

House impeachment team adviser and spokesperson Ace Barbers identified the two former security officers as Col. Raymund Dante Lachica and Col. Dennis Nolasco, who have both figured in testimonies on the handling of Duterte’s confidential funds at the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).

“The three allegations in this article have already been substantiated by the previous witnesses na iniharap, ‘yun nga ’yung sinasabi natin sa misuse, misappropriation, at saka irregular liquidation (presented on the misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds),” Barbers said during an online press briefing Friday.

“Sa prosecution panel, with the witnesses na iniharap, napatunayan na po natin ’yan (The prosecution panel had already proven that with the witnesses already presented) … So there is no need for additional witnesses like Col. Lachica, Col. Nolasco, and Madriaga,” he added.
Acosta testified as a hostile prosecution witness that Duterte instructed her to turn over four PHP125-million tranches, or a total of PHP500 million in OVP confidential funds, to Lachica.
She also disclaimed personal knowledge of how the money was ultimately distributed after turning it over to him.
Nolasco, meanwhile, was linked to DepEd’s confidential funds through the earlier House testimony of former DepEd SDO Edward Fajarda.

Fajarda testified during House proceedings that he turned over three PHP37.5-million confidential fund releases, totaling PHP112.5 million, to Nolasco upon Duterte’s instruction when she was education secretary.
Madriaga had been considered a potentially significant prosecution witness after identifying himself during House impeachment proceedings as Duterte’s former aide and alleged bagman.

In a sworn testimony before the House Committee on Justice in April, Madriaga claimed that he personally handled and distributed the first PHP125 million in OVP confidential funds released in December 2022 and disposed of the entire amount in less than 24 hours.

He alleged that he delivered bags containing millions of pesos to several locations upon Duterte’s instruction and implicated Lachica and Nolasco in the alleged movement of the money. Duterte has denied Madriaga’s allegations.

Despite Madriaga’s earlier inclusion among prospective witnesses, Barbers said the prosecution now believes his testimony, along with those of Lachica and Nolasco, would no longer be necessary given the evidence already on record.
The prosecution will instead proceed with its remaining witnesses as it seeks to complete its presentation of evidence on the confidential fund charge.

The witnesses are Fajarda and his wife, DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Charry Fajarda; Philippine Statistics Authority Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande; Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay; and Commission on Audit official Bresilio Sabaldan.
The Senate impeachment court has issued subpoenas for the five to appear as prosecution witnesses in the Sept. 7 to 9 trial proceedings.

Edward Fajarda’s personal appearance, however, could still be dispensed with because of his medical condition if the prosecution and defense agree to stipulate on the matters his testimony is intended to establish.

The prosecution is targeting Sept. 9 to finish presenting evidence on Article I, which covers the alleged misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of PHP612.5 million in confidential funds. (PNA)

articles.title: Nick Kyrgios gets month ban for cocaine, enters treatment program
articles.summary: SYDNEY–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios was cleared Friday to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for using cocaine and entering a treatment program. The 31-year-old, who reached the final…

blocks.text: FILE–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios reacts during the Australian Open first-round (AO1) singles match at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on January 14, 2026. (Photo by DAVID GRAY / AFP)
SYDNEY–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios was cleared Friday to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for using cocaine and entering a treatment program.
The 31-year-old, who reached the final at Wimbledon in 2022, failed a doping test during an ATP event in Mallorca on June 22.
He was provisionally suspended on August 4 by the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA), admitting he made “a huge mistake”.
In a statement Friday, the doping agency said Kyrgios had explained his use of the drug occurred socially during a night out before he was due to play in Mallorca.
The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory, who found his explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.
“As a result, the ITIA accepted that Kyrgios’ use of cocaine was outside of competition,” the ITIA said.
Under WADA rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be reduced to one month if an individual commits to a treatment program.
“Kyrgios has entered into a treatment programme,” the ITIA added.
“As such, the player’s suspension will end on September 3, 2026, subject to completion of the program. Prize-money and ranking points from the Mallorca event will be forfeited.”
Boasting a big serve and booming ground strokes, Kyrgios has won seven singles titles on the ATP Tour and rose to a high of 13 in the world in 2016. He is now ranked 918.
His finest performance was on the grass at Wimbledon in 2022, when he reached the championship match, losing in four sets to Novak Djokovic.
Despite his natural talents that is as good as it got, with a series of injuries taking their toll.
He has had numerous surgeries, the most serious a complete reconstruction of his right wrist in 2024.
The Australian last played as a wildcard entry in the men’s doubles at Wimbledon in July this year, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.
Kyrgios was contrite when the news of his cocaine use emerged last month.
“I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” he posted on Instagram at the time. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.
“I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me.
“I know the example this sets and I’m deeply disappointed in myself.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte no-show at QC court on Friday over grave threats case
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte failed to appear at the Quezon City (QC) Regional Trial Court on Friday following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her.

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 7:55pm
Vice President Sara Duterte failed to appear at the Quezon City (QC) Regional Trial Court on Friday following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her.
QC Regional Trial Court Branch 98 issued the arrest warrant over three counts of grave threats against Duterte after finding probable cause to hold the Vice President for trial.
In a “24 Oras” report by Joseph Morong, additional police forces arrived at the QC Regional Trial Court following a request made after the arrest warrant was issued.
A backdrop used for taking mugshots was also seen being brought inside the court in preparation for Duterte's possible arrival.
However, Duterte did not voluntarily appear before the court as of 6 p.m. on Friday.
Morong noted seeing the additional police forces and personnel from Branch 98 leaving the premises later that evening.
Duterte's lawyer stated that the Vice President has no intention of evading the law, adding that she will pursue all legal remedies.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” said Paul Lawrence Lim, Duterte’s counsel.
In early August, the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed three counts of grave threats against the Vice President.

The charges stem from her public statements claiming she had contracted someone to assassinate President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Martin Romualdez if an alleged plot against her succeeds.

Following this, Duterte filed a motion to quash on jurisdictional grounds, arguing that as an impeachable officer, she has limited procedural immunity from criminal prosecution while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
According to the DOJ, the court denied Duterte’s motion for lack of merit.
The court previously heard oral arguments on the motion in August.

Duterte’s alleged grave threats against Marcos and other officials is also the basis of one of the Articles of Impeachment against her in the ongoing trial before the Senate impeachment court. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Manuel Bonoan pleads not guilty to graft charge tied to flood control projects
articles.summary: Former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan on Friday pleaded not guilty to a graft charge related to the alleged conspiracy to insert allocations in the national budget for flood control projects,…

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 7:55pm

Former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan on Friday pleaded not guilty to a graft charge related to the alleged conspiracy to insert allocations in the national budget for flood control projects, from which kickbacks were collected.

Bonoan remained a co-accused of Sen. Jinggoy Estrada in the charges pending before the Second Division of the Sandiganbayan after the tribunal in August denied the motion to exclude him as among the accused.
He has since been discharged as a co-accused in a plunder case before the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division also related to the flood control scandal.
The Sandiganbayan ordered Bonoan's release after he was discharged as one of the accused in the case. Plunder is a non-bailable offense.
Bonoan was released from hospital detention on Friday.
He had been in hospital detention since the Sandiganbayan issued a warrant of arrest against him last May 29 due to multiple illnesses, including heart problems.
Asked by Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Geraldine Econg on Friday if he was still sick, Bonoan replied, “I am still taking medicines, Your Honor.” –NB, GMA News
