articles.title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
articles.summary: Germany has blamed Russia for an attack on Leipzig airport but there has been a series of suspicious incidents elsewhere.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in Europe
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent
As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records this summer and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.
Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.
This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.
A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".
Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".
But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.
Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.
Poland's interior minister is clear.

"There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.
August campaign across Europe
4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.
10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a factory of the defence firm EMCO, with initial reports that a truck ignited during a fuel delivery.
13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion.

The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".
15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.

25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.
30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires.
One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out".
An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".
The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms
Why is this happening now?
Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.
The novelty now is the concentration of cases.
"The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.
She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."
Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes.
After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.
There are other theories.
To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses.

"Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.
He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe.
"They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.
2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland.
One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport

blocks.text: Image source, Police handout
Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport
"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.
It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.
But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.
Who are the suspected saboteurs?
Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.
That would be unusual.
The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".
They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.
In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.
The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.
The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.
The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.
So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.
In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.
Nato faced with Soviet-style campaign

Russia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.
The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war.
"I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."
As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.
Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.
What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?
"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

articles.title: [Mind The Gap] A Pinoy TNT’s survival mode: ‘Weather-weather lang ‘yan!’
articles.summary: Targeted in the State Department's 'largest mass visa revocation in history' are those who tried to stay within legal channels by filing for political asylum Because the affirmative asylum backlog…

blocks.text: Either by air or by sea, the backdoor for thousands of Filipinos who overstay their visa, jump ship, or claim political asylum to buy time is slamming shut.

What has been a temporary bridge for generations of Filipino immigrants to American life — with the possibility of getting a Green Card that can lead to US citizenship — has now become a high-risk gamble amid heightened deportation risks.

In 2024 alone, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported that 9,433 individuals overstayed their visa out of the 313,654 Philippine passport holders who entered the US. These include 4,816 individuals on B-1/B-2 tourist and business visas, 3,601 on F, M, J student and exchange visas and 1,016 on H1-B workers and K-1 fiance visas.

The DHS estimated the overall annual overstay rate for Filipinos at 3%, or anywhere from 7,000 to 10,000 Pinoys staying behind past their stamped departure dates. They are the primary engine driving the total cumulative undocumented Filipino population in the US now estimated at about 350,000, and counting.
The choke point starts at the US Embassy in Manila, which recently paused and re-examined visa appointment scheduling in its efforts to reduce the flow of potential overstays right at the gate.

About a third of B1/B2 applicants are usually turned away at the embassy interview alone. Those who get a visa now face Customs and Border Protection officers at their US port of entry who can search luggage, phones, or social media for resumes, work gear, lease agreements, or messages discussing long-term job hunting, intent to marry, give birth, or seek asylum — any of which can trigger immediate refusal.

Facebook and other social media postings criticizing the Trump administration that are deemed by ICE agents stationed at the airports as “anti-American” can lead to being accosted to your next flight home.

Even those seeking medical help without proof of financial capacity or insurance face the same fate — a denial that closes off healthcare-driven travel as quietly and effectively as it closed off birth tourism.

Unlike those Filipinos who simply overstay their visas each year to join the shadow economy, targeted in the State Department’s “largest mass visa revocation in history” of up to 200,000 non-immigrant visas are those who tried to stay within legal channels by filing for political asylum.

Because the affirmative asylum backlog has climbed to over a million in pending cases across all nationalities, filing an asylum claim after entering on a B1/B2 tourist visa often buys applicants months or years of lawful presence and temporary work authorization while awaiting a hearing — even if the underlying claim is weak.

A credible asylum claim requires a well-founded fear of persecution, and the Philippines under President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. doesn’t fit the profile of a state actively persecuting its citizens for dissent.

That gap between the political story asylum seekers need to tell the immigration adjudicator and the reality in Manila is precisely why so many claims, even if filed in good faith, could be flagged as fraudulent.

Regardless of their immigration status, the Philippine Embassy in Washington, DC is advising those who are caught in this dragnet to consult an immigration lawyer. It said they have the legal rights to fight for their claim, noting that each case is different and assessed individually.
“Weather-weather lang ‘yan!” (Things change constantly.)

blocks.caption: [Mind the Gap] You’ve got mail, and a $1.8 M fine

blocks.text: Despite the dangers, the temptation is obvious, if only because a sub-minimum wage in the US pays more in a single week than many professions earn in months in the Philippines.

Besides, in big Filipino communities across California, New York, New Jersey, and Illinois, an informal safety net exists. Families, relatives and friends step in with shelter, provide leads on under-the-table, cash-in-hand jobs in care giving, construction, housekeeping and kitchen work.

Some even play matchmakers by marrying them to US citizens, usually in a transactional matrimony cloaked in the language of love to pass the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) scrutiny. Others share advice on keeping a low profile by staying away from snitching Pinoy MAGA TNTs (Turo Ng Turo).

That’s why the TNT pipeline won’t dry up so much as go deeper underground. As one Pinoy TNT told me, “Weder weder lang yan!,” adding he is determined to wait it out, keep working, keep sending money home, and hold on, hoping the next administration softens the enforcement climate again.

He said that even if enforcement tightens with the deployment of more ICE agents, herding 350,000 Pinoy TNTs scattered across kitchens, care homes, and construction sites in a dozen states is not an easy task.

It’s Russian roulette: ICE either gets you or it doesn’t, and until the loaded chamber lands on you, staying and working look like the rational bet – which is exactly why so many keep trying to get in and stay in the shadow.

The back door may be closing. But for those who got in and overstayed, the possibilities are endless, unfortunately, including the chance of getting killed in an ICE raid or thrown into a third-country ICE detention center in Eswatini, in Southern Africa. – Rappler.com
Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for the Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

articles.title: US diesel prices hit an all-time-high
articles.summary: Fuel prices have soared since the Iran conflict began at the end of February, mirroring the surge in wholesale oil prices.

blocks.text: Drivers in the US are paying more than ever for diesel at the pump as the US-Israel war with Iran continues to hit Americans' wallets.

The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US has hit $5.85, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago and above the previous high following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
Fuel prices have soared since the Iran conflict began at the end of February, mirroring the surge in wholesale oil prices.
In response, US President Donald Trump recently pledged to "substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans" through an oil deal with Venezuela, which the US invaded in January.

The agreement, announced on Saturday, calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65bn barrels, as well as "an investment of more than $100bn (£73.9bn) and more than $209bn in taxes" for Venezuela, according to Interim Venuzuela President Delcy Rodríguez.
The US government will retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela", a US official told the BBC's US partner CBS News.
But some analysts have reacted with scepticism, including questioning whether the deal would address long-running obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela's oil industry.

Oil is a key ingredient in car fuel and supplies have been limited by Iran responding to the war by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway south of the country through which a fifth of the world's oil is transported.
Rocketing pump prices have angered US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections in November.
According to recent Reuters/Ipsos polling, Trump's approval rating has fallen to 33%, ​with just 31% of Americans approving of the conflict.

However, not all Americans face the same level of price rises. According to the AAA's data, those in the Western states pay much more than those elsewhere, due to tax differences and distance from US oil producers.
For example, in Washington, average diesel prices are $6.81 a gallon, compared to $5.03 a gallon a year ago.
As well as high diesel prices, Americans also face historically high petrol costs, with the average price per gallon reaching $4.15 compared to $3.20 a year ago.

articles.title: Bonoan pleads not guilty to graft case, waives reading of charges
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Public Works (DPWH) chief Manuel Bonoan pleaded not guilty on Friday to graft charges before the Sandiganbayan Second Division. Bonoan’s graft case stemmed…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Public Works (DPWH) chief Manuel Bonoan pleaded not guilty on Friday to graft charges before the Sandiganbayan Second Division.

Bonoan’s graft case stemmed from his alleged conspiracy with Sen. Jinggoy Estrada to ensure the inclusion of flood control projects in Bulacan in the 2025 budget, where the senator allegedly received a P213.7 million kickback.
Bonoan’s counsel Stephanie Ong informed the court that they would waive the former DPWH chief’s right to have the formal charges read against him.
“May we request that the reading of information be waived as we already explained it to the counsel,” Ong told the court.
Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Geraldine Faith Econg, the Second Division chairperson, took note of the request, and the prosecution did not object.
“We received on record already the waiver,” Econg said. “May I know how the accused pleads?”
“Your Honor, not guilty po,” Bonoan said.
Earlier, Bonoan was released from hospital arrest at the Philippine National Police General Hospital in Camp Crame after the anti-graft court Fifth Division dropped his plunder case.

Bonoan’s plunder case led to his hospital arrest, so Ombudsman prosecutors filed a motion to amend the information to remove him from the charges before the Fifth Division. On Tuesday, the Fifth Division granted this motion.
Only Estrada and three other former DPWH officials remain as accused in the plunder case.
However, the anti-graft court Second Division denied the prosecutors’ motion to amend the information to discharge Bonoan, this time from the graft charge.
Bonoan has filed a motion for reconsideration to appeal this court ruling.
After the arraignment, Econg said the court would proceed to the pretrial proceedings.
But Ong noted that Bonoan is “not ready” for pretrial, saying they have yet to submit his pretrial brief.
Ong said they were “preventing ourselves” from submitting the pretrial brief should their MR be granted.
“Given the chance, we were able to submit this pretrial brief as soon as possible,” Ong said.
Estrada’s counsel said they would like the pretrial proceedings to begin.
The proceedings, which include the stipulation of facts between parties, still proceeded./coa

articles.title: 1 killed, 4 hurt as truck falls off ravine in Zamboanga del Sur town
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — A 63-year-old passenger was killed while four others were injured after a blue cargo truck lost its brakes and plunged into a deep ravine. The accident happened…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — A 63-year-old passenger was killed while four others were injured after a blue cargo truck lost its brakes and plunged into a deep ravine.
The accident happened along a downhill road in Barangay Kitaan Dagat, Kumalarang, Zamboanga del Sur on Thursday afternoon, local police said.
Police Captain Derf Jay Maquinta, spokesperson of the Zamboanga del Sur Police Provincial Office, reported that the mishap occurred at around 12:55 p.m. in Purok Tugas, Barangay Kitaan Dagat.
The vehicle, a blue Isuzu truck driven by a 43-year-old man, was carrying four passengers—all working as truck helpers, who are from Luuk town in Sulu province.

According to police reports, the truck was traveling from Zamboanga City toward Barangay Limamawan in Kumalarang when it encountered mechanical failure while negotiating a steep downhill stretch of the road.
Investigators said the truck’s brakes reportedly malfunctioned as it descended the sloping road, causing the driver to lose control of the steering wheel.
The vehicle veered off the road before plunging into a ravine.
The 63-year-old passenger died on the scene due to fatal injuries sustained from the impact.
Meanwhile, emergency responders rushed the surviving driver and the three other injured truck helpers to the Rural Health Unit of Kumalarang for medical treatment.
Local police said an investigation is ongoing to establish the full details of the incident. /apl

articles.title: After renewed US-Iran strikes - how could the conflict end?
articles.summary: Three experts give their BBC their thoughts on whether an imminent end to the conflict is likely.

blocks.text: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DC

The problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.
It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.
What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.

Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of statis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.
US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.

US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.
My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.
Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, London

I do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.

On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.
But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.

That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.
Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to Iran

The latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.
Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.
What is the White House's exit strategy?
Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.
Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.
There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.

What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.

Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.
For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

articles.title: UK ministers hit back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insist islands remain British
articles.summary: Defence secretary says ‘winds of change’ remarks by Argentina’s president are more about domestic politics

blocks.text: British ministers have hit back after the Argentinian president said “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the Falklands were “blowing around the world”.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the UK would “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the islands after the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, said his country needed to take them back.
Miliband said in a post on X: “The UK’s position on the Falkland Islands is unwavering.
“The islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders.
“Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it.”
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said Milei’s statement by “tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands”.
He added on X: “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.”
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, also insisted the islands were British, adding: “We will defend the right of those who live in the Falkland Islands to determine their own future.”
The latest diplomatic spat over the South Atlantic archipelago came after comments by the US president, Donald Trump, who has cast doubt on American support for British control of the islands.

blocks.caption: Mount Tumbledown behind Stanley on the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls Malvinas. Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/AP

blocks.text: The US has traditionally remained neutral on the Falklands’ sovereignty, while recognising Britain’s de facto control over them.
Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982, when British forces defeated Argentinian troops, who had landed there to stake a territorial claim.
In more recent years, the British oil company Rockhopper and the Israeli company Navitas have been developing the Sea Lion oil field, 140 miles to the north of the islands.
Asked on Monday whether he could review British sovereignty over the islands as a way to push the UK to spend more on defence, Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”

And on Thursday, when quizzed about whether the US would back the UK in the event of an Argentinian invasion, he referred to the government’s refusal to let him use British bases in his initial attack on Iran earlier this year.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”

He added: “The Falklands is very interesting because your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago. That was a long time [ago], you went there and you just took it back very quickly. There was no games, so I don’t know if you’re prepared to do that.”

In his statement on Thursday night, Milei highlighted Trump’s comments, saying: “President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas [the Argentinian name for the Falklands].”

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Rockhopper’s shares dropped 7% in early trading on Friday.

articles.title: Abante thinks it’s time to seek subpoena for Duterte to attend trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — It might be the right time to ask the Senate Impeachment Court to issue a subpoena against Vice President Sara Duterte to compel her to attend her trial and finally address the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — It might be the right time to ask the Senate Impeachment Court to issue a subpoena against Vice President Sara Duterte to compel her to attend her trial and finally address the allegations against her.
This is what Manila Rep. Bienvenido Abante Jr. said in an online press briefing on Friday.

The lawmaker believes that, instead of calling for other non-impeachable officers to attend the impeachment trial, Duterte herself should be subpoenaed and explain what happened to the confidential funds (CF).
The non-impeachable officers Abante is referring to are former Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG) officials Col. Raymund Dante Lachica and Col. Dennis Nolasco
“For me, they want us to call witnesses who are non-impeachable officers. Why not seek a subpoena for the impeachable officer herself?” Abante asked.
“Ask for a subpoena for Vice President Sara Duterte so that she will face these issues,” he continued.
“That’s what I have been saying. If she does not deserve to be impeached, she should address all the allegations, and say whether she should be impeached or not,” he added.

When asked to clarify whether a possible request for Duterte’s subpoena indicates that she will be called to the witness stand, Abante said it is his opinion that the vice president should be called to the court.
The lawmaker told the media that Duterte testifying in the trial will be a chance for her to defend herself.

A possible Duterte testimony will also be important, Abante said, because several witnesses close to the vice president have already said that they know nothing about the confidential expenditures made by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd).
“For me, that is what it should be. This will also be good for her because she will be able to answer all the allegations against her,” he said.

“What did the witnesses say? Ms. Gina (Acosta) already did all that she can do. (Lemuel) Ortonio did the same. They explained their side. Atty. (Michael) Poa also explained. So who else should we invite?” Abante asked.
“We really have to subpoena the vice president. She herself should face it,” said the legislator.
“And if she is issued a subpoena, this does not mean she is guilty already. We’re not actually saying that she is guilty. We are not talking about her criminal liability here,” he explained.
Prosecution spokesperson and impeachment advisor Robert Ace Barbers clarified later on that the panel is still considering what particular Article of Impeachment Duterte will be called for.
“The prosecution panel is discussing this, because she is ably represented by her 16 lawyers,” Barbers noted.
“If her presence is really required and answers are not being given from questions that are left hanging, maybe that’s the time that we will ask for the court to subpoena her,” he said.
Abante has been insistent about Duterte needing to attend the impeachment trial.
Last August 17, Abante said that, instead of letting her staff members explain how CFs were released and spent, Duterte herself should show up and address the issues hurled at her offices.

According to Abante, if Duterte is able to attend the proceedings for her perjury charge against ex-aide Ramil Madriaga, and the arraignment of brother Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte for his grave threats case, the vice president should also make time for the impeachment trial.
Abante thinks Duterte should not let her staffers alone be grilled.
Earlier, the prosecution panel for Duterte’s impeachment trial said it would no longer call to the witness stand three individuals believed to be capable of delivering key testimonies.
The team members believe they have already established a strong case.

In an online press briefing on Friday, Barbers said they will not call Lachica, Nolasco, as well as former Duterte aide Ramil Madriaga, believing that the three requirements under Article I of the Articles of Impeachment have been met.

Article I deals with the alleged misuse of CF lodged within Duterte’s offices, P500 million with the Office of the Vice President (OVP) from 2022 to 2023, and P112.5 million with the Department of Education for the first three quarters of 2023. /apl

articles.title: Sara Duterte headed for trial after QC court arrest warrant -DOJ
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The arrest warrant issued by a Quezon City court against Vice President Sara Duterte should pave the way for her grave threats case to proceed to trial soon, a Department of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The arrest warrant issued by a Quezon City court against Vice President Sara Duterte should pave the way for her grave threats case to proceed to trial soon, a Department of Justice (DOJ) official said on Friday.
DOJ spokesperson Polo Martinez said the resolution issued by Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) dismissed Duterte’s camp’s motion to defer or recall her arrest warrant.

Duterte is charged with three counts of grave threats over her outburst in an online press conference in November 2024 when she said that she allegedly arranged an assassination plot with a hitman to target President Marcos, the first lady, and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.
The offense, however, is bailable, which is set at P120,000 per count, the DOJ earlier noted.

“The case shall now proceed to trial,” Martinez said in a message to reporters. “As a matter of procedure, warrants of arrest are transmitted directly by the court to the appropriate law enforcement agencies for implementation.”
Martinez was referring to earlier motions sought by Duterte’s lawyers, led by Paul Lim, to quash the complaint and to block the issuance of any arrest warrant in connection with the case.
The DOJ filed the grave threats complaint in August after state prosecutors found a high quantum of proof that the country’s second-highest official may be found guilty of such offense.
For his part, Lim said in a statement on Friday that the Vice President would not try to dodge the enforcement of the arrest warrant against her.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Lim said./coa

articles.title: Forest fire-linked haze still present in Palawan, areas in Visayas, Mindanao

articles.title: ‘Stayin’ in Canada’: These artists halt sales to U.S. amid new 50% tariff on original art
articles.summary: Some N.S. artists have stopped selling their work to U.S. customers after President Donald Trump implemented a 50 per cent tariff on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods — including original…

image.caption: Chris Warburton Hulme is a mixed-media artist who sells her work online. Despite roughly half of her customers being American, she has halted all shipping to the U.S. as a result of the latest round of tariffs. (Celina Aalders/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

Some N.S. artists have stopped selling their work to U.S. customers after President Donald Trump implemented a 50 per cent tariff on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods — including original art.
Original art made in Canada now faces a 50% tariff when sold to U.S.
Chris Warburton Hulme was “appalled” when she learned that U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest round of 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods included original artwork.
For the mixed-media artist from Eastern Passage, N.S., that was the final straw. Despite about half of her customers being American, she will no longer ship her pieces south of the border.
“Sorry, it’s not going to the U.S. anymore. It’s stayin’ in Canada,” said Hulme.
“It’s original artwork. It should be free speech. It should be freedom of expression. And to tariff that … it restricts everything that an artist should be able to do.”
The new tariffs apply to a range of Canadian art, including paintings, drawings, collages, decorative plaques, engravings, prints, sculptures and more.
While the Canadian government announced dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on products imported from the U.S. effective Sept. 8, the retaliatory measures do not include original art.
Cole Harbour artist Miranda Jordan has also halted all sales to the states.
She said since the trade war first began, it’s been challenging to navigate the ever-changing rules and shipping restrictions.
“I don’t work for the U.S. government and I don’t want to be an unpaid customs clerk for them, so I’m just not doing it anymore,” she said.
“I would rather just do designs that appeal to Canadians and ship to Canadians.”
Journalist and former CBC Radio host Tod Maffin said he wanted to use his large social media following to support small businesses impacted by the latest tariffs.
He and his wife started an online directory where people can promote their products, while customers can browse locally made items.
Maffin said while the federal government has been offering financial support for larger industries, he doesn’t want the small players to be overlooked.

“That often leaves a lot of the smaller parts of the engine of our economy — which are the small businesses, the home businesses, the hobby businesses — that may not be employing five or 10 people, but may be a really important part of putting food on the table for that family,” said Maffin.
“I think that’s just as important.”
CARFAC National, a non-profit advocacy group for professional artists in Canada, said in a statement that artists “cannot be an afterthought” in the country’s response to the trade war.

“Canadian artists are independent workers and entrepreneurs," said interim executive director Jenna Faye. “Unlike large businesses and corporations, individual artists don’t have the financial resources to absorb new costs associated with these tariffs.”
Targeting Canadian buyers
While the new tariffs have already hindered their operations, Hulme and Jordan are both adapting and taking the opportunity to target Canadian buyers.
“I know that people want to support their creative community,” said Hulme. “Sometimes they can’t afford a $300 piece of art, but they can afford a $10 card.”
Hulme said she’s registering for more craft shows to get her work in front of local audiences, and she also plans to start a series of paintings inspired by trail-blazing Canadian women.
Jordan said she hopes people will make a concerted effort to buy local and engage with Canadian creators when possible.

“It doesn’t mean, of course, that we can all go out and spend all of our money on art before we start paying our mortgages, or rent, or food on the table. But I think art really does make life colourful,” she said.

articles.title: Nation in Motion, Ballots on Pause
articles.summary: Imagine a democratic country that treats your right to choose as a tentative date on a calendar. Something to be

blocks.text: Imagine a democratic country that treats your right to choose as a tentative date on a calendar. Something to be crossed out, erased, and rescheduled whenever it becomes convenient.

Out of eighteen scheduled village elections since 1982, only ten have successfully pushed through as planned. Let that sink in. The Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections are not just periodically delayed; they are the most fractured, disrespected democratic exercise in our country.
Perhaps postponing it once or twice can be an emergency measure, but doing it over and over again for decades is a symptom of a systemic addiction to control.

Now, we are told to sacrifice our ballots once more under the familiar guise of economic volatility. We are asked to accept that a nation facing financial strain must pay its debts by mortgaging its democracy

The very systems responsible for managing and often mishandling public funds are the ones canceling our civic participation under the banner of saving money. Since when did the right to vote become a budget item that the Congress can just slash as they please? A budget crisis does not give the Congress the right to hand out free, five-year unearned term extensions to politicians that the voters never agreed to.

The barangays are the pulse of this country, they are the direct link between the government and its people. Without them, there would be no municipalities, no regions, and no nation. They are the frontline of our communities.
Knowing that barangays are the ultimate grassroots mobilizers, is it truly a coincidence to hold the current local officials over until the 2028 national elections?

But in the middle of all these inconsistencies, it is the youth who loses the most. The Sangguniang Kabataan isn’t a democratic simulation that only shines with basketball leagues. It is a legitimate youth council that gives young people a direct voice in a nation that usually overlooks us.

With the postponement, the youth is denied the opportunity to participate until 2028—where some of our generation will already age out. This is our legal window to lead, yet we are being robbed of time. With the upcoming national elections, this is supposed to be a critical time of our lives—but instead, our civic participation is put on hold.

A five-year term extension is not a structural fix, it is a rebrand for carelessness and suppression. Lock the ballots and rewrite the calendar for convenience, but our country’s heart continues to beat. The nation doesn’t wait to move forward, and our right to choose who leads our immediate communities shouldn’t either.

Democracy isn’t a tentative date they get to cross out. Our local streets, our neighborhoods, our futures are happening today—no amount of political convenience will ever change the fact that the right to choose is a non-negotiable.
The 2026 BSKE must push through.

articles.title: 2 trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods
articles.summary: Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, raising hopes of reaching a dozen others believed to be trapped nine days after catastrophic floods devastated towns and…

image.caption: Sanjay Sah is carried by members of a search and rescue team after they rescued alive two people who had been trapped inside a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project after floods struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, Nepal. (Nepal Army/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, raising hopes of reaching a dozen others believed to be trapped nine days after catastrophic floods devastated towns and swept away villages.
One of the survivors told rescuers more people were still alive inside tunnel, says Nepal army spokesman

The two men were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A construction site. The rescued workers were Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha’s office said in a statement.
Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue.
Basnet said one of the survivors told rescuers that more people were still alive inside the tunnel.

items: Hundreds feared stuck in hydropower tunnels as flood deaths surpass 950 in Nepal, China
Hopes of finding survivors dim a week after catastrophic Nepal flood

blocks.text: Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, confirming that people were alive and allowing them to locate the two men, Neupane said.

Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer's shoulder. One of the survivors was in a critical condition, according to a statement from the Nepal prime minister's office. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.

"I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," Amir Maharjan, brother to one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.
Hundreds of other workers still missing

At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
Nepal's Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued.
"We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people," Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

At least 1,259 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country's disaster management agency. China said late Wednesday that 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

articles.title: Stage set for GCash’s record P92.3B IPO, October 20 listing eyed
articles.summary: The shares will be offered from October 6 to 12, with Mynt targeting an October 20 debut on the Philippine Stock Exchange under the ticker GCASH

blocks.text: The shares will be offered from October 6 to 12, with Mynt targeting an October 20 debut on the Philippine Stock Exchange under the ticker GCASH

MANILA, Philippines – GCash has obtained clearance from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to pursue what will likely become the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in Philippine stock market history.

The IPO will be conducted by Mynt Inc., the parent company of GCash, for up to P92.32 billion. Under the latest timetable submitted to regulators, the shares will be offered from October 6 to 12, with Mynt targeting an October 20 debut on the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) under the ticker GCASH.
While there is no final offer price yet, shares may be sold for as much as P10 apiece, giving the e-wallet giant an expected initial market capitalization of about P668.96 billion.

The base offer consists of up to 1.61 billion newly issued shares and another 6.42 billion shares being sold by an existing shareholder, alongside an overallotment option covering as many as 1.20 billion more shares.

While the entire transaction could reach P92.32 billion in gross proceeds, Mynt itself expects to receive only around P14.95 billion in net proceeds from the primary shares, which it plans to spend on “digital financial services growth, product development, and general corporate purposes,” according to the SEC.
The SEC clearance brings GCash a step closer to listing, though Mynt still has to comply with remaining requirements, such as obtaining final approval of its listing application from the PSE.

The GCash IPO will demand an unusually large amount of investor capital from the Philippine market. For this reason, Mynt will also become the first company to benefit from the SEC’s lower minimum initial public float requirement available for exceptionally large issuers valued at at least P200 billion. The SEC allowed Mynt to sell shares equivalent to only 12% of its post-IPO capitalization, below the normal 15% minimum for large issuers.

If the offer proceeds at its maximum size, GCash would comfortably surpass the current Philippine IPO record held by Monde Nissin, whose 2021 listing raised about P55.89 billion including primary and secondary shares. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bacolod creative hub-trained sewers produce market-ready creations
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY — Sewing artisans here have produced market-ready creations after an intensive training organized by the city’s Department of Local Economic Development and Investment Promotions…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY — Sewing artisans here have produced market-ready creations after an intensive training organized by the city’s Department of Local Economic Development and Investment Promotions (DLEDIP).
The project is a step toward building sustainable livelihoods and creative enterprises for Bacolodnons.
Five of the 24 graduates, who attended the pilot G-Hive Artisan Makers Bootcamp Sewing Track last week, received awards.
The recognition was in the spirit of “celebrating their potential transformed into skill, passion transformed into craft, and being artisans empowered to create with purpose.”
DLEDIP head and city investment officer Frances Mae Llamas said on Wednesday that through the G-Hive initiative, they provide training programs and learning opportunities for Bacolodnons.
Llamas said these actions are meant to develop practical skills, strengthen creativity, and explore pathways toward livelihood and entrepreneurship.

“G-Hive was created to provide our local talent with a clear pathway from grassroots passion to global opportunity,” the officer said. “These 24 graduates have proven that when our artisans receive systemic support, they become true entrepreneurs.”

At the G-Hive facility located in Mansilingan Activity Center, participants learned to transform canvas, hablon (handwoven textile), and other local materials into contemporary, market-oriented products, such as tote bags.
Vivo Handmade founder Vida Hayes, one of the first batches of participants, was awarded the Most Improved Artisan Award.
“As an entrepreneur, I really appreciate this opportunity. As an artisan, it is very important to learn and know your craft. This project is very valuable. It will help a lot of people,” she added.

Roselyn Olchondra received the Artisan Excellence Award; Jeanne Marie Alindog – Most Creative Maker Award; Elvira Prado – Master of Precision Award; and Elizabeth Abad – Outstanding Artisan Spirit Award.

Youngest participant Zoey Tuclaud, 23, said she is thankful for the opportunity to be part of the G-Hive Artisan Makers Bootcamp for free and invited those who are interested to learn to also enroll in the program.

“I can use the knowledge and skills I learned if ever I decide to proceed with putting up my own business. I learned so much in sewing, cutting, and how to use the sewing machine properly,” she added.
Interior designer and educator Jinky Cantancio, one of the trainers, said the instructors guided participants in transforming preloved canvas materials into beautiful and useful tote bags.

“As one of the trainers/facilitators of the pilot batch, I had the privilege to be part of something special. We are part of discovering the skills and creativity that can become opportunities for livelihood and entrepreneurship for Bacolodnons,” she shared.
After completing the bootcamp on Aug. 24 to 28, the first batch of graduates take with them a certified portfolio, a business/production plan, technical confidence, and a maker network.
The second batch of participants will undergo training on Sept. 28 to Oct. 2 and the third batch, on Oct. 26 to 30. /apl

articles.title: 4ID troops unearth arms cache in Surigao del Sur
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Military forces dealt another blow to armed elements in the Caraga region after troops on Thursday recovered buried high-powered rifles and assorted ammunition in a hinterland…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Military forces dealt another blow to armed elements in the Caraga region after troops on Thursday recovered buried high-powered rifles and assorted ammunition in a hinterland village of Cantilan, Surigao del Sur.
Soldiers from the Army’s 30th Infantry Battalion, under the 4th Infantry Division, uncovered the weapons cache in Signalnan, Sitio Katarugan, Barangay Lobo.
The seized cache yielded an M14 rifle, an M1 Garand rifle, five 20-round detachable box magazines, 32 rounds of .30 caliber ammunition, and 89 rounds of 7.62x51mm ammunition.
The weapons are believed to be from communist rebels.
The recovery forms part of the Army’s drive to secure local communities, block any resurgence of armed conflict, and lock down peace gains in previously conflict-affected zones.
Lt. Col. Rey Vergel Annogui, commanding officer of the 30th IB, said the operation reflects the troops’ resolve to safeguard the area from renewed violence.
“This successful operation demonstrates our troops’ unwavering commitment to protecting our communities and sustaining the gains we have achieved in our areas of responsibility,” Annogui said.
Maj. Gen. Marion Angcao, commander of the 4th Infantry Division, commended the 30th IB for sustaining the division’s security momentum.

Angcao emphasized that vigilance and close coordination among the military, local government units, communities, and key stakeholders remain critical to keeping communist terrorist groups from regaining access to firearms and destabilizing the Caraga region./coa

articles.title: 'Layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
articles.summary: From searching for a buried tunnel entrance to blowing up rocks the size of cars, rescuers had to surmount multiple challenges to reach survivors.

blocks.text: A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.

Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.
"It's like layer upon layer of layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given that the multiple challenges they faced.
The first hurdle was to locate the hydropower station, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.

"I've never known an rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.

Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters, and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.
They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors.
"We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.
Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to resort to using explosives to clear the way.
"We had to use explosives which we normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," said Dix.
He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.
At the same time, they discovered the tunnel was still full of water.
Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.
Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.
The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," said Dix.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.
But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.
Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.

Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood would not have reached the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".
The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers.

"Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," said Dix. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."
But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time.
"It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."
Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".
This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located.
"We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

articles.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home
articles.summary: The motto of this year's festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.

image.caption: After 10 years, the Beethovenfest in Bonn returns to its old home, the BeethovenhalleImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four trumpeters will be scattered throughout the concert hall, accompanied by organ music, promising a magnificent auditory experience in Bonn's newly renovated Beethovenhalle.

The piece "A Call to the Heavens" was composed by Stefan Behrisch specifically for the opening of this year's Beethovenfest. Additionally, the London Symphony Orchestra, led by principal conductor Sir Antonio Pappano, will perform Ludwig van Beethoven's "Die Weihe des Hauses" ("The Consecration of the House") as well as Bruckner's Symphony No. 9 at the opening concert on September 4.

blocks.caption: The Beethovenhalle aims to make everyone feel at home Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: For nine years, Bonn's Beethovenhalle, a designated historic landmark, was unavailable for the festival. But now, as Philipp Seliger, spokesperson for the Beethoven Festival explains, "we have a large concert hall again with its excellent original acoustics." He adds: "We can once again invite major renowned orchestras because we have the appropriate stage and infrastructure." This also prompted Hungarian star pianist, András Schiff, to perform at the festival this year.
A musical home for everyone

blocks.caption: Juri de Marco founded a community choir in Bonn's Tannenbusch neighborhoodImage: Beethovenfest Bonn

blocks.text: The new hall is not only intended to make stars and major orchestras feel at home — the audience and local musicians ought to feel that way too. Indeed, for local musicians, there is a specially designed "Festival Salon" where local communities and bands can create their own programs. And anyone can come by and participate in the "Meet your band" project, which is an accessible, free program for people who otherwise wouldn't visit a classical concert hall.

The Beethovenfest also reaches out to people in neighborhoods across the city, right where they live. For over a year, as a part of this effort, Juri de Marco and the "Community Choir" have been encouraging people to sing and improvise, regardless of whether they can read music.

blocks.caption: Steven Walter addresses the topic of home not only in his music, but also in lectures and in discussion forumsImage: Bjorn Kietzmann/DW

blocks.text: "For me, home is more a feeling than it is a place. It's where you can rely on a genuine social network, where people notice when you are absent," says festival director Steven Walter. who has lived in various places around the world himself. "Everywhere I go, my sense of well-being depends on my social connections."
Beethoven reinterpreted

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1850, and died in Vienna in 1827. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of his death, and to celebrate it, pianist Kit Armstrong with conductor Jan Caeyers, along with his orchestra "Le Concert Olympique," are launching "Beethoven 27," a major Beethoven cycle. In nine concerts, they will present entirely new interpretations of Beethoven's nine symphonies, as well as his sonatas and piano concertos.

blocks.caption: 'Beethoven 27' is the name of the project in which Kit Armstrong plays the pianoImage: SALVATORE DI NOLFI/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: The first three concerts will be presented at this year's Beethovenfest. Caeyers has devoted himself to Beethoven not only as a conductor but also as a musicologist. He is the author of the acclaimed biography "Beethoven: A life." Even so, Caeyers says he is far from finished discovering the composer.

"Every time I immerse myself in Beethoven, new and unexpected doors open. That's what keeps me fascinated," Caeyers told DW. Pianist Kit Armstrong feels the same way. "There isn't just one Beethoven," he said. "There are countless images and perspectives of Beethoven, including many that emerged long after his death. Those perspectives should also inform the way we interpret his music today."
Spotlight on Georgia

This year's Beethovenfest artists will introduce music from their homelands. Among them are Senegalese kora player Momi Maiga and Palestinian-Syrian pianist Aeham Ahmad, who gained global renown for playing the piano amid the rubble of the Syrian civil war.

blocks.caption: Violinist Lisa Batiashvili also supports young talent from her native Georgia, including composer Tsotne Zedginidze Image: picture-alliance/dpa/P. Zinken

blocks.text: Violinist Lisa Batiashvili, who was born in Georgia, is this year's artist in residence at the Beethovenfest. Performing with the Dresden Philharmonic, she will present works from her homeland as part of the program "City Lights" — a personal tribute to Georgia, which the festival is spotlighting this year.

As part of the festival's long-running "Campus" youth exchange program, young musicians from Georgia and Germany will collaborate, with Beethoven's music being performed alongside works by leading Georgian composers. The entire ensemble will also perform Heinrich Schütz's five-part motet "Verleih uns Frieden gnädiglich" ("Grant Us Gracious Peace").

Musicians from Germany's National Youth Orchestra and the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra held their joint rehearsal residency in June, developing their own artistic vision and program for Beethovenfest. The project also explores how young artists see themselves in a country facing political turmoil, where the path toward Europe has repeatedly shifted course.

blocks.caption: During rehearsals in Tbilisi, conductor Mirian Khukhunaishvili (left) and composer Tsotne Zedginidze (right) discuss his new workImage: Beethovenfest

blocks.text: 17-year-old composer and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze is regarded as one of Georgia's most extraordinary young musical talents. He was commissioned to write the Campus project's new work.
Beyond classical music

Crossovers, musical fusion and new ideas for the future of music remain central to this year's Beethovenfest. Two musical worlds will come together with kora player Momi Maiga joining the string orchestra "Ensemble Resonanz" to improvise on Beethoven's music.

blocks.caption: Composer and performer Brittany J. Green combines sound, video, movement and text in her workImage: Adley Haywood

blocks.text: American composer Brittany J. Green will experiment with artificial intelligence and visual effects in her work "gLitchED dreams//invisible BEINGS." Performed with the music collective "Alarm Will Sound," the piece creates a sonic landscape inspired by the digital age. "We're looking for the Beethovens of our time," says Philipp Seliger, "including people who aren't necessarily composers of classical music."
The Beethovenfest runs from Sept 3 through Oct 3, 2026. DW is a media partner and co-shareholder of the festival.
