articles.title: Remulla: Sara Duterte’s camp to post bail in grave threats case
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte intends to post bail in the grave threats case against her on Friday, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla. In a text message,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte intends to post bail in the grave threats case against her on Friday, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.
In a text message, Remulla told the Inquirer that Duterte’s lawyers “confirmed that they received the warrant.”
“They intend to post bail ASAP (as soon as possible),” he noted.
In a statement earlier on Friday, Duterte’s legal counsel Paul Lawrence Lim said the Quezon City Regional Trial Court had issued a warrant to arrest Duterte for grave threats.
Duterte’s camp has yet to answer reporters’ queries on whether they would post bail.
The warrant sets bail at P120,000 each for three counts of grave threats in relation to Section 6 of Republic Act No. 10175 or the Cybercrime Prevention Act, for a total of P360,000.
Duterte was charged with grave threats by the National Bureau of Investigation last August.

The case stemmed from her statements against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez during a virtual press conference in November 2024./coa

articles.title: Ridon: Sara Duterte arrest case separate from impeachment
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said that the criminal case against Vice President Sara Duterte is separate from her impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said that the criminal case against Vice President Sara Duterte is separate from her impeachment proceedings, noting that the prosecution panel will continue to press on.

Ridon on Friday said that the arrest warrant against Duterte is “not, by itself, a determination of guilt” and that the vice president “will have every opportunity to present her defenses before the proper court.”
“The impeachment proceedings are a separate constitutional accountability process. The Senate Impeachment Court will independently determine the matters properly before it,” he said.

Ridon made the statement as Duterte’s lawyer announced that a warrant of arrest was issued by the Quezon City Regional Trial Court this Friday over Duterte’s grave threats case before the National Bureau of Investigation.

He said the prosecution team took note of Duterte’s counsel’s statement, saying that the vice president has no intention of evading the law and will avail herself of the legal remedies available to her.

Duterte’s warrant came as her impeachment trial before the Senate is ongoing. In her impeachment trial, the vice president is likewise accused of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust for allegedly making kill threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, among others./coa

articles.title: Bond yields are soaring to multi-decade highs. What does that mean for Canadian consumers?
articles.summary: The bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off, creating waves for consumers and investors alike. Here's what you need to know about how the bond market can affect you.

image.caption: Traders gather on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in this 2010 file photo. The bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off. (Richard Drew/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business
The bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off, creating waves for consumers and investors alike. Here's what you need to know about how the bond market can affect you.
Canadians can expect higher mortgage rates, stronger returns on GICs
With global bond yields surging to multi-decade highs, a previously mundane corner of the financial world is now a hot topic on Wall Street.

For the average Canadian, it means higher borrowing costs for some products, such as mortgages and auto loans, but also stronger returns on other products, such as other guaranteed investment certificates (GICs) and money market funds.

Let's start with the basics. When you buy a bond, you're effectively lending money for a predetermined amount of time to the issuer. That could be the federal government, provinces, municipalities or a private company. Investors are typically paid interest until the maturity date, when they get the face value of the bond back.

So, what's a bond yield? It's the annual return an investor earns from holding a bond, expressed as a percentage. After bonds are issued, they can be traded on the open market, causing their prices to shift. When bond prices drop, yields rise. This is because investors get the same interest payments for a lower buy-in price.

Until recently, the global bond market was pretty sleepy. That's because central bankers around the world kept interest rates at near-zero for more than a decade following the 2008 financial crisis. Now, a growing number of investors see rate hikes on the horizon as central banks look to tamp down sticky inflation.
When a central bank raises interest rates, newly issued bonds offer higher payouts, making existing lower-paying bonds less valuable.
Higher inflation puts pressure on central banks
Right now, the bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off. From the United States, to Germany, Japan and Canada, yields have jumped to multi-year or even multi-decade highs.

"What's going on there? Well, when you see a substantial movement, usually it's because there is more than one thing happening at once," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Wednesday, after the central bank's latest interest rate decision was announced.
Inflation fears and concerns about ballooning government debt are feeding expectations for the Bank of Canada and its global peers to raise their trend-setting interest rates.
"Central banks' tolerance for higher inflation is limited," said Macklem. "That is causing the market to build in the possibility of future interest rate hikes."

According to the latest Statistics Canada data, gas prices were a key driver of higher inflation in July. On Wednesday, the Bank of Canada said global oil prices are persistently high, with no end in sight for the U.S.-led war with Iran, which has disrupted seaborne crude traffic in the region. U.S. benchmark oil prices have soared nearly 60 per cent year-to-date.

items: Inflation risks rise with higher fuel costs and new U.S. tariffs, Bank of Canada governor warns
'Measured confidence': RBC, TD Bank, CIBC share optimistic outlook for Canada's economy

blocks.text: At the same time, the bank sees the Canada-U.S. trade war pushing up costs for businesses, which could feed into consumer prices over time. Macklem noted the AI infrastructure buildout is stoking demand for new corporate bond issuance, lowering prices for previously issued bonds.
"All those things are tending to work in the same direction to boost global bond yields," Macklem said.
Inflationary impact of counter-tariffs expected to be 'relatively modest': Bank of Canada governor
Canada's 10-year government bond yield hit a two-year high on Wednesday, after the Bank of Canada signalled inflation risks are rising.

Because Canadian banks can invest risk-free with the government, government bond yields set the floor for all other lending. Fixed-rate mortgages, auto loans and other forms of credit are linked to five-year and 10-year government bonds, meaning the higher the yields for those bonds are, the higher the banks set their interest rates for those loans.
For those looking to invest their savings, rising bond yields force banks to raise their GIC rates to stay competitive, boosting guaranteed returns.
'A good time to lock in your mortgage'
True North Mortgage founder and CEO Dan Eisner says savvy borrowers are locking in rates.

"Fixed mortgage rates won't drop substantially until yields do. Yields aren't likely to enter a sustained downward trend unless signs of deeper economic softening gain momentum and inflation pressures ease," Eisner wrote in a blog post on Wednesday.

"It's a good time to lock in your mortgage rate if you're looking to buy a home or renew your mortgage, as fixed rate movement is likely to resemble a rollercoaster for the next while, or at least until we see some clarity on geopolitical activity and U.S. trade."

Google Trends data show Canadians are taking a keen interest in the ongoing bond market upheaval. The volume of inquiries about the bond market over the past month is up 5,000 per cent on a yearly basis, according to the search engine giant.
No 'dysfunction' in Canada's bond market
Macklem said while there has been some "spillover" from higher global yields into Canada's bond market, Canada's yield curve sits well below that of U.S. government bonds.

Speaking at Wednesday's press conference in Ottawa, Bank of Canada Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers reassured investors that Canada's bond market, while affected by global trends, is not necessarily in dangerous territory.
"I think it's important to distinguish between volatility and dysfunction or instability when prices and yields are moving, because investors are repricing risk," she told reporters.

"The vulnerability that we have talked about in our previous financial stability reports really comes when you get leveraged investors unwinding their positions quickly, and liquidity starts to dry up," she added, referring to investors such as hedge funds and non-bank asset managers who use borrowed money to fund their investment strategies.
"That's the risk we worry about. We don't see that happening right now."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: Mark Critch promises a 'very special' send-off for Son of a Critch
articles.summary: The cast of Son of a Critch is reflecting on how they’ve all grown over five seasons of working together ahead of it's final season.

blocks.text: Entertainment
The cast of Son of a Critch is reflecting on how they’ve all grown over five seasons of working together ahead of it's final season.
The CBC comedy is back for its fifth and final season on Sept. 8
Son of a Critch says goodbye with Season 5
It's the beginning of the end for Son of a Critch, and Mark Critch is promising fans a send-off worth waiting for.
"I was quite happy with the way it ended. I think the last episode is gonna be very, very special. Maybe my favourite part of the whole series," he told CBC News.

The beloved CBC comedy is back for its fifth and final season Sept. 8, returning for one last trip to Newfoundland. Based on Critch's bestselling memoir, the eight-time CSA nominated show follows him through the chaos of growing up in '80s St. John's.
The show may be built on memories of his past, but Critch — who plays his own father — said he has "made so many new memories I'll cherish forever with this group of people."

In this final season, Mark's last year of high school collides with Newfoundland's cod moratorium. As his world is thrown into chaos, he navigates messy first love, changing friendships and family turmoil — all while chasing his dream of becoming an actor.
Benjamin Evan Ainsworth, who stars as young Critch, has spent nearly a third of his life playing the role — something he calls a "terrific journey."
Fans may recognize him from season three of HBO's House of the Dragon. He's also set to star as Link in the live-action The Legend of Zelda movie.

"It's really exciting. We've just filmed in New Zealand, and so I'm really excited to see kind of where that goes," he told CBC News, adding that he's proud of how the show wraps up and is "just really happy to be back here ... to come to such a familiar place with familiar people."
End of an era
For the rest of the cast, it also felt like the end of an era.
"I think it's the feeling of, like, all those years that you went to summer camp and now you're finally too old to go to summer camp anymore," said Claire Rankin, who plays Mary, Critch's mother.

"You know, you have to let that go, but it doesn't mean you have to let those friendships go. And so I think we'll all walk away with these incredible relationships and memories that last a lifetime."
That connection became even more personal for Rankin when she began hearing stories from locals about the woman she had been playing.

"There's quite a few people in St. John's who knew Mark's mom and knew her well," she told CBC News. "It was all these tiny moments that I would get these little glimpses of who Mary was through other people's eyes as well. And — and to know that they somehow saw enough of that in me was really — it was really good for my soul."
Endorsement from a Hollywood heavyweight

Rounding out the family tree is screen icon Malcolm McDowell. Known for his roles in A ClockWork Orange, if.... and Star Trek: Generations, McDowell plays Critch's grandfather — a role he calls one of the "absolute fondest memories" of any show he's done.
"And, you know, I'm at the end of my career — towards the end, you know, I'm getting up there. So, to finish, you know, doing something like this for five years was a real blessing."
Malcolm McDowell calls Son of a Critch one of his 'absolute fondest memories'
McDowell also puts Critch among the greats.

"I'm in awe of his writing, and I've done some pretty damn good writers in my career, you know, and he's up there with the very, very best," McDowell said. "I've loved it. I've loved every minute of it."
The fifth and final season of Son of a Critch premieres Sept. 8 on CBC and CBC Gem.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: German far-right party could use win in upcoming state election to try to overhaul key aspects of society
articles.summary: Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is soaring in popularity in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. It could form government in an upcoming regional election and become the first…

image.caption: Thousands gather in Quedlinburg, Germany, on Aug. 23 to support the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. The party is soaring in opinion polls in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where an election will be held on Sunday. (Malte Broyer/CBC)

blocks.text: On a warm August afternoon in the quiet eastern German town of Quedlinburg, thousands gathered to hear what a popular far-right leader had to say about the country's future.

Many came on their Simson motorcycles, which have become a cultural symbol for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, to meet Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's candidate to lead the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The party is soaring in opinion polls and in a regional election on Sunday, it could become the first far-right party to hold state power in Germany since the Second World War.

Experts say the AfD would gain significant political leverage over state resources in areas such as education, where it hopes to achieve goals such as creating separate classrooms for refugees, normalizing relations with Russia through student exchange programs and promoting a patriotism agenda that includes focusing less on the country's Nazi past.
"I think [Siegmund] speaks from his heart, from our hearts," Luca Stemmler, 17, said during the gathering in Quedlinburg.
"He's an idol for me."

Across the street from the motorcycle rally, counter-protesters waved rainbow flags and sang All You Need Is Love by The Beatles — a show of solidarity against a party some fear will challenge basic human rights and overhaul key aspects of Germany's postwar democratic order.

"I think this is something that might have ripple effects throughout Germany, throughout the European Union and thus also on a global stage," said Marcus Böick, a University of Cambridge historian who is from Saxony-Anhalt.
"Once they're in power, it's very hard to get rid of them."
How the AfD could hold state power

The country's major political parties refuse to collaborate with extremist parties in a strategy known as "the firewall," which is meant to safeguard Germany's postwar democracy. If opinion polls translate to votes — which experts say is possible, but not certain — the other parties may not be able to block the AfD out of the state government.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD is leading in opinion polls at 42 per cent, according to German election research company Infratest-Dimap, which surveyed 1,511 eligible voters online and over the phone between Aug. 24 and 25.
The party also leads national opinion polls at 28 per cent, according to Infratest-Dimap, and secured the second highest number of seats in the 2025 federal election.

The AfD began in 2013 as an anti-Euro party, but shifted its focus to issues surrounding migration in 2015, when then chancellor Angela Merkel welcomed hundreds of thousands of refugees from countries such as Syria into Germany.
Germany’s AfD party, explained
What are the AfD's goals?

The AfD calls for "remigration," a term often used in right-wing circles to refer to mass deportations of people who come from a migration background. In Saxony-Anhalt, it promises to ban immigration from non-European Union countries it deems problematic, establish hundreds of detention centres for deportees and create separate classrooms for refugee children.

Akinola Sanyaolu, who moved to Saxony-Anhalt's capital city of Magdeburg six years ago from Nigeria, says many people he works with blame immigrants for the country's political or economic problems. He said he's experienced many instances of racism in the city, but tries to remain positive because he wants to stay in the country where he's built a home.
"I feel attacked, but what can I do?" said Sanyaolu.
"They are not in my shoes. They don't know what it is to be a foreigner. I know what it is. I'm the one feeling it."
States have autonomy in many areas including environment, education, cultural policy and policing.

The Saxony-Anhalt AfD lists its specific goals in a lengthy government manifesto. They include banning Pride flags in schools and revising the state's history curricula to focus more on what it says are the positive aspects of Germany's past.
The party also defines a "healthy family" as a father, mother and children.
I would say, 'Make Saxony-Anhalt great again.'- Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, AfD politician in Saxony-Anhalt

Anki Wolf and Miriam Siemon recently got engaged, but their celebrations have been tainted by fear of rising political extremism. The lesbian couple live part-time in the state's small city of Dessau and they want to have kids. But they question whether it's safe to raise a family in Germany while fighting increasing homophobia.
"What is happening when there is a child involved? Can I say with my heart, I can stay here and I can protect this child?" said Wolf.
How far right is the AfD?
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is designated as right-wing extremist by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which monitors extremist threats.
Party members have come under fire for using language associated with Nazi groups and experts say many have ties to far-right, ethnonationalist movements.

If the AfD holds state power it could control state-level domestic intelligence services, which is reportedly raising concerns in part due to the party's ties to Russia. Party lawmakers have reportedly praised and visited the country, and in the Saxony-Anhalt AfD's government manifesto, it states that it has a strong interest in good relations with Russia both "economically and culturally."

A few days before the motorcycle rally, hundreds of AfD supporters congregated in the town of Querfurt. Many lined up for hours to get a signed T-shirt with Siegmund's face on the front. The polished 35-year-old is from a small town in Saxony-Anhalt and has more than 800,000 TikTok followers.
"Here, no one is a right-wing extremist," he said in German to his supporters at the festival.
"Here, everyone is extremely in their right."
Why is the AfD so popular?

While far-right populism has been rising in other European countries, what makes Germany unique is a lingering divide between the country's west and east, where AfD support is the strongest, said Böick, who researches modern German history.
LISTEN | How a regional election in Germany is testing the country's postwar firewall:
Front Burner30:48Is Germany's firewall against the far right crumbling?

Citizens in the formerly communist East Germany were promised increased freedoms through reunification, but inequality and unemployment remained rampant after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Many in the east left for job opportunities in the west, said Böick.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a member of the governing CDU, is also facing widespread unpopularity.

If people are dissatisfied with mainstream political parties and are also dealing with political uncertainty fuelled by international wars and economic instability, they may feel motivated to vote for something new, said Oliver Schmidtke, former director of the Centre for Global Studies at the University of Victoria.
The party also has support from outside political actors. In 2025, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance publicly criticized Germany's firewall strategy and Elon Musk endorsed the party.

Saxony-Anhalt AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is often described by experts as the brain behind the party's cultural policies. He told reporters at a family festival he hosted in the town of Querfurt, his voting district, that he's inspired by U.S. President Donald Trump.
"I would say 'Make Saxony-Anhalt great again,'" said Tillschneider.
What happens if the AfD wins?

Some experts worry the AfD's potential success could also increase the party's leverage federally. If it holds state power, it will sit in the Bundesrat, the second federal legislative chamber representing the country's 16 states. There, it could try to undermine attempts to pass legislation, said Schmidtke.

Schmidtke said Germany's robust constitution would make it difficult for the AfD to make sweeping changes, but winning a state election would further normalize the party as a legitimate political force.

items: As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
65 years after the Berlin Wall was built, Germany’s east-west scars help feed a rising far-right party

blocks.text: If the AfD secures the highest number of votes on Sunday but is blocked out of government by the other political parties, Böick said it could use this outcome to its advantage.
"This leads to their own narrative of being victimized, of being mistreated, of being undemocratically mistreated," said Böick.
"I think both ways they will win. This is the hard truth."

articles.title: South Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claims

South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military…

blocks.text: South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Donald Trump over Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.

Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reportspublished on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing have not been agreed.

But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.

An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”

According to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.
One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.
Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.
South Korea is highly dependent on the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.

blocks.caption: The office of South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, said ‘nothing related to the matter has been decided’ in response to the media reports. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: In 2020, the government of the then president Moon Jae-in expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.

South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.

The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran, claiming in August that South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationing tens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.
Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back, shortening the drills by six days.

Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US had restricted intelligence sharing with South Korea, and by a dispute over a data breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.
Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signals openness to another meeting with Kim Jong-un.

articles.title: Labour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations after undercover report – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Two key aides to Nigel Farage have stepped down pending an internal investigation

Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, has said that James Orr and Dan…

blocks.text: Two aides suspended over donations allegations have 'no chance of coming back', says Reform UK's chair Lee Anderson

Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, has said that James Orr and Dan Jukes – the two aides primarily involved in the apparent plot exposed by an undercover investigation to evade electoral law – were suspended and won’t be coming back.
In an interview on Sky News this morning, Anderson said:
double quotation mark[Orr and Jukes] were told they had to step down. They have stepped down. And that’s got to be the right thing to do.

The presenter, Kamali Melbourne, put it to Anderson that Orr, head of policy at the party, and Jukes, a key aide to Nigel Farage, were both very important figures in the party and asked if there was any chance they could “come back”. Anderson replied:

double quotation markNo, there’s no chance of them coming back. They’ve stepped aside. We’re a serious party, you know, and sometimes in politics, you have to make tough decisions, harsh decisions. I think this probably was an easier decision, being given the option to stand down. They have gone. Like I said, they’ve left the building and our focus now is on the conference today.
Key events

items: nowAnderson says Farage won't quit over undercover report into donations, and 'country needs him'
16m agoTwo aides suspended over donations allegations have 'no chance of coming back', says Reform UK's chair Lee Anderson
28m agoFarage personally has 'serious questions to answer' over alleged Reform UK plot to evade electoral law, Ed Davey says
39m agoLabour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations, as two party aides involved step down

blocks.text: Anderson says Farage won't quit over undercover report into donations, and 'country needs him'

In a separate interview, on Times Radio, Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, insisted there was no chance of Nigel Farage resigning over the undercover investigation into party donations.
Anderson said:

double quotation markI don’t think Nigel has got any questions on this. The two people involved, they have gone. They have left the building. I keep saying this time and time again. They have gone. That is the right thing to do. They are not coming back and Nigel is going nowhere … Nigel is an honest man. I have known him for many years now. The party has done the right thing by launching this investigation. Nigel will be on the main stage later on explaining our first 100 days in government. He is not going anywhere. The country needs him.

While James Orr and Dan Jukes are the main focus of the investigation, the film shown by Channel 4 News suggests Farage himself also had some knowledge of the proposal for a US-based supporter to donate £500,000 to the party by channelling it through his UK-based son. Foreigners are not allowed to donate to UK political parties, and donating via proxies in this manner is also banned.
Farage is filmed attending an oyster bar lunch where he thought he was meeting the father and son. But the ‘son’ was an undercover reporter, and the ‘father’ an actor hired to play the part.
After discussion of how the money from the UK might be given to the party via the son, Farage is recorded telling them: “Thank you both.”
Farage personally has 'serious questions to answer' over alleged Reform UK plot to evade electoral law, Ed Davey says

Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, says Nigel Farage was ultimately responsible for the apparent attempt to evade electoral law on donations exposed by the undercover investigation shown on Channel 4 News.
In a post on social media this morning, he says:
double quotation markSo much for this being a “hoax” then. Clearly very serious questions for Farage to answer given his role in the meeting. The buck stops with him.

Davey was referring to the way Reform UK, in its first response to the undercover report last night, said it had “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors”.
Labour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations, as two party aides involved step down

Good morning. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, is speaking on the main day of his party’s conference in Birmingham. It has been a bad summer for the party. After having a large lead over the other parties in opinion polls for over a year, the lead collapsed after Andy Burnham became PM, and now Reform UK and Labour are basically neck and neck. Farage has been embroiled in the scandal over his failure to declare a £5m donation. And last night, on the eve of Farage’s big speech, Channel 4 News broadcast the findings of a long, undercover investigation showing leading Reform UK figures apparently plotting to evade UK law on electoral donations.
Here is Rowena Mason’s story.
You can read the Channel 4 News write-up here. But to fully appreciate how strong the evidence against Reform UK is, it is best to watch the half-hour report in full.
There are two developments this morning.

items: Reform UK says the two senior Reform officials most implicated in the apparent plot to evade electoral law are stepping down pending an investigation. In a statement released about half an hour ago, a Reform UK spokesperson said:

blocks.text: double quotation markReform UK has launched an investigation following the broadcast of a Channel 4 News programme. Both individuals involved have stepped down from their respective positions pending the outcome of the investigation. The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing.
This is a reference to James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage.

items: The Labour party has written to the Metropolitan police calling for a criminal investigation. In her letter to Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, says:

blocks.text: double quotation markWe … believe there is a proper basis for a police investigation into whether offences under PPERA [Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000] have been committed, including, but not necessarily limited to: (a) offences under section 61(1) concerning evasion of restrictions on donations; (b) any offence arising from knowingly providing false information to, or withholding material information from, the registered treasurer in circumstances falling within section 61(2); (c) any offence arising from Reform UK’s acceptance or retention of impermissible donations, including the £32,500 of polling expenditure, if the evidential and reporting facts establish the necessary elements; and (d) any related offence concerning the accuracy or completeness of statutory donation returns. We understand that political finance matters also fall within the regulatory remit of the Electoral Commission. We are not suggesting that a police investigation should displace the commission’s role; rather, given the apparent possibility of criminal conduct, we believe the allegations should be brought formally to the attention of the police so that the appropriate authorities can determine the proper investigative route.
Here is the agenda for the day.

11.05am: The main day of Reform UK’s conference opens with tributes to Ann Widdecombe. After that the main speakers on the stage are chief whip Lee Anderson at 11.30am; Welsh leader Dan Thomas at 11.45am; home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf at noon; Jordon Bardella, president of the French National Rally party at 12.30pm: Matt Goodwin at 3pm; Sarah Pochin MP at 3.15pm; deputy leader Richard Tice at 3.30pm: and Nigel Farage at 3.50pm. There are also fringe meetings through the day.
1pm: Farage and Bardella hold a press conference.
Afternoon: Kemi Badenoch is on a visit in West Sussex.

I will be blogging until around lunchtime, and then colleagues will be taking over. I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. articles.title: Meloni government becomes longest-serving in postwar Italy
articles.summary: The hard-right government has officially beaten the record set by media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi. Meloni and her party are using the opportunity to celebrate and also rally for the 2027 election.

image.caption: Meloni and her far-right Brothers of Italy (Fdl) party are planning a celebration on Friday evening in the port city of Bari [FILE: Jul 20, 2026]Image: Stefano Costantino/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: The right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni on Friday became the longest-serving since the Italian Republic was established 80 years ago.
Meloni's government, the most-right wing to have ruled Italy since World War II, has been in charge for 1,413 days.

That's one day more than billionaire media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi, who still holds the record for collectively serving longest as prime minister with nine years in office, albeit under different governments.
Since Italy became a republic after the end of the war, it has had 68 governments within 80 years, with governments lasting around 13 months on average.
How is Meloni celebrating her record tenure?
Meloni and her far-right Brothers of Italy (Fdl) party are planning a celebration on Friday in the port city of Bari in the southern Puglia region.
Some 80 coaches will transport supporters there, with Meloni due to address the gathering in the evening.
Deputy Prime Ministers Matteo Salvini and Antonio Tajani are also due to appear via video link. The event is effectively an opportunity to campaign for Italy's 2027 election.
What does the Meloni government and its supporters say?
The Meloni government boasts one million extra people in employment in its four years in power, unemployment below 6% as well as a €21 billion ($24 billion) reduction in personal income taxes.
They are also especially proud of what they say is a sharp decline in migrant arrivals.
The prime minister, whose party has neo-Fascist roots, also says Italy's influence on the world stage has grown.

Meloni's nationalist streak was celebrated at home on more than one occasion. One notable example was when US President Donald Trump, with whom the Italian leader had initially and unusually enjoyed a cordial relationship, said she had begged him for a photo.
"Italy doesn't beg," Meloni said of Trump's claim, much to the satisfaction of many Italians.
Trump-Meloni feud escalating
What do Meloni's critics say?
Critics of Italy's first female prime minister and her longest-serving government however argue that despite the numbers, the country's persistent problems remain.
They list weak productivity, demographic decline and long-standing inefficiencies in healthcare, education and public administration. The rising cost of living is also a major criticism.

"Have wages increased? No. Petrol costs more, job insecurity has increased, people are retiring less and the healthcare system is functioning less effectively," Maurizio Landini, head of the CGIL trade union, said ahead of the celebrations.
Italian unions strike to protest new budget priorities

Parallel to the Meloni party in Bari, her opponents are also planning a gathering across the city. Organizers accuse her government of creating a "war and weapons economy" and a "police state," as well as fueling a climate of hate against migrants.
Meanwhile, others think the prime minister strayed from her election campaign and has become too moderate, including a potential challenger in the coming vote.
Retired army general Roberto Vannacci, whose party is further to the far right than Meloni's, is known for hard-line positions on immigration and national identity.
Polls show his party has overtaken both the anti-immigrant League and right-wing Forza Italia parties, both members of Meloni's ruling coalition.

articles.title: PNP studying possible amendments to SIM Registration Law
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it was studying possible amendments to Republic Act No. 11934 or the Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) Registration Law. “The…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it was studying possible amendments to Republic Act No. 11934 or the Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) Registration Law.

“The PNP is ready to provide its insights and data that will push for the amendment of the law, making it more effective when it comes to crime prevention,” the agency’s chief, Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., said in a statement.
“I have directed our legal team to look into this and make the necessary recommendations,” he noted.

The top cop’s instruction came after concerns raised by the Anti-Cybercrime Group (ACG) about frequent arrests of individuals allegedly selling pre-registered SIM cards and the possibility that pre-registered SIM cards are being used in cybercrimes.
The ACG made this pronouncement last week, while detailing the arrest of a 26-year-old man in Obando, Bulacan, for the alleged illegal sale of 400 pre-registered SIM cards.

“Innovations in digital technology are fast evolving, and we really need to keep up [with] more efficient and effective approaches in running after illegal activities and eventually make cyberspace safe for every Filipino,” Nartatez explained./coa

In a statement, lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim said, “Today, the Quezon City RTC has issued a warrant of arrest against the vice president.”
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Lim added.
Lim is Duterte’s counsel in her National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) grave threats cases.

articles.title: NBI considers ethics complaint vs. Leviste after trafficking raps
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is considering filing an ethics complaint against Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste before the House of Representatives next week,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is considering filing an ethics complaint against Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste before the House of Representatives next week, Director Melvin Matibag said on Friday.

Matibag said this after announcing that the bureau will file on Friday afternoon “qualified human trafficking” charges against the congressman and six others after completing its investigation into the supposed “honey trap” plot against Executive Secretary Ralph Recto.
“Next week we will be considering also filing […] a case to the ethics committee of the House of Representatives against Congressman Leandro Leviste,” Matibag noted in an ambush interview on Friday.
The NBI director said he does not know Leviste’s exact current location but noted that he is “definitely still out of the country.”
“Last time that we monitored him, he was in France; hindi ko lang alam ngayon kung nasaan na siya,” he said.
(Last time that we monitored him, he was in France; I just don’t know where he is now.)
The Inquirer reached out to Leviste regarding the matter, but he has yet to respond as of this writing.
Last August 6, Matibag and the Bureau of Immigration confirmed in separate statements that Leviste and his mother, Sen. Loren Legarda, have left the country through separate flights on August 2.
Leviste was implicated by a nabbed talent manager—Alias Ken—as the alleged “financer” in the “honey trap plot” against Recto.

Aside from Leviste, Negros Oriental Rep. Jacinto “Jing” Paras, alias Ken, and four lawyers from the Rondain and Mendiola Law Firm who were supposedly tasked to create fabricated statements against Recto were implicated.
The congressman and other implicated individuals have since denied Alias Ken’s allegations of a supposed plot against the executive secretary./coa

articles.title: DENR eyes monitoring system for endangered Samar Rafflesia flower
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Samar Island Natural Park (DENR-SINP) is developing a Biodiversity Monitoring System (BMS) to conserve the endangered Samar…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Samar Island Natural Park (DENR-SINP) is developing a Biodiversity Monitoring System (BMS) to conserve the endangered Samar Rafflesia (Rafflesia manillana) in Basey, Samar.
The initiative follows the rediscovery and documentation of the rare flowering plant in Sitio Bagong Silang, Barangay Guirang in Basey town, about 15 years after it was last recorded there.
DENR is also collaborating with experts on further research about the specie.

The Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) – SINP said in a statement on Friday that the monitoring system will provide a more systematic way to track the rare plant, its habitat and potential threats to its survival.

“The DENR-SINP also plans to work with experts to generate additional scientific information that could guide conservation measures for the specie, including its habitat requirements and relationship with its host vine,” the agency stated.
A DENR-SINP team documented 24 visible buds and flowers, including one fully bloomed flower, during surveys conducted in the upland area of Guirang village on May 26-28 and June 9-11.
According to available records, the site is currently the only confirmed location of Rafflesia manillana.

“The 2026 documentation is significant because it confirms that Rafflesia manillana continues to survive in its natural habitat after approximately 15 years without a known documented record,” the DENR-SINP added.
The Samar Rafflesia is endemic to Samar and is classified as endangered under DENR Administrative Order 2026-20.
To complement scientific monitoring, the PAMO-SINP, in partnership with Basey’s local government unit, recently conducted a communication, education, and public awareness campaign.
The activity is meant to encourage residents to help protect the specie and its habitat.
Residents were briefed on the ecological importance and conservation status of the Rafflesia, and its dependence on a specific forest habitat and host vine.
DENR officials said disturbing surrounding vegetation could threaten the plant’s survival.
The awareness campaign highlighted threat indicators near the Rafflesia habitat, such as signs of illegal timber poaching and human activities that could cause forest degradation.
Residents were encouraged to report activities that could threaten the Rafflesia and its habitat.

Experts also discussed Republic Act 11038, or the Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System Act of 2018, which prohibits unauthorized activities that may damage protected habitats and wildlife.

The DENR-SINP emphasized that ongoing monitoring, research and collaboration with conservation experts and local communities are crucial for creating long-term measures to protect the Samar Rafflesia. /apl

articles.title: How Volkswagen's huge workforce became a costly burden
articles.summary: The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV…

image.caption: VW has 60% more employees than Toyota, which makes a similar number of carsImage: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volkswagen has built one of the largest workforces in the global auto industry.
At nearly 630,000 people — 680,000 if you count joint ventures in China — VW employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, 140% more than Stellantis and nearly 240% more than Ford.

That headcount was once a sign of Germany's industrial might and VW's huge profits. Now, it's become a massive burden, one that's forcing the company to make painful job cuts to survive against agile Chinese competitors.

After already trimming thousands of positions last year as profits came under pressure, Volkswagen is now preparing to slash 50,000 additional jobs worldwide, including tens of thousands in Germany. The proposal got the backing of the VW Supervisory Board on Thursday, September 2.
VW also wants to close four German factories, a plan that the supervisory board on Thursday stopped short of agreeing to implement right away.

These cuts include VW luxury brands like Porsche and Audi. Other German automakers and suppliers are facing similar pressures. Mercedes-Benz is planning to cut several thousand jobs, and suppliers like Bosch have announced large cost savings.
How VW got to this point
Much of VW's headcount issue stems from long-standing strategic decisions.

Meghan Ostertag, an analyst for economic policy at the US-based Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, says VW's much larger workforce was needed because the firm chose to control more stages of production than its peers.

"The company makes many of its components and software internally, increasing the demand for labor and, of course, labor costs," Ostertag told DW, adding that factory expenses in Germany can be "up to twice those of the competition."
Other experts point to an aggressive acquisition strategy over the years, which brought brands including Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti into the VW fold — not to mention several truck makers.

"That strategy worked to some extent, but the complexities of integrating all those brands, supply chains and different designs make VW very complicated to operate," Daniel Harrison, senior automotive analyst at the London-based Ultima Media, told DW.
Can Volkswagen's 'legacy' help restore its former glory?
Why the VW model broke
Although Volkswagen survived the 2015 Dieselgate emissions scandal without suffering lasting financial damage, the company incurred massive costs and soon faced a new set of problems.

The company was slow to transition its production to electric vehicles (EVs) — just as Chinese EV makers gained serious traction and a technological edge. That delay contributed to slower sales in China, which accounted for a third of total VW sales, as well as softening demand in Europe and other key markets.

VW also repeated a mistake made by the US auto industry decades earlier. In the 1960s and 1970s, the Big Three — Ford, GM, and Chrysler (now part of Stellantis) — were bloated and slow to adapt when Japanese and European competitors began eating into their market share.
By the time US carmakers shifted toward leaner production methods, a decade had passed, and they had fallen significantly behind, noted Ostertag.
Toyota, which produces a similar number of vehicles as VW, operates with nearly half the workers by relying more on suppliers, higher automation, and a simpler management structure.

blocks.caption: Four German plants, including this one at Zwickau, are facing closureImage: AAPimages/Wehnert/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a research note, auto industry analyst Matthias Schmidt pointed to another factor: the "stranglehold" that trade unions and a key shareholder have over VW. This, he said, had helped cause "years of neglect in readjusting workforce numbers."

The northern German state of Lower Saxony — home to Volkswagen's global headquarters in Wolfsburg — holds 20% of voting rights in the company, can veto major decisions, and has previously pressured executives not to close plants or lay off staff, notably during the Dieselgate and COVID supply chain crises. It's ramping up the pressure this time, too.
Over the decades, Germany's powerful unions, meanwhile, have repeatedly held out for high wage increases and generous benefits, which have made VW staff among the best-paid autoworkers in the world.

blocks.caption: With plants in Thailand and Brazil, China's BYD opening a factory in HungaryImage: Jin Haoyuan/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Is VW's turnaround plan enough?
Analysts warn that the company may have to cut more than the annual €4 billion the firm hopes to save to secure its future.

The current proposals to cut 50,000 additional jobs, they say, will bring savings and help improve short-term profitability. But VW's underlying cost base and slow decision-making culture mean deeper, more radical reforms may well be needed.

VW should "invest more heavily in automation," Ostertag told DW, adding that it would allow the carmaker to "better compete with leaner firms," such as China's BYD, one of the fastest-growing EV brands in Europe.

Analysts say VW has lagged peers in plant automation levels but has stepped up investments in robotics and digital upgrades for its EV production. The company is also planning its first sub-€20,000 EV next year.

With China responsible for around 30% of VW's global vehicle output, Harrison predicts more production shifts to Asia and the potential to share VW's European plants with Chinese EV producers, a move previously seen as "unthinkable."
Chinese EV maker BYD goes Europe
German government, EU offer a lifeline
On the policy front, the German government is providing subsidies and loans for domestic EV battery plants to help cut reliance on Chinese imports.

The European Union, meanwhile, is advancing the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA is meant to boost the bloc's competitiveness and shield strategic industries from unfair competition from China.
The EU has already imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese-made EVs. But they are far below the 100% levies that the US charges, which have largely shut Chinese competitors out of the US auto market.
Historian Niall Ferguson from Harvard University warned that Europe has been slow to respond to China's strategy of giving huge subsidies to EV makers that help undercut European rivals.
"Unless there's radical change, I predict: Europeans will be driving Chinese cars on a massive scale very soon," Ferguson told Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper earlier this year.

During the same interview, economist Moritz Schularick, President of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, suggested using market access as leverage — only allowing Chinese brands to sell in Europe if they produce locally.
Schularick responded provocatively when questioned on VW's long-term future, predicting that Germany's auto giant would "likely be bought by a Chinese car maker like BYD."
Editor's note: The article, originally published on July 7, 2026, has been updated to include the VW Supervisory Board's backing for a restructuring plan calling for an additional 50,000 job cuts.
Are AI-powered robots German carmaker BMW's future?

articles.title: 100 influencers invited to US Open spark debate on 'tennis etiquette'
articles.summary: The behaviour of influencers and content creators has become a major talking point at this year's US Open amid incidents of matches being disrupted.

blocks.text: Lights. Camera. Quiet please...
When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.
Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes.
As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.
Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.
Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette.
"I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said.
"But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans.
"I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."
During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.
The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.
When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet.
"Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said.
"I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly.
"I think it bothered my opponent, too."
In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop.
"I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said.
"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette.

"It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match.
"Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport.
"I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."
Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.
Some players love it. Some do not.
Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing.
"I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said.
"The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing.
"I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."
American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York.
"I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said.
"All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that.
"I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."
American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful".
"I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said.
"But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.
"People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful.
"I think it's become a little too much this year.
"I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."
The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.

A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.
It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".

Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today.
"The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."

Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".
The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport".
"We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added.
"We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

articles.title: ICYMI: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Week 9 highlights
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Education chief of staff Michael Poa, now part of Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team, was declared a hostile witness for the prosecution as the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Education chief of staff Michael Poa, now part of Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team, was declared a hostile witness for the prosecution as the Senate impeachment court examined how P112.5 million in confidential funds was spent during Duterte’s tenure as education secretary.
His testimony on Day 21 on Sept. 2 followed two Philippine Army officers who questioned DepEd’s use of military certifications to justify its confidential fund expenses.
The prosecution, meanwhile, is weighing whether to drop the bribery allegations under Article III to speed up the trial and proceed to the unexplained wealth allegations under Article II.

The developments came as senator-judges also discussed the 16-vote threshold for conviction or acquittal, while the Senate adjusted its schedule to accommodate impeachment proceedings alongside budget hearings and plenary sessions.
Key developments

items: Col. Manaros Boransing II testified that the Philippine Army received no regular or confidential funds from Duterte’s offices for the 2023 Youth Leadership Summit and Information Education Communication activities.
Col. Magtangol Panopio said his certification only confirmed that the Army conducted youth summits in its area of operations and did not validate how DepEd spent its confidential funds.
Panopio said he personally considered it improper for DepEd to use his certification to support its confidential fund liquidation.
Both officers said they were shocked to learn during a House committee hearing in October 2024 that DepEd had cited Army programs to justify its confidential fund expenses.

Presiding Officer Francis Escudero barred witnesses from bringing earpieces, mobile phones, smartwatches and similar communication devices while testifying after the court determined that a viral image allegedly showing a witness wearing an earpiece was AI-generated.
Sen. Vicente Sotto III said names appearing on acknowledgment receipts can be considered aliases only if there is a real person behind them. Otherwise, they should be treated as fictitious names.
The Senate impeachment court declared Poa a hostile witness for the prosecution, allowing prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. to ask leading questions.
Poa was called to testify on the disbursement of P112.5 million in DepEd confidential funds during Duterte’s tenure as education secretary from 2022 to 2024.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison criticized the prosecution’s 13-point offer of testimony, saying it sounded like rhetoric intended to add drama to the proceedings.

Poa acknowledged that he could potentially face personal liability if Duterte is found guilty of misusing confidential funds, but maintained that he had no personal knowledge of how the money was spent.
He said he only learned during a House committee hearing in October 2024 that confidential funds had been handed to officials of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group.
Poa also confirmed that not a single peso from DepEd’s confidential funds went to the military’s Youth Leadership Summits.
The court reprimanded lawyers over a prolonged exchange during Poa’s testimony, with Escudero urging them to avoid wasting time.
Outside the court, the prosecution panel said it was considering dropping Article III, which covers alleged bribery involving DepEd procurement officials, to expedite the impeachment trial.
Lead public prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro said no final decision had been made but that proceeding directly to Article II, the unexplained wealth allegations, was being seriously considered.
Rep. Joel Chua said dropping the article would be a matter of prioritization rather than weakness, citing a similar move during the impeachment trial of former Chief Justice Renato Corona.

The prosecution also received bank documents and tax records involving Duterte, her husband Manases Carpio and associated companies. Rep. Terry Ridon described these as the final key pillar of evidence for the unexplained wealth allegations.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri confirmed that some senator-judges had discussed the possibility of revisiting the 16-vote threshold needed to convict or acquit Duterte.
The Senate also approved a scheduling arrangement allowing budget hearings and plenary sessions to proceed alongside afternoon impeachment proceedings.
Escudero separately floated holding whole-day impeachment sessions in October, with the trial potentially suspended in November to make way for the Senate’s legislative calendar. /dp

articles.title: Nepal: Two pulled alive from tunnel nine days after floods
articles.summary: Crews are racing to find hundreds more people still believed to be trapped after a glacier collapse triggered floods that killed more than 1,200 people.

image.caption: Rescue workers are racing to find hundreds of people still missing in the aftermath of the floods in NepalImage: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

blocks.text: Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after catastrophic floods swept through the country's border region with China.
Emergency teams are continuing efforts to reach hundreds more believed trapped inside similar tunnels.

The men, identified as mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah and mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, were freed from the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station's tunnel along the Trishuli River, according to a statement from the office of Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha.

"As long as there is breath, there is hope!" Shrestha said in a statement. "Rescue operations are continuing in all the affected tunnels. Let everyone's efforts and prayers continue. We have not lost hope."
What do we know about the rescue?
Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, authorities said.

blocks.caption: The two survivors rescued from the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project were flown to KathmanduImage: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

blocks.text: Video and photos showed Maharjan, 45, pulled from a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered. Images showed him being placed on a stretcher, while Shah, 30, whose face was covered in mud, was carried out on a worker's back to a rescue tent, where army doctors fitted him with an oxygen mask and checked his vitals.
An aide to the energy minister said Maharjan could not move his hands or legs, while Shah's injuries were not considered critical. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.

Family members reacted with relief. Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, told the Associated Press, "I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," adding that the family was heading to the hospital to see him.
What is happening at the hydropower project sites?

These were the first successful rescues concerning the hydropower projects along the Trishuli River. Officials say as many as 900 workers remain missing across a number of project sites, with roughly 500 believed trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.
Nepal floods trap hundreds in hydropower tunnels
At the Trishuli 3A project specifically, the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal put the number of missing workers at 557, with about 115 believed trapped in the main tunnel.
Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remained hopeful more survivors would be found: "We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people," he said.
A team of experts coordinating through a WhatsApp group has been guiding rescue crews at the sites, becoming a key tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the search effort.
What is the scale of damage caused by the Nepal floods?

Separately, Nepal's disaster authority estimated the floods caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.56 billion, €2.20 billion) in damage to property, housing and infrastructure, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Reuters.
He said the first four months of early recovery — including rebuilding roads, setting up temporary shelters, and restoring water and power — would cost an estimated $52.6 million.

"These are estimated amounts. We have calculated this in coordination with different concerned agencies and departments," Upreti said, noting a more detailed assessment would follow. He said Nepal would need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-affected areas, with at least 7,500 destroyed outright.
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes
The floods on August 26 were triggered by the collapse of a glacier upstream on the Trishuli River that sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through towns and villages near the Nepal-China border.
At least 1,259 people have been killed in Nepal, according to the country's disaster management agency, with more than 5,000 still missing.
China reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing on the Tibet side of the border as of late Wednesday.
