articles.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
articles.summary: Reduced but resilient, girl group Katseye received a hero's welcome in London.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Only two-thirds of the girl band made it to London, but fans seemed thrilled nonetheless (L-R: Megan, Yoonchae, Lara and Daniela)
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.
The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.
The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.
"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.
"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.
The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.
There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her., external

blocks.caption: Image caption, Daniela recovered from her stage fall in Dublin with no injuries.

blocks.text: Image source, Katseye / Hybe / UMG
Daniela recovered from her stage fall in Dublin with no injuries.
Such adulation - and scrutiny - has come quickly for Katseye.
Based in Los Angeles, the multinational girl group were only formed in 2023 as part of the online reality competition show The Debut: Dream Academy.

The contest was created by Hybe, the South Korean entertainment company behind acts like BTS and Le Sserafim, and the US record label Geffen, home to Olivia Rodrigo and the Rolling Stones. Of the 120,000 who initially applied for the show, only six made it through.

Trained under the rigorous K-Pop system, they had a breakout year in 2025, first with the hyperactive electro-skronk of their single Gnarly, then with its follow-up, a slinky ballad called Gabriela that highlighted Daniella's Cuban-Venezuelan roots.
In London, their audience skewed young: The queue for pick and mix was longer than the one for the bar.
When Megan asked, "Whose first concert is this?" the air curdled with screams.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The group’s first world tour is scheduled to run until the end of the year.

blocks.text: The group’s first world tour is scheduled to run until the end of the year.
Throughout the show, fans shook lightsticks, parroted Katseye's dance moves and, in some cases, spontaneously burst into tears.
Many concert-goers also wore bindis, inspired by Lara, who has proudly incorporated her Asian heritage into her aesthetic.
One individual also came dressed as a courgette, a reference to Internet Girl's so-weird-it-almost-works refrain, "Eat zucchini".
The energy was infectious. And, if you looked closely, the parents were enjoying the show as much as their kids.
Even Spice Girl Melanie C is a fan, hosting a Q&A with the band during their first UK trip last October.
"They're incredible girls," she told the BBC earlier this summer. "They've got great music, they've got a great work ethic, and they're really beautiful, you know?
"Obviously, they've had a little drama, as happens with all bands, but they work so goddamn hard."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sophia Laforteza, officially the band's leader, said she needed to take a break from the band's gruelling schedule

blocks.text: Sophia Laforteza, officially the band's leader, said she needed to take a break from the band's gruelling schedule
The drama began in February, when Manon announced she was taking a hiatus from the band to "focus on her health and wellbeing".

It came after the Swiss-Ghanaian singer told BBC News the band had been subject to racism and death threats; but fans also highlighted Katseye's gruelling schedule, suggesting they were being overworked.
In April, she posted a message to fans saying she was having "positive conversations" with Katseye's management, but not before she removed references to the band from her Instagram biography.
Then, just months after Manon stepped back, Sophia announced she was also going on hiatus to protect her "mental health and wellness".
"You can't pour from an empty cup," she posted on social media. "It's important to care for yourself."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The group were nominated for best new artist at the 2026 Grammys (L-R): Yoonchae, Megan, Lara, Manon, Sophia and Daniella

blocks.text: The group were nominated for best new artist at the 2026 Grammys (L-R): Yoonchae, Megan, Lara, Manon, Sophia and Daniella
Although it was hoped Sophia would return for the European leg of the Wildworld tour, that's proved impossible.
Her mother assured fans the absence is only temporary.
"Don't worry, this is for her own good," she told ABS-CBN News, external. "This is what I love about her management. They realise when the girls are tired.
"It's a good thing that she is resting so that she's stronger when she comes back."
It is not unusual for members of K-Pop bands to take a break when the mental or physical demands of the job become overwhelming.

Lia from the girl group Itzy took more than a year off work to seek treatment for "extreme levels of anxiety" in 2023-24; while Moka, a singer from Katseye's labelmates Illit, is currently on extended hiatus, also for anxiety.
In keeping with K-Pop tradition, Katseye honoured Sophia's place in the band during Tuesday's show, retaining her pre-recorded vocals on songs like Mean Girls and Pinky Up.
Manon's lyrics, however, were sung by other members of the band - presumably because her hiatus pre-dated production and rehearsals
Vocal criticisms
Which brings me to a related point. After the tour's opened in Dublin on Tuesday, Katseye were accused of miming throughout their set.
But from what I could tell on Thursday, the member's microphones were live all night, with a backing track doubling their vocals at crucial moments.
On slower songs like Tonight I Might and My Way they proved more than capable as live performers.

Meanwhile, Lara's vocals on the solo showcase unloveu (proudly introduced as "the first Katseye song written by a member of Katseye") mixed power and emotion in a way that suggested the band have potential beyond the ear candy pop that's become their trademark.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Katseye will play a second night in London, before heading to Manchester and then to Europe

blocks.text: Katseye will play a second night in London, before heading to Manchester and then to Europe
Other highlights included Daniela's death-defying dance break, complete with aerial splits, that led into Gabriella; and Megan's technotronic shakedown at the end of Pinky Up.

For Yoonchae, the show's high point was Time Lapse, where she got to sing in her native Korean, while mingling with the crowd. ("Keep your hands to yourselves and don't throw any gifts on the stage for our safety," warned Lara, spoiling the atmosphere just a little).
The show ended on a powerful note, with Iconic By Mistake - the band's defiant response to an online hate campaign - and an extended romp through Gnarly, complete with a leather-studded rock remix.
All told, it was a stunningly confident and self-assured show from a band who could easily been diminished by personnel problems.
"This is not a goodbye," promised Yooncahe as Katseye waved goodbye. "We'll come back."
Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage would be a perfect fit.

articles.title: Transplanted pig kidney works in US man's body for record 271 days
articles.summary: A man has lived for a record nine months with a transplanted pig kidney while waiting for a human transplant.

blocks.text: A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.
Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.
The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.
But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.
Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.
In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list.
Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis.
"I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.
But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel".
"Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

articles.title: US investigating if missile hit Iran wedding, Vance says
articles.summary: The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony and killed four people on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Watch: JD Vance "extremely sceptical" over alleged strike on Iranian wedding
The US military is investigating Iranian claims that its strikes killed at least four people including two children at a wedding in southern Iran, Vice-President JD Vance has said.

The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) - a humanitarian group - said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony at a home in Sirik on Tuesday, prompting Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei to declare it a "war crime".
US missiles were fired the same day over "attempted attacks" by Iran on American forces, but a US Central Command spokesperson said it "never targets civilians".
Speaking on Thursday, Vance said he was "extremely sceptical" over reports of the alleged strike but confirmed the US would investigate.
"I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far. So I'm extremely sceptical of this," Vance told a White House briefing.
"I know that we're investigating."
Iran has launched fresh attacks on US bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates in response to the alleged strike.

The IRCS said 67 people were hurt when shrapnel from the missile hit a family wedding ceremony, killing at least four people. Iranian state media said a fifth person, a woman aged 22, had died in hospital shortly after.
The four people killed were named locally as Zarkhatoon Taheri, 50; Kolsum Mallahi Nazhdnia, 43; Mohammad Mallahi, 16; and Amirali Karimi, four.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A picture distributed by the Iranian Red Crescent Society purportedly showing the remains of a building which was hosting the wedding ceremony

blocks.text: Image source, Iranian Red Crescent Society
A picture distributed by the Iranian Red Crescent Society purportedly showing the remains of a building which was hosting the wedding ceremony

BBC Verify confirmed a video and two images taken on Tuesday near Kuhestak's coast that showed a telecommunications tower being destroyed, and other videos from Tuesday and Wednesday showed severely damaged houses about 130m (427ft) north of the tower.

articles.title: DMW: 2 Filipinos dead in Strait of Hormuz attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified projectiles as it was about to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Cacdac said in a press briefing on Wednesday that the victims were among 16 Filipino seafarers on the vessel when it was attacked on Aug. 31. The rest were unharmed with the vessel now off the coast of Oman.
“Unfortunately, we have two crew members who died as a result of the attack,” Cacdac told reporters, adding that a fire broke out on the tanker but it was contained by the crew.
“We are already working on the immediate repatriation of all the crew members, including the two fatalities,” he said.
According to the DMW chief, he would personally visit the families of the victims although he did not disclose where they reside, citing privacy concerns.

The DMW and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration will also provide assistance to the families while government agencies coordinate with authorities in Oman on the repatriation of the Filipino seafarers, Cacdac said.
President Marcos has likewise ordered that assistance be given to the victims’ families, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Thursday.

“First and foremost, the President and the administration extend their condolences to the families of the two seafarers from Cabuyao, Laguna, and Daanbantayan, Cebu. The President has also ordered immediate assistance for the families of our two fellow citizens who perished, as well as the provision of all necessary support—including the benefits, compensation and insurance proceeds—rightfully due to them,” Castro said in a briefing at the Malancañang.
“The government will not neglect the families left behind by our two fellow citizens. Once again, we extend our condolences to the families of our two seafarers,” she added.

The DMW, meanwhile, remains on red alert amid continuing security risks in the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said. According to him, they were coordinating with the Department of National Defense and the Department of Foreign Affairs on the security situation involving Filipino seafarers in the region.
About 3,000 Filipino seafarers remain aboard vessels in the wider Persian Gulf, although they are not necessarily all within the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said.
High-risk area

Since Feb. 28, when the United States and Israel launched an attack on Iran, triggering the Middle East conflict, about 31 ships carrying 421 Filipino seafarers have been attacked while entering or leaving the strait.
Cacdac said that 268 of those seafarers have since returned to the Philippines. Of the 421, 406 were unharmed, 10 were injured but had recovered, three had died and one remains officially missing.

The DMW, however, is not imposing a blanket deployment ban on Filipino seafarers passing through the Strait of Hormuz unlike its policy covering the Northern Black Sea, because of the strategic importance of the waterway and the principle of freedom of navigation, he added.

Instead, shipowners must conduct risk assessments before voyages and ensure that adequate security measures are in place, including security protocols, possible escorts, armed guards and reporting mechanisms, he said.
“We are disallowing deployment to the extent that there is a refusal of sailing by the seafarer,” Cacdac stressed.
He said that the right of Filipino seafarers to refuse sailing in high-risk areas must be respected.
The DMW will investigate the incident, including whether the appropriate safety and risk-assessment measures were followed.

Cacdac said the SIDR appeared to have been heading toward the Strait of Hormuz after coming from the eastern coast of the United Arab Emirates and sailing northward off Oman, but the vessel’s exact route remains subject to further determination.
For now, it is still too early to provide details on how the two Filipino seafarers died, he noted.
“It is not yet clear how exactly that happened. Usually, when we are still 24 to 48 hours removed from the event, we will find out the details as we go along,” Cacdac said.

He added that the DMW remains in contact with Bahri, the Saudi shipping company in charge of the vessel, and would meet with its top management to discuss the incident and the safety of Filipino crew members. /das

articles.title: Iran war is not a war, US VP Vance says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the conflict.
Vance’s comments came amid growing signs that President Donald Trump is trying to draw a line under the conflict that has bogged down his administration.
“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting,” Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Vance added that “I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” but said major combat operations only lasted for six weeks after the U.S.-Israel war started on Feb. 28.

“But when you ask when will this end, you’re asking me a question like when will the Iranians stop shooting at ships? I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians,” he said.
After several weeks of calm, fresh clashes began with U.S. raids on Sunday, deepening the impasse in the six-month war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Vance insisted that the United States would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping.

But with fuel prices threatening to cost Trump’s Republicans their control of Congress at the ballot box, his administration has begun pushing the message that oil flows through the waterway are now returning to pre-war levels.
Wedding strike probe
“Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone,” Vance said of Iran.

“If you go back three months ago, how much oil and gas was coming out of the strait under Iranian threats? It was virtually nothing. Now, it’s almost back to where it was before the conflict even started,” Vance said.
Trump’s approval ratings are near record lows as the president who vowed to keep the United States out of any more foreign wars finds himself in a quagmire with the Islamic Republic.
Eighteen U.S. troops and thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon have died in the conflict since February.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was now discussing with senior aides whether to declare the Iran war over. He posted a photo of a banner saying “Mission Accomplished” last week.
Iran pressed on with fresh attacks on Thursday, saying it hit U.S. military bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates to avenge a strike on a wedding that it blamed on Washington.
Vance said the United States was probing the wedding strike but cast doubt on Iranian reporting of the incident.

“I know that we’re investigating,” Vance said. “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good source of information about what’s happened in the conflict thus far. So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
The Iranian Red Crescent said the missile attack on the wedding in the Iranian coastal town of Kuhestak killed four people late Tuesday, including a child, and wounded more than 50. /das

articles.title: ‘Friend-for-hire’ services gain traction in Thailand
articles.summary: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people. The service is a new…

blocks.text: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people.
The service is a new type of gig work in which people are paid to act as companions, for instance accompanying someone on a trip to take photos or even joining them in indoor rock climbing.

Although no official figures are available, industry players say demand for professional companions has increased in recent years due to the rise in people living alone, changing lifestyles and the influence of social media.
According to global market research company Euromonitor International, 29.5 percent of Thai households were single-person households in 2025, exceeding the global average of 21.9 percent.
And that growing segment has created rising demand for products and services designed for independent living, such as single-seat restaurant tables and solo travel.
For many clients, however, the motivation for hiring a companion is convenience rather than loneliness.

Ainthuon Rattanawaraporn, a university student and content creator from Bangkok, said she initially used the service out of curiosity but soon found it solved a problem—friends were sometimes too busy to come with her on trips but she was not yet comfortable traveling alone.
“I also wanted someone to take pictures for me,” she said.
Unlike asking friends for favors, hiring a companion allowed her to freely request specific photo angles and compositions because photography was part of the service.
“I don’t want to bother my friends by asking them to take hundreds of photos during a trip,” she said. “With a hired companion, I can tell them exactly what kind of pictures I want.”
Growing demand
The growing demand has created new income opportunities for people like Thanaporn Charoenchuea, a 20-year-old university student who started her “Snap Like a Bestie” service.
Within about two months, she had served more than 50 clients. She said her customers are not simply looking for someone to take photographs.
“They want someone who can make them feel comfortable while capturing natural-looking photos,” she said.
Apart from taking photos, Thanaporn spends much of her time chatting with clients, helping shy or introverted people relax before posing for pictures.

“The biggest challenge is making sure every client enjoys both the experience and the final photos,” she said. “I love photography and meeting new people, so I find the job both enjoyable and rewarding.”
On busy days, she accepts up to three appointments, each lasting between one and three hours. She only accepts bookings in public places after screening clients through their social media accounts.
For another companion service provider, Penkawin Wangniwetkul, known as Ice, the business has evolved well beyond photography.

After leaving her full-time job as a television coproducer, Ice spent several years working as a presenter, master of ceremonies, and online marketing host before entering the companionship business about three months ago.
The opportunity came unexpectedly after relatives suggested she accompany two elderly women on shopping trips and outings.
“I realized there was genuine demand for someone who could simply accompany people,” she said, adding that she later began posting about the experience on social media, leading to more referrals.

Today, clients hire her for activities, including running, gym workouts, aerobics, shopping, spa visits, cafe hopping, and even indoor rock climbing. A typical booking lasts two to three hours, and she charges 1,000 baht ($30) per hour.
Ice has served more than 10 clients and intentionally limits bookings because she continues to work as an MC and presenter. She also screens every client before accepting an assignment.

Her clients have included public figures, including an actress she accompanied to a veterinary clinic. She has also received requests to attend wedding receptions as a companion, although she was too busy to accept.

Despite growing demand, Ice is selective. She turns down requests that could compromise her safety or make her feel uncomfortable, including accompanying male clients to late-night entertainment venues.
Outside city trips
The service has also expanded to trips outside the city. Company employee Sasiprapa Nookong is among those who hired a companion during a trip to Chiang Mai.

Sasiprapa said that while traveling with a friend, they decided to spend one day pursuing different interests. Her friend planned to go hiking, while she preferred visiting cafes around the city, so she contacted a university student offering the service after seeing reviews on TikTok.

“I believe this service meets the needs of people who occasionally want company, not long-term companionship,” she said, echoing others in stressing that safety should always come first when hiring strangers.

Sociologist Narupon Duangwises of the Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn Anthropology Centre wrote in a report that interacting with hired companions may provide emotional comfort for people who find it difficult to make friends in everyday life.

But he noted that one feature distinguishing “friends for hire” from traditional friendship is the ability to choose a companion based on physical appearance, unlike friendships that develop naturally.
He therefore suggested that service providers establish clear rules and boundaries to protect themselves and prevent situations, such as sexual harassment or other forms of violence. /das

articles.title: El Niño could be strongest in decades, UN warns
articles.summary: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world…

blocks.text: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world was in the “danger zone of extreme weather.”
The weather phenomenon is set to become “very strong” in the months ahead and is almost certain to persist through February, the World Meteorological Organization said.
“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began,” WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.
El Niño will peak toward the end of this year — though its knock-on effects on the climate will continue well into 2027, said the WMO.
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.
Heat in the oceans is released more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the year after it develops.
The powerful 2023-24 El Niño contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and “we should not be surprised if this record is broken,” Saulo added.

“El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat,” the WMO said.
Highway to the danger zone
El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amplifying weather extremes.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres.

“The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
WMO chief Saulo urged disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, fisheries, health, energy and water to prepare themselves.
“This exceptional El Niño … has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” she said.
“We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”
El Niño typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite, La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away from the tropical Pacific.
Pacific Ocean heating up

Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, the WMO’s climate prediction chief, said some places would be affected before, some during and some after the peak later this year — though the strength of the peak is not an indicator of the severity of the impact.
For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures “across almost all land areas.”
The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened from an average 1.5°C above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2°C to 2.6°C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.
The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong — meaning this one is set to reach the highest level out of four.
Moufouma-Okia said the classification meant a sea surface temperature anomaly of more than 2°C.
“That category is open: We know where it starts; we don’t know where it ends,” he told AFP.
The average forecast is pointing toward an anomaly peaking at 3.6°C — way higher than the last two very strong El Niños in 1997-98 and 2015-16.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8°C above average during July and early August.
Saulo called this a huge reservoir of “very warm ocean waters that will fuel the intensity of El Niño.”
The UN’s International Organization for Migration agency appealed Thursday for $110 million to protect 4.9 million people from the potentially severe impacts of the phenomenon. /das

articles.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins ‘tricky’ arrival
articles.summary: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet. The…

blocks.text: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet.
The BepiColombo mission set off from Earth in 2018 on a winding path to study the smallest and least understood planet in our solar system, with the aim of releasing the two probes into its orbit.
On Thursday, it began its arrival phase, described by the European Space Agency (ESA) as its “most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequence ever attempted.”

Mercury’s relatively tiny mass — it is only slightly bigger than the moon — means its gravitational pull is extremely weak compared with the Sun’s, making it complicated for spacecraft to approach the planet without ending up incinerated or lost in space.
“It’s a very ambitious mission,” Santa Martinez, the mission manager at ESA, told a press conference ahead of its arrival.
The spacecraft had to travel more than 10 billion kilometers (miles), executing a series of nine flybys, to speed up, slow down and perfect its trajectory.
The two probes, which are attached to each other, finally separated on Thursday from the transfer module that has propelled them — a crucial first step in the final approach.

It was the equivalent of “launching a new spacecraft. Only this spacecraft happens to be around a different planet,” explained Ignacio Tanco, ESA’s head of inner solar system mission operations, before the separation began.
All went to plan
On Thursday, Mercury was some 63 million km from the Sun and 200 million km from Earth.

“At these distances … any real-time operation becomes impossible,” Tanco said, explaining there was about a 30-minute delay between checks being performed and commands being executed from the ground to the spacecraft.
It meant the spacecraft had to check and execute the separation autonomously — a “tricky business,” Tanco said.
But all went to plan.
The spacecraft autonomously cut the four mechanical struts connecting the orbiters to the module.
Spring mechanisms then gently pushed them away.
The separation took place at a speed of 40 centimeters (16 inches) per second, leaving the two entities relatively close given the vastness of space.

Due to the distance between the probes and Earth, the signal confirming the operation’s success reached the control center in Darmstadt, Germany, nearly two hours later — at 1353 GMT — sparking rounds of applause and cheers.
“This is the best-case scenario, that the telemetry comes exactly at the moment we expect it,” said Elsa Montagnon, in charge of module operations at ESA.
“The spacecraft has completed its reconfiguration as expected,” she said with relief.
The probes are due to enter Mercury’s orbit on Nov. 21.
The next tricky phase will come on Dec. 9 and 10, when the two probes separate into their respective orbits.
From April, the ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) will begin studying the planet closest to the Sun with unprecedented precision, passing just 480 km from its surface.
The Japanese Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio) will focus on its space environment and magnetic field, following an elliptical orbit that will carry it as far as 11,000 km away.
New chapter
Mercury is the least studied of the four rocky, innermost planets in our solar system, which include Venus, Earth and Mars.
NASA’s Mariner 10 was the first probe to capture a close image of its lunar-looking surface in 1974.
The MESSENGER probe then orbited the planet in 2011.
But many mysteries remain about its magnetic field, iron core and surface marked by hollows.

With its 16 instruments and 1.7-billion-euro ($2.0-billion) budget, BepiColombo “is going to bring to humanity and to the scientific community unprecedented views of Mercury … and it’s going to open a new chapter in our understanding of the solar system,” Martinez said. /das

articles.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
articles.summary: Police have given the all-clear at Terminal 1 at Berlin's BER Airport following an earlier security scare and evacuation. The airport said some flights had been delayed but they were trying to avoid…

image.caption: Crowds waited outside the terminal building amid the police operationImage: Ann-Marie Utz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare.
"The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman.

Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage.
"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency.
Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point.
Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days.
Berlin: BER operations remain restricted
Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening.
"Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman.
She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport.
"Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays.
"Regular operations will resume on Friday."

blocks.caption: Various emergency services were in action at the scene as dusk fell on ThursdayImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the airport say about departures and arrivals?
The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.
Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said.
Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website.
An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2.

blocks.caption: Specialist personnel could be seen in action near the buildingImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year.

The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.

blocks.caption: Personnel responding to the alert went through decontamination procedures on leaving the buildingImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Australia news live: Pauline Hanson to make cost of living ‘worse’, new union boss warns; Labor scraps course citing ‘integrity’
articles.summary:
The new ACTU secretary, Melissa Donnelly, says One Nation ‘says one thing and does another’

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoWorkers should have a say in when and how AI is used, ACTU secretary says
23m agoWelcome

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor
Asked if she saw her role as one of countering One Nation on the cost of living, Donnelly said Pauline Hanson’s party “says one thing and does another”.

double quotation markThe reality is that Pauline Hanson’s track record is voting against penalty rates, voting against rights for casual and gig workers. She’s opposed the minimum wage. She’s most recently suggested it should be easier to sack workers. Our job, as the union movement, is to make sure our members and workers understand that is what she stands for. And if you’re worried about cost of living, Pauline Hanson is going to make it worse.
Workers should have a say in when and how AI is used, ACTU secretary says
The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, Melissa Donnelly, has said cost of living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role.
Donnelly told ABC’s 7.30 program workers “absolutely deserve” a say on AI in their workplaces, but it would not amount to a veto.
She said unions will test the existing laws demanding workers are consulted over significant impacts of new technology before suggesting the laws need to be strengthened for AI.
double quotation markThere are a whole range of workplace issues, and workers’ rights issues, that arise with the advent of AI.
The stronger guardrails Donnelly said, would include the capacity of workers to have a say on “when it’s used and how it’s used”.

double quotation markThere’s a broader conversation that we should be having as a nation about what AI means and how we regulate it. It’s not a tropical cyclone bearing down on the coast. It is technology. We’ve seen governments step in on issues like social media and set some guardrails. We have all sorts of commentators from Bill Gates to others saying that we’ve got to have some rules around how this works, we’ve got to have protections, because we need to protect workers into there future. We need to make sure there are meaningful and quality jobs going forward.

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji
Labor says it will shut down a management course amid fears it is being “misused by shonks” and providing a back door into Australia.

As the government faces increased pressure to curb overseas migration, Labor says the graduate diploma of management (learning) which is registered at 452 institutions showed students either were enrolled but weren’t even starting the course, weren’t completing the course or were transferring out of it.
It’s the first time the government will use powers to shut down courses due to concerns over their integrity – though students currently completing the course will be able to finish it.
The assistant minister in charge, Julian Hill, pinned the blame on the Coalition:

double quotation markThe Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks. Australia continues to welcome genuine international students seeking a premium education and must maintain a ruthless focus on quality, integrity and a great student experience.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.

The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, Melissa Donnelly, has said cost of living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role. More coming up.

articles.title: Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village
articles.summary:
Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues

Israelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled…

blocks.text: Israelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupied West Bank.

The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer.

The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said.
Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted.

blocks.caption: Mourners at the funeral ceremony of Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Al-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both had died before they made it to hospital.

A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods.

When Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.”
Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler.

blocks.caption: Mourners at the funeral ceremony of Abu Alia and al-Nassan in al-Mughayyir. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Israeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year.

The other victims were a 17-year-old player from the Palestinian youth football team shot in June, a 14-year-old gunned down at the school gate in April, and another 14-year-old killed outside the village mosque in January.

“We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April.

“This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound.
They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the last two weeks.

blocks.caption: Funeral attenders look out from their village of al-Mughayyir at an Israeli hilltop settlement. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: Since late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outposts surround it in all directions.
In late August soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening.
At least eight families have fled in the last week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said.
The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday.

blocks.caption: Israeli troops raiding al-Mughayyir in July after settler attacks. Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/Reuters

blocks.text: In the South Hebron Hills Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet a-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children.
Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement.

It is the 66th Palestinian community that has been wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.

“Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” said Yuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.”

A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency which manages civilian affairs in occupied Palestine, said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone.

In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet a-Taban, as Firing Zone 918. It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions.

As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the most notoriously violent Israeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal.

articles.title: Data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost?
articles.summary: Advocates say data centres will bring jobs but others worry they will suck up resources while providing little advantage.

blocks.text: Data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost?
Image source, Reuters
Locals in the Sydney suburb of Lane Cove are concerned about the planned construction of four new data centres
The sheer size and noise of data centres are what people tend to notice first. Some say they sound like a jet plane about to take off, others complain of a high-pitched whine.
When Lucy* puts her child to bed, she hears a constant humming. "I'll hear it and think, 'What is that? What is going on?'," she says.

And then she'll remember that the noise is a data centre just 350m (0.2 miles) from her front door in the desirable suburb of Lane Cove, in Sydney's lower north-shore. Another four are in the pipeline at the local industrial park.

Australia has quickly become a global destination for data centres, with investors attracted to the country's abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land to power and house their technologies.
Earlier this year, OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman said Australia could become a data centre capital of the world, if it wanted to.

Australia is already headed in the direction of big tech's wishes. There are 162 data centres across the country, with plans for 90 more, and an estimated more than A$155bn (£80bn) of investment money lined up.
If approved, one of the world's biggest data centres will be built in western Sydney. At one gigawatt, it is expected to be Australia's largest single energy user.
And in Marsden Park, also in western Sydney, the biggest data centre in the Southern Hemisphere is already under construction only 100m away from a local community.

But as more Australians find themselves living next door to data centres - triggering concerns about water supplies, energy use and the environment - many are asking whether joining the artificial intelligence (AI) race is worth it.
'What happens if we don't?'

blocks.caption: Image caption, Data centres, like this one in Lane Cove, are becoming a more familiar sight in Australia

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
Data centres, like this one in Lane Cove, are becoming a more familiar sight in Australia
Data centres have been essential to the digital economy since the arrival of the internet.

They were originally built to process and store data for things like emails, online banking and cloud services. But everything changed after 2022 when ChatGPT launched and AI exploded in popularity. This prompted a sudden race to build more data centres to power the technology.
The location of these large, windowless buildings filled with beeping servers and cables also became important to latency – the time it takes for data to travel from its source to its destination.
Delays for things like air traffic control, robotic surgery or even Netflix would not be tolerated today, Belinda Dennett, CEO of Data Centres Australia, says.
Australia has roughly 13.6 million users of AI every month, making them the sixth most active users of the tech globally.
And experts say having data centres in Australia will lower the barrier to building more of its own AI companies.

"If we think about it in reverse, what happens if we don't build infrastructure here", Dennett says. "We get none of the value chain, we are just importing tools from someone else and we become just a user."
Australia is also an attractive market for foreign investment, as "we've got availability of land, we've got political stability, and we've got the Five Eyes security alliance," Dennett says.
"We've also got a skilled workforce, a pretty stable energy grid, and an abundance of renewable energy potential."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jon Whittle says the government has no choice but to lean into data centres

blocks.text: Image source, Adrien Rossignol
Jon Whittle says the government has no choice but to lean into data centres
Leading business experts and economists say that without Australia's data centre boom over the last couple of years, the country would likely have headed into a recession.

Jon Whittle, a former director of the digital research centre at the country's national science agency CSIRO, who is now a leading voice in AI and business, agrees with this. He says the government doesn't really have a choice but to continue down the investment path.
"There's some very serious considerations around this, but my main message would be we need to lean into it," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Residents in Sydney's lower north shore fear the national park and river will be affected by a new cluster of data centres

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied to BBC
Residents in Sydney's lower north shore fear the national park and river will be affected by a new cluster of data centres
Fears over power and water supplies
But leading energy and environmental experts argue Australia has little capacity to meet the massive energy and water demands of new data centres.
The Australian Energy Market Operator says data centre energy demands could triple by 2030 nationwide.

Without significant new renewable generation and storage, data centres could push power prices 26% higher in New South Wales (NSW) by 2035, according to the Climate Council, an independent non-profit that provides expert advice.
Because data centres need uninterrupted power at a scale and speed that wind and solar cannot match, there are fears the current boom will trigger a new generation of coal and gas power plants.
No data centre operator analysed in a recent report by Greenpeace Australia Pacific adequately proved their claim of driving the country's renewable energy growth.
In the US, many data centres are not waiting to build more renewable energy and have found it cheaper to build new gas-fired power stations instead.

Just a 90-minute drive from Sydney's central business district, the Australian-owned data group Cloud Carrier plans to build three gas-fired power stations to generate energy for an existing data centre and two more in the future.
Moreover, if energy demands place too much pressure on the grid or there is a power outage, data centres, like in Lane Cove, will rely on backup diesel generators.
But NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey says Australia's investment boom in data centres is being accompanied by a boom in renewable energy.

"We don't see the two [as] unrelated," he tells the BBC. "We see data centres allowing us to replace a lot of our old coal-fired power with clean, green renewable energy with the private sector picking up a large amount of the tab because otherwise households would."
The new private investment will help with renewable energy and create "new industries that are likely to employ future generations", Mookhey says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A data centre in Artarmon, Sydney. The huge windowless buildings use massive amounts of energy and water

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
A data centre in Artarmon, Sydney. The huge windowless buildings use massive amounts of energy and water

But data centres also consume large amounts of water - some up to 40 million litres a day, which is equivalent to 80,000 households - to prevent their servers from overheating. In a drought-prone country that is a potentially huge problem.
Sydney already needs to increase its drinking water supply over the next five to 10 years in order to provide for its growing population, according to Water Services Association of Australia (WSAA).
But if that water is used for data centres, households are likely to pay the price for sourcing water from elsewhere, such as through desalination, which costs more than traditional water sources.
Sydney Water, Australia's largest water utility, says data centres could use up to 25% of Sydney's drinking water by 2035.

In July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a new legal obligation for "large-scale" data centres to underwrite power supplies, limit water use, and pay for any extra water infrastructure needed.
But the prime minister also told media that the legislation, which will be introduced in 2027, would only apply to new proposals, not projects that were already built or under construction.
In response, environmental and community groups want a pause on all data centre development.
"We've got the government rolling out the red carpet saying we want to be the data centre capital of the world," Sydney's Lane Cove deputy mayor, Rochelle Flood, says.
"But can we actually do that sustainably or is it going to set us back in terms of net zero and our water storage targets?"

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lane Cove Deputy mayor Rochelle Flood outside the proposed data centre space at 12 Mars Road

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied by Rochelle Flood
Lane Cove Deputy mayor Rochelle Flood outside the proposed data centre space at 12 Mars Road
'What is it for?'
On a rainy Monday night during a town hall event led by Greenpeace Australia Pacific at the Lane Cove library, locals say they were never consulted on their area becoming a data centre hub.
One of the proposed centres from the cluster is 16m from the nearest home and 160m from a local primary school.
In addition, Flood says if the four data centres get approved in the industrial park, 50% of the current businesses will have to move - taking their jobs with them.
Felipe Tanaka, 40, is a manager of a business in the industrial park who has been told he must relocate for a data centre.
"We never knew that something like this would happen," Tanaka tells the BBC. "Thousands of jobs are going to be gone from this area in the next few years."
While a large data centre can employ more than a thousand workers during construction, research says that number drops to more like 100 jobs once the centre is operational.
"Most of our 300 to 400 workers here are locals," Tanaka says. "Having to move will probably see half of my employees gone."
NSW Treasurer Mookhey says the jobs that data centres will bring come not from those who work in them but from those who use them.
"When Microsoft and Amazon do business here in NSW, it's pleasing to see they are committed to providing some of their more skilled operations and locating them here," he says.

But what other skilled jobs might be created is not clear, and effectively what the data centres will be used for. As some critics have pointed out, many AI users are making cat GIFs, which uses the equivalent amount of energy as running a microwave for an hour.
"They're telling us this is essential... that we need to have these centres in our neighbourhood but they're not saying what it's for," Flood says.
"When our drinking water, energy and land is being used for generative AI slop, that is not giving any value back."
*Names have been changed to protect identities

articles.title: US billionaire Leon Black defies summons and sues Epstein panel
articles.summary: The lawsuit calls the House Oversight Committee's subpoenas, which ordered him to share nondisclosure agreements, "invalid".

blocks.text: Billionaire investor Leon Black has failed to appear before a US congressional committee investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein - instead filing a lawsuit challenging the committee's efforts to summon him.
The lawsuit calls the subpoenas issued by the House Oversight Committee "invalid" and says they hold "no legitimate connection" to the committee's legislative aim.
Black walked out of the committee in June while giving voluntary testimony after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.
Black has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.
The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.

His lawsuit opposing these summonses, which was filed in federal court in Washington on Thursday, argued that revealing the NDAs might "expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it".
NDAs are contracts where both parties agree to keep information confidential, often as part of a settlement or employment agreement.
"This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black," Susan Estrich, an attorney for Black, said in a press release on Thursday.
"We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power."
"By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two Congressional subpoenas," Robert Garcia, who sits on the committee, said in a statement after Black failed to appear.
"His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable. We must hold him in contempt immediately," Garcia added.
Contempt of Congress could result in the committee referring Black to the justice department for potential prosecution.
"It's a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people," Chairman Jomes Comer said. "Mr Black's testimony is crucial to our investigation."

Black has said he employed Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling the House Oversight Committee in June that he had paid Epstein $158m (£120m) for legitimate purposes over the course of their years-long association.
He has said he did not know about Epstein's "nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019".
Black appears in the Epstein files released by the justice department, which include photos, videos and investigative documents relating to the disgraced late financier.
There is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.
Black had a six-year affair with a former Russian model, Guzel Ganieva, which ended in allegations of abuse, court records show.
According to a lawsuit filed by Ganieva against Black, which was later dismissed, he prepared a nondisclosure agreement in 2015 to secure her silence.

Epstein offered Black advice, including suggesting in an email to his assistant that Black hire former law enforcement officers to approach Ganieva, according to files released by the US justice department.
Estrich, Black's attorney, has dismissed Ganieva's accusation as "demonstrably false". Black himself has previously said he was the victim of extortion.
A judge ultimately dismissed Ganieva's lawsuit, citing the NDA she signed and about $9m (£6.6m) that she had received in the years after entering the agreement.

Black left Apollo Global Management, a company he co-founded, in 2021 - saying at the time that "relentless public attention and media scrutiny" of his ties with Epstein had taken "a toll" on his health.

articles.title: Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from Gaza
articles.summary:
Itamar Ben-Gvir claims proposal for illegal forced displacement of 2 million people is ‘realistic’ and ‘concrete’

Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the…

blocks.text: Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, with the intention of sending them abroad.

Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of its population of roughly 2 million over the next six years.
“It’s realistic,” Ben-Gvir said, claiming there were countries that were “ready” to take in Palestinians from Gaza, without naming which ones.

While the forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, Israeli political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for Gaza, rebuffing efforts by the US president, Donald Trump, to advance a half-baked and largely moribund ceasefire deal that has been marked by continuing Israeli attacks.

Ben-Gvir said the far-right Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and … is concrete”.

blocks.caption: Ben-Gvir speaks at a rally in the Israeli city of Netanya this week. Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images

blocks.text: The proposal is contained in a euphemistically titled 20-page document titled National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip.

Despite the use of the word “voluntary”, the plan will be seen as coercive by the international community because of the dire conditions imposed on Gaza’s population by Israel and because of Ben-Gvir’s explicit intention: to remove Gaza’s Palestinian population.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

Ben-Gvir’s comments follow hard on the heels of comments by Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the approval of the Trump administration to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he claimed was still under discussion after being “frozen” by Trump.
Katz, at a conference hosted by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion.

Trump himself provoked international outrage at the beginning of his second term with a suggestion that all 2 million Palestinians leave Gaza and that the US redevelop the territory, a proposal he later walked back.

With elections in Israel in October, Ben-Gvir has made a series of inflammatory interventions aimed at his far-right base, including sharing footage from a site where Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks by Israeli military courts – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – are to be executed. In another video, he revelled in the mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli custody.

Polling suggests that Jewish Power, the party led by Ben-Gvir – who has convictions for incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and who has been put under sanctions by various countries – would gain about seven seats.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part staged a visit to a military outpost in Gaza on Wednesday to insist that Israel would not withdraw from the areas of Gaza that it occupies.

“We are not withdrawing. We are staying on this line. We control 60% of the strip. And there is still more to come, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us – we do this day in and day out,” he said.
According to Israel’s deputy chief of general staff, Maj Gen Tamir Yadai, the country now controls 65% of Gaza. This is far beyond the 53% agreed under the ceasefire brokered last year by Trump.

As well as pushing for the expulsion of Gaza’s population, Ben-Gvir has called for the deportation of two MPs and others “who are disloyal to the state of Israel” – including Jews – saying he would promote such a policy if he is included in the next government.

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition leader questions US oil deal with ‘illegitimate regime’
articles.summary:
María Corina Machado says interim government does not have democratic mandate to negotiate natural resources

The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has questioned Donald…

blocks.text: The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has questioned Donald Trump’s oil deal with Venezuela’s interim government, declaring that the country’s natural resources do not belong to “an illegitimate regime”.

In her first public comments since Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela last Friday, Machado walked a diplomatic tightrope between challenging the controversial agreement and trying not to rile the White House.

In a video posted on social media, the Nobel peace prize winner said: “Of course the United States is the principal partner Venezuela needs to fully develop its strategic potential. This is what the majority of Venezuelans believe … and it is something I’ve spent my whole life defending.”

However, Machado said the current occupants of the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas were “enemies of the US” and claimed they did not have the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources. “The wealth of our subsoil does not belong to an illegitimate regime – it belongs to the Venezuelan people,” said Machado, recognising that supporters felt “sadness and anger” at being excluded from the decision-making process.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels – more than 65bn barrels of which are involved in the agreement.
Trump’s deal was struck with the un-elected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January after her strongman predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces.

Many observers expected Trump to replace Maduro with Machado, a conservative democracy activist who later gave the US president her Nobel prize award. But Trump instead backed Rodríguez, warning: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price – probably bigger than Maduro.” Machado has been sidelined.

The White House claims the oil deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves.

Speaking outside the Miraflores palace on Wednesday, the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said the aim was “to massively grow production and economic opportunities in Venezuela”. “President Trump has a clear mission in Venezuela. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity, and prosperity to everyone in Venezuela,” Wright told reporters.

But there has been widespread condemnation of what critics have called a predatory and colonial-style land grab. Machado’s supporters fear the deal makes Washington far less inclined to push for fresh presidential elections.

Machado’s movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro by a landslide in the last such vote, in 2024, but he refused to accept the result and clung to power until his dramatic rendition on 3 January 2026.
On Wednesday, both Trump and Rodríguez brushed off questions about when an election might be held.
“You had a very powerful, very nasty dictatorship in Venezuela – and they’re just not going to be ready for it yet,” Trump told reporters, before adding vaguely: “But soon.”
Asked when an election would be held, Rodríguez said: “There will be an electoral process, but when Venezuela is ready.”
“I don’t set dates,” she added.

articles.title: Around 2,000 fall ill in Indonesia after eating free school meals
articles.summary: Authorities are investigating several suspected outbreaks amid growing criticism of the scheme.

blocks.text: Around 2,000 students and teachers across Indonesia have fallen ill with food poisoning over the past three days linked to the government's free school meals programme.
In the latest case, 777 people became unwell after consuming the food at a high school in Rembang, Central Java, the institution's headteacher said.
The meals were provided through a multibillion-dollar scheme that is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, aiming to improve nutrition for Indonesia's schoolchildren.
But, as well as being the suspected source of a string of mass food poisonings, the programme has been dogged by allegations of corruption and criticism of its cost.

A total of 752 students and 25 teachers experienced symptoms of food poisoning after eating meals provided through the Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) programme at the high school in Lasem on Wednesday lunchtime.
"They had diarrhoea and took turns using the toilet," headteacher Juhartutik told BBC News Indonesia. "There are 40 toilets in total, so they can't accommodate everyone."
The school has since sent nearly 1,200 pupils and 95 members of staff home, while several were taken to hospital.
Juhartutik said the government would cover any medical costs and that the local food distributor had come to the school to "take responsibility".
The suspected outbreak came after 730 people fell ill after consuming MBG meals at an Islamic boarding school in Sidoarjo, East Java, on Tuesday, a local health official said.
Reni said their child felt dizzy and nauseous before developing stomach problems after eating the meal.
Some of those affected required hospital treatment, with some students being transported in wheelchairs because they were too weak to stand.
Hundreds of others have been affected by suspected cases of food poisoning linked to the free school meals this week, including hundreds across several schools in Tana Toraja, South Sulawesi.
Improper storage or poorly prepared food are often to blame for cases of food poisoning, in which the body rejects the contaminated food.
Parents and teachers have told reporters of slimy chicken, as well as food that appeared undercooked and had a fishy odour.
Local authorities are investigating the cause of the suspected outbreaks, with food samples being tested for possible contamination.
The head of the food distribution unit in Lasem, Achmad Sholeh Syarifudin, apologised and took "full responsibility for the recovery of students and teachers".
He said the unit would conduct a comprehensive evaluation of its operation following the incident.
The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency has said: "If it is identified that there was negligence and there are criminal elements, I apologise, we cannot help."

articles.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
articles.summary: Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to…

image.caption: The research vessel was taking a group of researchers to Barentsburg, a Russian coal mining settlement on the Arctic Svalbard archipelagoImage: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.
Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday.
Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions.
Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

blocks.caption: Around two thirds of Svalbard is designated as national parks and nature reserves, but the coal mining settlement of Barentsburg is home to about a tenth of the archipelago's populationImage: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded?

The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023.

Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead.
"Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived.
The end of coal mining in Svalbard
The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.

"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement.
Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo.
"Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said.
How did Russia respond?
Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.
"We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.
The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint.
Is Svalbard Russia's real leverage in the Arctic?
The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.

"The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website.
He said that for the time being, "the Professor Mochanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case.

blocks.caption: Prior to the war in Ukraine Barentsburg was also home to Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. But most have since left, Ukrainians in particular were told to accept an offer of Russian citizenship or leave. Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement?
Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people.
It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century.

The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions.

The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades.
Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago.

articles.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
articles.summary: Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. People forget that, over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a…

image.caption: A statue in the port of Bremerhaven commemorates the millions of Germans who emigrated abroadImage: S. Ziese/blickwinkel/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."
